teile.einleitung: Montesquieu was a French philosopher and writer of the Enlightenment in the 18th century. He is known above all for the idea of the separation of powers. This idea still shapes almost all democratic states today, Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Montesquieu lived from 1689 to 1755 and came from the area around Bordeaux.
In 1716 he inherited from his uncle the office of president at the Parlement of Bordeaux.
In the “Persian Letters” of 1721 he had two fictional Persians describe their impressions of France.
His main work “The Spirit of the Laws” appeared in 1748.
He demanded that state power be divided, because power must be limited by power.
England served him as a model of a free constitution.
In 1751 the Catholic Church put his main work on the Index of Forbidden Books.

abschnitte.text: Montesquieu was actually called Charles-Louis de Secondat and bore the title Baron de Montesquieu. He was born on 18 January 1689 at the château of **La Brède** near Bordeaux. He studied law and in 1716 inherited from his uncle the office of president at the **Parlement of Bordeaux**, a high court. He died on 10 February 1755 in Paris.

In 1721 Montesquieu published the **Persian Letters**. In them two invented Persians describe in letters their impressions of France. With their foreign eyes they made fun of the king, the Church and the customs in Paris. In this way Montesquieu could criticise without directly passing the criticism off as his own opinion.

After long journeys through Europe Montesquieu wrote his main work **The Spirit of the Laws**, which appeared anonymously in **Geneva** in 1748. In it he investigated why different peoples have different laws. He thought that factors such as **climate** and geography shape the customs and thus the suitable laws of a people. In 1751 the Catholic Church put the work on the Index of Forbidden Books.

Montesquieu distinguished three forms of state: the republic, the monarchy and **despotism**. To each he assigned a principle that holds it together. The republic needs the virtue of its citizens, the monarchy honour. Despotism, the rule of a single arbitrary ruler, is based on fear.

Most famous is his teaching of the **separation of powers**. State power is to be divided among three powers: the **legislative**, which makes laws, the executive, which carries them out, and the judiciary, which gives judgment. Because power can only be limited by power, the powers are to check one another. His model was England, where he had stayed for a long time on his journey.

Montesquieu’s ideas influenced the constitution of the USA of 1787 and the French Revolution. The Swiss **Federal Constitution** is also based on the separation of powers. In Switzerland the Federal Assembly makes the laws, the Federal Council governs and the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne gives judgment. In this way nobody can seize all the power for themselves alone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement in the 18th century that relied on reason, knowledge and freedom.
The division of state power among lawmaking, government and courts.
The lawmaking power, in Switzerland the parliament.
The rule of one individual who governs arbitrarily and without control.
The list of books that the Catholic Church used to forbid people to read.

gewusst: Montesquieu’s main work was so extensive that it appeared divided into several volumes.
Montesquieu was also a winegrower and sold wine from his estate, among other places to England.
Montesquieu’s face is on postage stamps and used to appear on a French banknote.

teile.einleitung: The Mexican Revolution began in 1910 and lasted about ten years. At first it was directed against the long-serving president Porfirio Díaz. It turned into a long civil war in which various leaders fought for power and for land for the peasants.
wichtigste: From 1910 the revolution was directed against President Porfirio Díaz.
Francisco Madero called for an uprising with the Plan of San Luis Potosí.
General Victoriano Huerta overthrew Madero in 1913.
Emiliano Zapata demanded land for the peasants in the Plan of Ayala.
Pancho Villa raided the US town of Columbus in 1916.
The constitution of 1917 is still in force today.
The party PRI governed Mexico until the year 2000.

abschnitte.text: **Porfirio Díaz** ruled Mexico, with a short interruption, from 1876. He ruled **authoritarian**-style, that is, he tolerated hardly any contradiction and allowed no free elections. Under him railways were built, and foreign companies invested in the country. But most of the land belonged to a few rich large landowners. Most peasants were poor and owned no land of their own.

In 1910 the politician **Francisco Madero** stood against Díaz in the election and was arrested. After that he called for an armed uprising with the **Plan of San Luis Potosí**. People rose up all over the country. In 1911 Díaz resigned and went to Europe. Madero became president. But as early as 1913 General **Victoriano Huerta** overthrew him, and Madero was murdered shortly afterwards.

Two revolutionary leaders became especially well known. **Emiliano Zapata** came from the state of Morelos. In the **Plan of Ayala** he demanded that the peasants get their land back. His cry was “Land and Freedom”. In the north **Pancho Villa** fought with a large cavalry force. In 1916 he raided the US border town of Columbus in New Mexico. The USA then sent soldiers to Mexico to catch him, but without success.

In 1917 Mexico received a new **constitution**, which is still in force today. It promised a land reform, rights for workers and a school for everyone. Mineral resources were to belong to the state. But the fighting did not stop at once. Zapata was killed in 1919, Villa in 1923. Around 1920 the revolution is regarded as over. It had cost a great many people their lives.

From the revolution came a party that has been called the **PRI** since 1946. The abbreviation stands for “Institutional Revolutionary Party”. It governed Mexico without a break until the year 2000. Then for the first time a candidate of another party won the presidential election. The revolution is still very important in Mexico today, for example in the large murals of the painter Diego Rivera.

gewusst: The start of the revolution on 20 November is marked every year in Mexico as a public holiday.
Many women also fought in the revolution; they were called “Adelitas”.

teile.einleitung: Neoliberalism is a school of thought in economics. Its supporters find that free markets and competition promote prosperity best and that the state should interfere less. From about 1980 these ideas shaped the politics of many countries, but they are still controversial today.
wichtigste: Neoliberals rely on free markets, competition and fewer state rules.
In 1947 the Mont Pèlerin Society was founded in Switzerland.
Friedrich August von Hayek published “The Road to Serfdom” in 1944.
Milton Friedman taught at the University of Chicago.
Margaret Thatcher was British Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990.
The economic policy of Ronald Reagan is called Reaganomics.
In 1989 the Washington Consensus arose, with reform recommendations for developing countries.

abschnitte.text: Neoliberals believe that the **free market** decides best what is produced and what it costs. The state is to ensure order and competition, but otherwise interfere little. Important demands are lower taxes, fewer regulations, which is called **deregulation**, and the sale of state firms to private owners, **privatisation**. The word “neo” means “new”.

In 1944 the Austrian economist **Friedrich August von Hayek** published the book **“The Road to Serfdom”**. In it he warned that too much state planning endangers freedom. In 1947 he invited scholars to **Mont Pèlerin** above Vevey in the canton of Vaud. There they founded the **Mont Pèlerin Society**, an important network of neoliberal thinkers. Hayek received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1974.

The American **Milton Friedman** taught at the **University of Chicago**. He and his students thought that the state should above all keep the money supply stable. This doctrine is called **monetarism**. Friedman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1976. His ideas had great influence on governments in many countries.

From 1979 **Margaret Thatcher** was British Prime Minister, until 1990. Her government sold many state companies, in 1984 for example **British Telecom**, with a large share sale. On 27 October 1986 she loosened the rules for the London financial centre, which is called the **Big Bang**. In the USA President **Ronald Reagan** cut taxes and removed regulations. His policy is called **Reaganomics**.

In 1989 ten recommendations for developing countries were formulated, the **Washington Consensus**. They included saving in the state budget, free trade and privatisation. Supporters say that such reforms brought growth and new prosperity. Critics think they widened the gap between rich and poor and weakened the state. How much market and how much state is good is still fiercely debated today.

gewusst: The German economist Wilhelm Röpke, a co-founder of the Mont Pèlerin Society, taught for many years in Geneva.
The name “Big Bang” in German is “Urknall”.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Stalingrad was one of the most important battles of the Second World War. In 1942 and 1943 German and Soviet troops fought over the city on the Volga, and the battle ended in a heavy German defeat.
wichtigste: Stalingrad lies on the Volga and is today called Volgograd.
With Operation Uranus the Red Army encircled the German troops in November 1942.
The German 6th Army under Friedrich Paulus was encircled.
At the beginning of February 1943 the last German troops surrendered.
Of around 90,000 prisoners only about 6,000 returned home.
After that the Wehrmacht was in retreat in the east.

abschnitte.text: **Stalingrad** lies on the river **Volga** in the south of Russia. The city was named after the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin. Since 1961 it has been called **Volgograd**. In 1941 Germany had attacked the **Soviet Union**. In the summer of 1942 the German Wehrmacht attacked Stalingrad. The city was important because of its factories and because the Volga was an important transport route.

The German **6th Army** pushed into the city. There there was fighting for every street and every house. The city was almost completely destroyed in the process. The Soviet troops, however, held parts of the city on the bank of the Volga. Both sides suffered very high losses. The civilian population also suffered badly.

In **November 1942** the Red Army began a great offensive, **Operation Uranus**. Within a few days it encircled the German 6th Army. This is called a **pocket**. The commander **Friedrich Paulus** was not allowed to break out on Hitler’s orders. In the icy winter there was a shortage of food, ammunition and warm clothing. Shortly before the end Paulus was still promoted to **field marshal**.

At the end of January and **the beginning of February 1943** the last German troops surrendered. Around **90,000** German soldiers went into **captivity**. Many were sick and exhausted. Only **about 6,000** of them returned home after the war, the last not until the middle of the 1950s.

The Battle of Stalingrad is regarded as an important **turning point** of the Second World War. After it the **Wehrmacht** was mostly in **retreat** in the east. The defeat showed many people that Germany could lose the war. In Volgograd a huge statue, the **“Motherland Calls”**, recalls the battle today.

gewusst: The statue “The Motherland Calls” in Volgograd is 85 metres tall including the sword.
At the end of the battle the city lay almost completely in ruins and was afterwards rebuilt.

teile.einleitung: Roald Amundsen was a Norwegian polar explorer. In December 1911 he became the first person to reach the South Pole, and thereby won a famous race against the Briton Robert Scott.
wichtigste: Roald Amundsen came from Norway.
On 14 December 1911 he became the first person to reach the South Pole.
He sailed to Antarctica with the ship “Fram”.
Dogs pulled his sledges.
Robert Scott reached the South Pole shortly after him.
Amundsen was also the first to sail through the Northwest Passage.

abschnitte.text: **Roald Amundsen** was born in 1872 in **Norway**. Even as a boy he wanted to become a polar explorer. He prepared thoroughly, learned to sail and got used to cold. From 1903 to 1906 he was the first to sail through the **Northwest Passage** with a small ship. That is a sea route north of America between the Atlantic and the Pacific.

Actually Amundsen wanted to go to the North Pole. When he heard that others claimed to have arrived there already, he secretly changed his plan and went to **Antarctica**. His ship was called **“Fram”**, which means “forward”. The Fram was built especially sturdily so that it would not be crushed by the ice. In Antarctica Amundsen’s crew built a camp and waited out the winter.

Amundsen relied on **dogs** that pulled his **sledges**. He had learned from the Inuit in the Arctic how to move and dress in great cold. His men wore warm fur clothing and travelled on skis. Along the way they laid down depots of supplies. This good preparation was an important reason for his success.

abschnitte.titel: The race to the South Pole
abschnitte.text: On **14 December 1911** Amundsen reached the **South Pole** with four companions. They put up a tent with the Norwegian flag. The Briton **Robert Scott** arrived with his group only in January 1912. Scott relied above all on ponies and motor sledges, which failed in the cold. He and his companions died on the way back in ice and storm. Amundsen’s group returned healthy.

gewusst: The Fram stands today in a museum of its own in Oslo.
Amundsen disappeared in 1928 with an aircraft over the Arctic Ocean when he wanted to help in the search for explorers who had crashed.

teile.einleitung: Valentina Tereshkova from the Soviet Union was the first woman in space. In June 1963 she orbited the Earth alone for almost three days.
wichtigste: Valentina Tereshkova was born in 1937 in the Soviet Union.
Before she became a cosmonaut she worked in a textile factory.
She was a skilled parachutist.
On 16 June 1963 she launched with the spacecraft Vostok 6.
Her radio call sign was “Chaika”, which means seagull.
She spent almost 71 hours in space and orbited the Earth 48 times.
She flew entirely alone in her capsule.

abschnitte.text: Valentina Tereshkova grew up in simple circumstances. As a young woman she worked in a **textile factory** where fabrics were made. In her free time she learned **parachuting** in a club. At that time the Soviet Union was looking for women to be trained as cosmonauts. Because Tereshkova had a lot of experience with parachutes, she was chosen.

On **16 June 1963** Tereshkova launched with the spacecraft **Vostok 6**. She was 26 years old at the time. Over the radio she called herself **“Chaika”**, which is Russian for seagull. She spent almost **71 hours** in space, which is nearly three days. In that time she orbited the Earth **48 times**.

The Vostok spacecraft could not land gently. So Tereshkova had to eject from the capsule shortly before reaching the ground and float down to Earth by **parachute**. Here her experience as a parachutist helped her. She sat **alone** in her capsule. To this day she is the only woman who has made a spaceflight completely alone.

After her flight Tereshkova became famous in the Soviet Union and all over the world. She travelled to many countries and received high honours. Later she also became a **politician**. The next woman in space, in 1982, was again a cosmonaut from the Soviet Union. Today women from many countries fly into space.

gewusst: Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space, only about two years after the first human in space, Yuri Gagarin.
With her one flight she spent longer in space than all the American astronauts before her put together.

teile.einleitung: The Anabaptists were a Christian movement that arose in Zurich in 1525. They baptised only adults who had consciously decided for the faith. For this they were persecuted for a long time, but their successors such as the Mennonites and the Amish exist to this day.
wichtigste: The first adult baptism took place on 21 January 1525 in Zurich.
The first Anabaptists quarrelled with the reformer Ulrich Zwingli.
Conrad Grebel is regarded as the most important co-founder.
In 1527 the Schleitheim Confession arose in the canton of Schaffhausen.
The Mennonites are named after Menno Simons.
The Amish go back to Jakob Ammann of Bern.
In Münster radical Anabaptists set up a rule of their own in 1534.

abschnitte.text: At the time of the **Reformation** many people wanted to renew the Church. In Zurich the reformer **Ulrich Zwingli** was at work. Some of his followers wanted to reform faster and more radically, especially on **baptism**. On 21 January 1525 a few young men in a house in Zurich baptised one another, although they had already been baptised as children. With that the **Anabaptist movement** began.

The most important co-founder is regarded as **Conrad Grebel**. He came from a respected Zurich council family and had studied in Vienna and Paris. The Anabaptists held that only someone who believes himself should be baptised. Small children cannot yet do that. Grebel died already in 1526 of the plague.

In 1527 Anabaptists in the Schaffhausen village of **Schleitheim** wrote an important confession of faith. It goes back to **Michael Sattler**. In it the Anabaptists rejected, for example, the **oath** and **military service**. In doing so they came into conflict with the authorities, because oath and military service were compulsory at that time. The Anabaptists were therefore harshly persecuted in many places.

Most Anabaptists rejected violence. But a radical group set up a rule of its own in 1534 in **Münster** in Westphalia. It is called the **Anabaptist kingdom of Münster**. In 1535 the city was conquered, and the leaders were executed. After that all Anabaptists counted as dangerous to many people, although most were peaceful.

**Menno Simons**, a former Catholic priest from Friesland, gathered the peaceful Anabaptists in northern Germany and the Netherlands. After him they are called **Mennonites**. The **Amish** go back to **Jakob Ammann** from Erlenbach in the Simmental in the canton of Bern. Many later emigrated to America. Today the Amish in the USA often live without cars and without electricity from the grid.

gewusst: Many Amish in the USA still speak an old German dialect today.
In the Bernese Jura and in the Emmental there are still Anabaptist communities today, which are called Mennonites.

teile.einleitung: The League of Nations was the first worldwide organisation of states, meant to secure peace after the First World War. It had its seat in Geneva and began its work on 10 January 1920. Although it could not prevent the Second World War, it was the model for today's United Nations.
wichtigste: The League of Nations was founded with the Treaty of Versailles and worked from 10 January 1920.
Its seat was Geneva in Switzerland.
The USA never became a member because its Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles.
Switzerland joined after a popular vote on 16 May 1920.
Japan, Germany and Italy left in the 1930s.
The League of Nations had no army of its own and could hardly stop aggressors.
On 18 April 1946 it was formally dissolved and replaced by the UN.

abschnitte.text: After the First World War, with its millions of dead, such a war was never to happen again. US President **Woodrow Wilson** promoted the idea of a league of all nations especially strongly. The charter of the League of Nations became part of the Treaty of Versailles. The states promised to settle disputes peacefully and to stand by one another against aggressors. This principle is called **collective security**.

The League of Nations chose neutral Switzerland and the city of **Geneva** as its seat. At first it worked in a former hotel on Lake Geneva, today's Palais Wilson. In the 1930s the great **Palais des Nations** was built, which is now the second most important seat of the UN. The main bodies were the Assembly of all members, the Council and the Secretariat. The International Labour Organization was also linked to it.

abschnitte.titel: Switzerland in the League of Nations
abschnitte.text: On 16 May 1920 the Swiss people voted on joining. About 56 per cent said yes, and among the cantons there was only a narrow **majority of the cantons**. Switzerland was allowed to stay neutral and did not have to take part in military measures. This model was called **differential neutrality**. In 1938 Switzerland returned to full neutrality.

The League of Nations settled a few smaller conflicts, for example in 1921 the dispute between Finland and Sweden over the **Åland Islands**. The Norwegian Fridtjof Nansen helped hundreds of thousands of people as refugee commissioner and introduced the **Nansen passport** for stateless people. For this he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922. The League of Nations also worked against slavery, human trafficking and epidemics.

The League of Nations had no army of its own, and important decisions had to be unanimous. When Japan occupied Manchuria in 1931 and was criticised, it left on 27 March 1933. Germany was a permanent member of the Council from 1926 to 1933 and left the League under Hitler. In the **Abyssinian War** of 1935 the League imposed sanctions on Italy, but because oil was exempt, they had no effect. In 1939 the Soviet Union was expelled because of its attack on Finland.

The League of Nations could not prevent the Second World War. As early as 1945 the victorious powers founded the **United Nations**, which was meant to learn from the mistakes. On 18 April 1946 the League of Nations was formally dissolved, and its buildings and archives passed to the UN. Geneva owes it largely to the League of Nations that it is now a city of international organisations.

begriffe.erklaerung: All members help together when a state is attacked.
Punitive measures against a state, for example a trade ban.
The majority of the cantons in a Swiss popular vote.
A state does not take part in the wars of other states.

gewusst: Although the League of Nations was the idea of US President Wilson, the USA never became a member.
The Palais des Nations in Geneva is so large that, after Versailles, it is said to be one of the largest building complexes in Europe.
In 1919 Wilson received the Nobel Peace Prize for his work for the League of Nations.

teile.einleitung: The Peace of Westphalia is a series of peace treaties that ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648. They were negotiated in the Westphalian cities of Münster and Osnabrück. It is especially important for Switzerland, because with it the Confederation separated legally from the Holy Roman Empire.
wichtigste: The peace treaties were signed on 24 October 1648.
Negotiations took place in Münster and Osnabrück.
The peace ended the Thirty Years' War, which had devastated Central Europe.
The Reformed were given the same legal standing as the Lutherans and Catholics.
Sweden received Western Pomerania, and France the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun.
The mayor of Basel, Johann Rudolf Wettstein, secured the detachment of the Confederation from the Empire.
In 1648 the Netherlands were also finally recognised as independent of Spain.

abschnitte.text: From 1618 to 1648 Catholic and Protestant powers fought one another in Central Europe. What began as a religious dispute in Bohemia became a war for power in which Sweden, France and Spain also took part. Armies of mercenaries plundered villages, and disease and hunger followed. In some parts of Germany a third of the people or more died. The Confederation was largely spared, and only the Grisons was drawn heavily into the fighting.

From 1643 envoys from all over Europe met for the **peace congress**. In **Münster** the emperor and France mainly negotiated with the Catholic powers, and in Osnabrück the emperor and the Empire with Sweden and the Protestants. The treaty with Sweden is called the Instrumentum Pacis Osnabrugense. The negotiations lasted about five years, because there were many disputed questions and issues of rank. The treaties were signed on 24 October 1648.

The **Reformed**, that is, the followers of Zwingli and Calvin, were given the same legal standing in the Empire as the Lutherans and Catholics. The **normative year** was 1624: whoever owned a church or monastery then was allowed to keep it. The princes and cities in the Empire gained more rights, and could even make alliances with foreign countries. For the Palatinate a new, eighth electoral dignity was created, that is, another right to elect the emperor.

**Sweden** received Western Pomerania and other territories on the Baltic and North Seas. France was given the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun for good, as well as territories in Alsace. France and Sweden also became **guarantor powers** of the peace. In the Peace of Münster the Republic of the United Netherlands was finally recognised as independent of Spain. That also ended the Dutch Eighty Years' War.

The mayor of Basel, **Johann Rudolf Wettstein**, travelled to Westphalia in 1646. The occasion was a dispute, because an imperial court demanded money from Basel merchants. Wettstein succeeded in having the Confederation exempted from the jurisdiction of the Empire. With that it was legally independent of the **Holy Roman Empire**, although in fact it had long been self-governing. In Basel the Wettstein Bridge now recalls him.

The Peace of Westphalia is regarded as the beginning of a new order in Europe. States were to be **sovereign**, that is, decide their own affairs, and to recognise one another as equals. Conflicts were to be solved as far as possible by negotiation. The Peace Hall in the town hall of Münster still recalls the event today and can be visited.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right of a prince to help elect the German king and later emperor.
A state that makes sure a treaty is kept.
A cut-off year used to decide who owned churches and church property.
The right of a state to decide independently for itself.

gewusst: The news of the peace took days to arrive everywhere, and some troops carried on fighting.
Because many envoys cared about their rank, people argued for a long time over who was allowed to enter a room first.
Wettstein travelled to Westphalia without a mandate from all the Swiss cantons, but came back with the most important success.

teile.einleitung: For many generations people from Africa and their descendants were enslaved in the United States. They had to work without pay and without rights. Only in 1865 was slavery abolished throughout the USA.
wichtigste: Especially many enslaved people worked in the South on cotton plantations.
From 1808 the import of new slaves from Africa was banned.
People who demanded abolition were called abolitionists.
Frederick Douglass was a famous speaker against slavery.
The novel “Uncle Tom’s Cabin” of 1852 drew many people’s attention to the suffering.
The 13th Amendment to the Constitution abolished slavery in 1865.
Juneteenth on 19 June recalls the liberation in Texas.

abschnitte.text: Enslaved people counted as the property of their masters and could be sold. In the south of the USA they worked above all in large fields, the **plantations**. Especially important was **cotton**, the most important export of the Southern states. Its cultivation rested on the work of millions of enslaved people. Families were often torn apart.

From 1 January 1808 it was banned to bring new slaves from Africa into the USA. Slavery within the country, however, continued. Enslaved people continued to be sold between states. Their children too were unfree from birth.

People who demanded the abolition of slavery were called **abolitionists**. The word comes from the English “abolish”, to do away with. A well-known abolitionist was **Frederick Douglass**. He escaped from slavery in 1838 and became a famous speaker and writer. William Lloyd Garrison also fought against slavery with his newspaper.

In 1852 the novel **“Uncle Tom’s Cabin”** by Harriet Beecher Stowe appeared. It tells of the suffering of enslaved people. The book became a huge success and was translated into many languages. In the North it strengthened resistance to slavery. The dispute between North and South finally led to the Civil War.

After the Civil War the **13th Amendment** to the Constitution came into force in December 1865. Since then slavery has been banned throughout the USA. Already on 19 June 1865 Union troops in Galveston, Texas, had announced the freedom of the enslaved. This is recalled by the holiday **Juneteenth**, which has been a national holiday since 2021. Equal rights, however, were fought for by their descendants only much later.

gewusst: The name “Juneteenth” is put together from the English words for June and nineteenth.
Frederick Douglass wrote down his own life story, and the book made him world famous.

teile.einleitung: Mikhail Gorbachev was the most powerful politician in the Soviet Union from 1985 to 1991. With his reforms of glasnost and perestroika he wanted to renew his country. He contributed substantially to the peaceful end of the Cold War and received the Nobel Peace Prize for it.
wichtigste: Mikhail Gorbachev came from the Stavropol region in the North Caucasus.
In 1985 he became General Secretary of the CPSU as successor to Konstantin Chernenko.
Glasnost means openness and transparency, perestroika the restructuring of economy and society.
In November 1985 he met US President Ronald Reagan for the first time in Geneva.
In December 1987 the two signed the INF Treaty on intermediate-range missiles in the White House.
In February 1989 the last Soviet troops left Afghanistan.
In 1990 Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize.

abschnitte.text: Mikhail Gorbachev was born on 2 March 1931 in a village in the **Stavropol region** in the North Caucasus. As a teenager he helped with the harvest on combine harvesters. He studied law in Moscow and met his wife Raisa there. In the Communist Party he rose quickly, supported especially by **Yuri Andropov**.

abschnitte.titel: At the head of the Soviet Union
abschnitte.text: In March 1985 Konstantin Chernenko died, and Gorbachev became **General Secretary of the CPSU**. At 54 he was much younger than his predecessors. The Soviet Union was then in a serious crisis, and the economy worked badly. The expensive war in Afghanistan and the arms race with the USA also burdened the country.

With **glasnost** Gorbachev allowed more openness, and newspapers were allowed to criticise abuses. With **perestroika** he wanted to restructure economy and society. After the nuclear disaster at Chernobyl in April 1986 it became even clearer to him how dangerous secrecy is. Later there were elections with several candidates for the first time, and in 1990 he became President of the Soviet Union.

In November 1985 Gorbachev and US President **Ronald Reagan** met for the first time in **Geneva**. The most important result was a new thread of talks between the superpowers. In October 1986 they negotiated in Reykjavík about far-reaching disarmament. In December 1987 they signed the **INF Treaty** in the White House in Washington, which banned land-based intermediate-range missiles.

Gorbachev withdrew the Soviet troops from Afghanistan, the last of them leaving the country in February 1989. He allowed the states of Eastern Europe to go their own way in 1989, without sending tanks. In this way the Berlin Wall could fall and Germany be reunified in 1990. For his role in peace he received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1990.

In August 1991 opponents of his reforms tried to overthrow him with a **coup**, which failed. After that, however, Boris Yeltsin became more and more powerful, and the constituent republics declared themselves independent. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned, and the Soviet Union dissolved. He died on 30 August 2022 in Moscow; in the West he is still mostly held in high regard, while in Russia he is often viewed critically.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Communist Party of the Soviet Union, which governed the country alone.
The head of the Communist Party and thus the most powerful man in the Soviet Union.
Russian for openness, the policy of more freedom of speech and transparency.
Russian for restructuring, the reform of economy and society.
The reducing or destroying of weapons by agreement between states.

gewusst: Gorbachev had a conspicuous birthmark on his forehead, by which he is instantly recognised in photographs.
The Geneva meeting of 1985 took place, among other places, in the Villa Fleur d’Eau on Lake Geneva.
After his resignation Gorbachev even appeared in an advertisement for a pizza chain.

teile.einleitung: Robert Koch was a German physician and one of the founders of modern research on bacteria. In 1882 he discovered the cause of tuberculosis and later received the Nobel Prize for it.
wichtigste: Robert Koch was a physician from Germany.
With the microscope he searched for bacteria.
In 1882 he discovered the cause of tuberculosis, a bacterium.
Tuberculosis mostly attacks the lungs.
In 1883 he investigated cholera in Egypt and India.
In 1905 he received the Nobel Prize.
Every year 24 March is World Tuberculosis Day.

abschnitte.text: **Robert Koch** was born in 1843 in **Germany** and became a **physician**. At first he worked as a country doctor. Alongside his work he did research with a **microscope**, which his wife is said to have given him. At that time little was yet known about how diseases arise. Koch was able to show that a particular **bacterium** causes the animal disease anthrax.

On **24 March 1882** Koch presented in Berlin his greatest discovery: the **cause of tuberculosis**. It is a tiny **bacterium**. Tuberculosis was then one of the most common causes of death. It mostly attacks the **lungs**, and the sick cough badly. Because the cause was now known, one could search better for remedies against the disease. In memory of this day 24 March is today **World Tuberculosis Day**.

In 1883 Koch travelled to **Egypt** and **India** to investigate **cholera**. This disease causes severe diarrhoea and often spread through polluted water. In India Koch found the cause of cholera. He recognised how important **clean drinking water** is. After that many cities paid more attention to a good water supply and sewers.

For his research on tuberculosis Koch received the **Nobel Prize** for Medicine in **1905**. In **Berlin** he headed an institute for infectious diseases, which today is called the **Robert Koch Institute**. It still monitors contagious diseases in Germany today. Koch died in 1910. His rules for how to prove reliably that a germ causes a disease are still used by researchers today.

gewusst: Koch and his colleagues grew bacteria on solid culture media, among other things in the flat dishes that are now called Petri dishes.
Today there are medicines against tuberculosis, but even so many people around the world still fall ill with it.

teile.einleitung: Nikola Tesla was an inventor and engineer. He became famous above all for alternating current, which is used today to distribute electricity almost everywhere in the world. A unit of measurement, a machine and even a car company are named after him.
wichtigste: Tesla was born in 1856 in what is now Croatia.
In 1884 he emigrated to the USA.
There he worked briefly for Thomas Edison.
He became famous for alternating current.
At Niagara Falls he helped to build a power station that used alternating current.
The Tesla coil bears his name.
The tesla is a unit of measurement in physics.

abschnitte.text: Nikola Tesla was born in 1856 in the village of Smiljan. At that time it belonged to the Austrian Empire and today it lies in **Croatia**. His family was Serbian and his father was a priest. Even as a child Tesla was very curious and had a good memory. He studied engineering in Graz and afterwards worked in Budapest and Paris.

In 1884 Tesla emigrated to the **USA**. In New York he first worked for the famous inventor **Thomas Edison**. The two did not get on well, however, and Tesla left after a short time. Edison backed **direct current**, in which the electricity always flows in the same direction. Tesla thought **alternating current** was better.

With **alternating current** the electricity changes direction very many times a second. It can easily be brought to a high voltage and so transported over long distances. Tesla invented a special motor for it. The businessman George Westinghouse bought his ideas. A fierce quarrel arose between Edison and Westinghouse, the **War of the Currents**. In the end alternating current won through.

abschnitte.titel: The power station at Niagara Falls
abschnitte.text: In the 1890s a large **hydroelectric power station** was built at **Niagara Falls**. It worked with Tesla’s alternating current. From 1896 it supplied electricity to the city of Buffalo. This was a great success and showed that electricity from water power can be transported far. In Switzerland too the electricity from the socket is alternating current.

abschnitte.titel: Coil, pigeons and a unit of measurement
abschnitte.text: In 1891 Tesla invented the **Tesla coil**. With it one can produce very high voltages and see long flashes of lightning. In his later years Tesla lived in hotels in New York. He liked to feed **pigeons** in the park and looked after sick birds. He died in 1943 in New York. Since 1960 a **unit of measurement** for the strength of magnetic fields has been called the **tesla**.

gewusst: Tesla held around 300 patents in various countries.
The car company Tesla was founded in 2003 and named after him, but he himself had nothing to do with it.

teile.einleitung: The White Rose was a resistance group of students in Munich. With leaflets they fought against Hitler and the war in 1942 and 1943.
wichtigste: The siblings Hans and Sophie Scholl belonged to the White Rose.
The group was active mainly at the University of Munich.
It resisted the Nazi regime with leaflets.
In all, the White Rose wrote six leaflets.
On 18 February 1943 the Scholl siblings were discovered in the atrium of the university.
Judge Roland Freisler sentenced them to death at the People's Court.
Professor Kurt Huber also supported the group and was executed in 1943.

abschnitte.text: From 1933 the **Nazis** under Adolf Hitler ruled in Germany. Anyone who disagreed was persecuted. In **Munich** students came together who did not want to accept this. They included **Hans and Sophie Scholl**, Alexander Schmorell, Christoph Probst and Willi Graf. They called themselves the **White Rose**. They were supported by Professor **Kurt Huber**, who taught philosophy and musicology.

The group wrote and distributed **leaflets** against Hitler and the war. In them they called on people to offer **passive resistance**. They also sent the leaflets by post to other cities. From 1942 to 1943 a total of **six leaflets** were produced. Kurt Huber helped write the sixth. This was very dangerous, because resistance was punishable by death.

On **18 February 1943** Hans and Sophie Scholl laid out leaflets in the university. They threw the rest into the **atrium**, a large hall with a glass roof. A **caretaker** saw them and reported them. The siblings were arrested. Only a few days later they stood before the **People's Court**.

Judge **Roland Freisler** was president of the People's Court and notorious for his **show trials**. He often shouted at the accused. On 22 February 1943 he sentenced Hans and Sophie Scholl and Christoph Probst to death, and they were executed the same day. Later Kurt Huber, Alexander Schmorell and Willi Graf were also sentenced and executed. Kurt Huber died in July 1943.

The sixth leaflet reached England. Aircraft of the **Allies** dropped it over Germany in great numbers. Today many schools, streets and squares recall the White Rose. The square in front of the University of Munich is called **Geschwister-Scholl-Platz**. The group is regarded as an example of courage and civil courage.

gewusst: Sophie Scholl was only 21 years old when she was executed.
In the atrium of the University of Munich a memorial now commemorates the White Rose.

teile.einleitung: National Socialism was an inhuman political movement that ruled in Germany from 1933 to 1945 under Adolf Hitler. It was based on racism, hatred of Jews and belief in an all-powerful leader. The National Socialists started the Second World War and murdered millions of people in the Holocaust.
wichtigste: The NSDAP emerged in 1920 from the German Workers’ Party.
Racism was a central core of Nazi ideology, which divided people into “worth” and “worthlessness”.
National Socialism was directed especially against liberalism, democracy and Marxism.
The Führer principle meant orders from the top down without democratic control.
In the Reichstag election of 5 March 1933 the NSDAP won 43.9 per cent.
After 1934 the SS developed into the regime’s central organisation of terror and extermination.
The rule ended with Germany’s defeat in May 1945.

abschnitte.text: After the First World War there was hardship in Germany, anger over the lost war and political unrest. In 1920 the **NSDAP** emerged from the **German Workers’ Party**, and soon Adolf Hitler stood at its head. In 1923 an attempted coup in Munich failed. Only in the world economic crisis from 1929, when millions of people were unemployed, did the party become very strong.

A central core was **racism**, which divided people into supposedly “valuable” and “worthless” ones. Jews in particular were declared enemies; this hatred of Jews is called antisemitism. The “national community” was meant to exclude everyone supposedly “foreign” and all opponents. By “living space in the east” was meant the conquest and Germanisation of Eastern European territories.

Before 1933 the **SA** was the NSDAP’s troop of thugs and hall guards, which intimidated and attacked political opponents. In 1934 Hitler had the SA leadership murdered in order to secure his power. After that the **SS** under Heinrich Himmler developed into the regime’s central organisation of terror and extermination. It ran the concentration and extermination camps.

On 30 January 1933 Hitler became Reich Chancellor. In the Reichstag election of 5 March 1933 the NSDAP won 43.9 per cent, so not an absolute majority. With the **Enabling Act** in March 1933 it switched off parliament, and after that all other parties were banned. According to the **Führer principle** all orders ran from the top down, without democratic control.

With the invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 the Second World War began. In the **Holocaust** the National Socialists murdered around six million Jews from all over Europe. Sinti and Roma, people with disabilities, political opponents and many others were also persecuted and killed. On 8 May 1945 Germany surrendered, and Nazi rule was at an end.

In Switzerland too in the 1930s there were so-called **Fronts** that stood close to National Socialism, but found only few followers. Switzerland, on the other hand, strengthened its own democratic values with Spiritual National Defence. After the war leading National Socialists were convicted in the Nuremberg trials. Today memorial sites and school lessons recall it, so that such crimes are never repeated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed body of ideas with which a group explains the world and justifies its aims.
Hatred of and prejudice against Jews.
Rule in which one person or party has all the power and allows no free elections.
The murder of around six million Jews by the National Socialists.
The principle that all power lies with one leader and everyone must obey.

gewusst: The NSDAP never won an absolute majority of the votes in a free election.
The abbreviation NSDAP stands for National Socialist German Workers’ Party.
In Germany today the public display of swastikas and other Nazi symbols is largely banned.

teile.einleitung: Toussaint Louverture was the most important leader of the Haitian Revolution. He had himself been born into slavery. He fought for the freedom of the enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, which is now Haiti.
wichtigste: Toussaint Louverture was born enslaved and later became free.
He led the rebels in Saint-Domingue.
In 1794 France abolished slavery in its colonies.
For a time he governed the colony.
In 1802 Napoleon sent troops under General Leclerc against him.
He died in 1803 in the Fort de Joux in the Jura, close to the Swiss border.

abschnitte.text: **Saint-Domingue** was a French colony in the Caribbean, today's **Haiti**. It was very rich, above all thanks to sugar and coffee. The work on the plantations was done by hundreds of thousands of **enslaved people**. From 1791 they rose up against their oppressors. This was the beginning of the **Haitian Revolution**.

**Toussaint Louverture** had himself been born into slavery and later became free. He was well educated and a skilful military leader. He became the most important leader of the rebels. Partly because of the uprising, the French **National Convention** abolished slavery in all colonies in 1794. After that Toussaint governed the colony for a time.

**Napoleon Bonaparte** wanted to win back control of the rich colony. In 1802 he sent a large army under **General Leclerc** to Saint-Domingue. Toussaint was taken prisoner and brought to France. Napoleon reintroduced slavery in some colonies.

The French locked Toussaint up in the **Fort de Joux** near Pontarlier. This fortress lies in the French Jura, close to the border with the canton of Neuchâtel. It was cold and damp there. Toussaint died in April 1803 of cold and illness. He did not live to see his victory: in 1804 Haiti became independent.

gewusst: Toussaint Louverture died in a fortress in the Jura, only a few kilometres from the Swiss border.
In 1804 Haiti became the first state to emerge from a successful uprising of enslaved people.

teile.einleitung: Trench warfare is war in which the fronts hardly move and the soldiers dig themselves into trenches. Best known is the trench warfare on the Western Front in the First World War. There millions of soldiers fought for years over a few kilometres of ground.
wichtigste: In trench warfare the fronts hardly move, and the troops entrench themselves in trenches.
From the end of 1914 the frozen Western Front stretched from the Belgian North Sea coast to the Swiss border.
The space between the opposing trenches was called No Man’s Land.
Machine guns, barbed wire and trenches made attacks very costly in lives.
In battles of material enormous quantities of ammunition and war matériel were used.
Before attacks there was often a non-stop artillery barrage, the drumfire.
Many soldiers became seriously ill in mind; they were called war tremblers.
At Christmas 1914 soldiers at some sections of the front spontaneously agreed a truce.

abschnitte.text: In August 1914 the German army marched through Belgium into France. It wanted to capture Paris quickly, but was stopped in September in the **Battle of the Marne**. After that both sides tried to outflank one another, and dug in. So arose a **Western Front** about 700 kilometres long, which reached the Swiss border at Bonfol in the Jura.

The **trenches** were deep ditches in a zigzag, protected by sandbags and barbed wire. The soldiers slept in damp dugouts and often lived for weeks in mud. Rats, lice and cold tormented them. Many got **trench foot**, a painful disease caused by constantly wet feet.

Anyone who wanted to attack had to run out of the trench across **No Man’s Land**. There barbed wire and **machine guns** were waiting, which could kill very many people in a short time. That is why defence was usually much stronger than attack. Often thousands of soldiers died in order to gain only a few hundred metres of ground.

To wear down their opponents the armies relied on huge **battles of material**. Before an attack the artillery often fired for days as **drumfire**. In the Battle of Verdun in 1916 and the Battle of the Somme in 1916 hundreds of thousands of soldiers were killed or wounded. From 1915 **poison gas** was also used, and in 1916 the first tanks appeared on the Somme.

The constant noise, the fear and the death of comrades weighed heavily on the soldiers. Some afterwards trembled uncontrollably and were called **war tremblers**. Today this is understood as an injury of the mind, as **trauma**. Many returning soldiers suffered from it all their lives.

abschnitte.titel: The Christmas Truce and the end of the war
abschnitte.text: At Christmas 1914 soldiers at some sections spontaneously laid down their weapons, sang songs and exchanged small presents. This **Christmas Truce** remained an exception. Only in 1918 did the front move again, also thanks to tanks and fresh troops from the USA. On 11 November 1918 the war ended with an **armistice**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dug ditch in which soldiers seek protection from shelling.
The area between the trenches of the opponents, which nobody controls.
A battle with huge quantities of ammunition and military equipment.
Non-stop shelling with cannon before an attack.
A serious injury of the mind after a terrible experience.

gewusst: In north-western Switzerland the thunder of the guns of the Western Front could at times be heard.
Added together, the trenches on the Western Front were many thousands of kilometres long.
In the Christmas Truce of 1914 soldiers of both sides are said even to have played football in No Man’s Land.

teile.einleitung: Mount Everest is the highest mountain on Earth. It lies in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and China. In 1953 Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first people to stand on its summit.
wichtigste: Mount Everest lies in the Himalayas.
It is 8,849 metres high.
Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first to climb it, in 1953.
Hillary came from New Zealand.
Tenzing Norgay belonged to the Sherpa mountain people.
The two breathed with oxygen bottles.
In 1952 a Swiss expedition had already got almost to the summit.

abschnitte.text: **Mount Everest** lies in the **Himalayas**, the highest mountain range in the world. It is **8,849 metres** high. Nepal and China announced this height in 2020 after a joint measurement. The mountain is named after George Everest, a British surveyor. In Nepal it is called **Sagarmatha**, in Tibet **Chomolungma**. On the summit it is extremely cold and windy.

In 1952 a **Swiss expedition** tried to reach the summit. The Geneva mountaineer Raymond Lambert climbed together with the Sherpa **Tenzing Norgay** up to about 8,600 metres. Then they had to turn back because of exhaustion and poor equipment. The experiences of the Swiss helped the next expedition. In 1956 two Swiss then also stood on the summit, as the second rope team ever.

In 1953 Britain sent a large expedition. On 29 May **Edmund Hillary** from **New Zealand** and **Tenzing Norgay** reached the summit. Tenzing belonged to the **Sherpa**, a mountain people from Nepal who know their way around at great height. The two stayed at the top for about a quarter of an hour. Hillary took photos, and Tenzing laid small gifts in the snow.

The higher you climb, the **thinner the air** is. On the summit there is only about a third as much oxygen as at sea level. Hillary and Tenzing therefore carried **oxygen bottles** on their backs. The zone above about 8,000 metres is called the **death zone** by mountaineers, because the body can no longer recover there. In 1978 Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler climbed Everest for the first time without additional oxygen.

gewusst: Mount Everest grows a tiny bit higher every year, because the Earth’s plates under the Himalayas are pushing together.
The Swiss expedition of 1956 was also the first to climb the neighbouring mountain Lhotse.

teile.einleitung: The Sistine Chapel is a famous chapel in the Vatican in Rome. Its ceiling was painted by Michelangelo. Here the cardinals also elect the new Pope.
wichtigste: The chapel belongs to the Pope’s palace in Vatican City.
Michelangelo painted the ceiling from 1508 to 1512, so for about 4 years.
The best-known picture is the Creation of Adam.
Later Michelangelo painted the Last Judgement on the altar wall.
The pictures are frescoes, painted on fresh, wet plaster.
In the chapel the cardinals elect the Pope.

abschnitte.text: **Vatican City** is a tiny state in the middle of Rome. Here lives the Pope, the head of the Catholic Church. The Sistine Chapel belongs to the Pope’s palace. It is named after Pope Sixtus IV, who had it built. Every year millions of people visit the chapel.

**Michelangelo** received the commission from the Pope to paint the huge ceiling. He worked on it from 1508 to 1512. For this he had a high wooden **scaffold** built so that he could get close to the ceiling. The work high up was very tiring. The pictures tell stories from the Bible.

The most famous ceiling picture is called **The Creation of Adam**. God stretches his hand out towards Adam. Their fingers almost touch. This picture is known all over the world and is often copied. Later Michelangelo painted another huge picture on the altar wall: **The Last Judgement**.

The pictures in the chapel are **frescoes**. In a fresco the paint is applied to fresh, wet plaster. As it dries the paint bonds firmly with the wall. That is why frescoes last a very long time. But one has to work quickly, before the plaster is dry.

When a new Pope is elected the **cardinals** meet in the Sistine Chapel. This election is called the **conclave**. After the rounds of voting the ballot papers are burned. If **white smoke** rises from the chimney, a new Pope has been elected. Black smoke means: no decision yet. By the way, the Pope is guarded by the Swiss Guard.

gewusst: Michelangelo was also a sculptor: his marble statue of David in Florence is over 5 metres tall.
For over 500 years the Pope has been protected by the Swiss Guard, whose soldiers are Swiss.

teile.einleitung: On 1 September 1939 Nazi Germany attacked Poland. With this invasion the Second World War began in Europe. Shortly afterwards the Soviet Union also marched into Poland, and the country was divided up between the two dictatorships.
wichtigste: On 1 September 1939 the German invasion of Poland began the Second World War in Europe.
A staged attack on the Gleiwitz radio station on 31 August 1939 served as a pretext.
The training ship Schleswig-Holstein shelled the Polish garrison on the Westerplatte near Danzig.
In the Hitler-Stalin Pact, Germany and the Soviet Union had secretly divided up Central and Eastern Europe.
Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939.
On 17 September 1939 the Red Army marched into eastern Poland.
Warsaw surrendered on 28 September 1939.
In Switzerland the Federal Assembly elected Henri Guisan as General on 30 August 1939.

abschnitte.text: After the First World War Poland had become an independent state again. The city of **Danzig** was a Free City, and Poland had access to the Baltic Sea through the so-called **Polish Corridor**. Adolf Hitler demanded these territories back. In spring 1939 Britain and France had promised Poland to stand by it in the event of an attack.

On 23 August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a **non-aggression pact**. In a **secret additional protocol** they divided Central and Eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres of interest. Poland was to be divided between them. This meant Hitler did not have to fear a war against the Soviet Union.

On the evening of 31 August 1939 SS men in Polish uniforms attacked the German **Gleiwitz radio station**. Nazi propaganda then claimed that Poland had attacked Germany. In reality the attack was **staged**, in other words acted out. It was meant to justify the attack on Poland.

In the early morning of 1 September 1939 the training ship **Schleswig-Holstein** opened fire on the Polish garrison on the **Westerplatte** near Danzig. At the same time German troops attacked from the west, north and south, and aircraft bombed cities such as Wieluń. The small garrison on the Westerplatte held out for a whole week. On 3 September Britain and France declared war on Germany, but hardly attacked.

On 17 September 1939 the **Red Army** marched into eastern Poland. The Polish army now had to fight on two fronts. On 28 September the capital **Warsaw** surrendered after heavy bombing. The Polish government fled and formed a **government in exile**, first in France and later in London. Under the two **occupying powers**, Jews and many other people were persecuted and murdered, and over the whole war about one sixth of Poland's inhabitants died.

Already on 30 August 1939 the **Federal Assembly** elected Henri Guisan as General of the army. On 2 September the **general mobilisation** began, and hundreds of thousands of soldiers reported for duty. Switzerland declared itself neutral. The borders were guarded, and the supply of food was planned.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sudden attack without a declaration of war.
Deliberate influencing of people, often with lies.
A treaty in which states promise not to attack one another.
When a country calls up its soldiers for service.
A government that had to leave its country and carries on working from abroad.

gewusst: When it attacked, the Schleswig-Holstein was a training ship that was in Danzig on a visit.
Polish mathematicians had already broken parts of the German Enigma cipher machine before the war and passed their knowledge on to the British and French.
In Germany, 1 September is observed as Anti-War Day.

teile.einleitung: A Montgolfière is a hot-air balloon. The name recalls the French Montgolfier brothers, who invented it. In 1783 humans flew freely through the air for the first time in their balloon.
wichtigste: The Montgolfier brothers from France invented the hot-air balloon.
Their family owned a paper factory.
A hot-air balloon rises because warm air is lighter than cold air.
The brothers made the air hot with a fire.
Their first balloons rose in 1783.
In Versailles a sheep, a duck and a rooster flew along, and King Louis XVI watched.
In November 1783 humans flew over Paris in a hot-air balloon for the first time.

abschnitte.titel: Two brothers from the paper factory
abschnitte.text: **Joseph-Michel** and **Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier** came from Annonay in **France**. Their family earned its living from a **paper factory**. The brothers observed that smoke and warm air rise upwards. They built envelopes of cloth and paper and filled them with hot air. In June 1783 a large balloon without passengers rose in Annonay in front of many spectators.

The brothers made the air in the balloon hot with a **fire** of straw and wool. Warm air expands. That is why it is **lighter than cold air** in the same amount. The balloon full of warm air is pushed upwards by the colder air all around it, much like a cork in water. When the air cools, the balloon sinks again.

Nobody knew whether you could even breathe at that height. That is why the brothers sent animals up first. On 19 September 1783 a balloon with a **sheep**, a **duck** and a **rooster** rose in **Versailles**. King **Louis XVI** and many people from the court watched. After a few minutes the balloon landed, and the animals had survived the flight.

abschnitte.titel: The first humans in the air
abschnitte.text: On 21 November 1783 the time had come: over **Paris** humans flew freely in a hot-air balloon for the first time. The passengers were Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d’Arlandes. They travelled for about 25 minutes over the city. After the inventors, a hot-air balloon is also called a **Montgolfière**. Today the balloons are heated with gas burners.

gewusst: Soon after the Montgolfiers, a balloon filled with the light gas hydrogen also flew in Paris.
In Château-d’Œx in the canton of Vaud, balloonists from all over the world meet every winter.
In 1999 the Swiss Bertrand Piccard, together with Brian Jones, was the first to fly around the Earth non-stop in a balloon.

teile.einleitung: In the late 19th century European powers divided up almost the whole of Africa among themselves. This rapid conquest is called the Scramble for Africa.
wichtigste: From about 1880 European states conquered almost the whole of Africa in a short time.
At the Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885 they laid down rules for the partition.
France conquered Algeria from 1830, and Portugal held Angola and Mozambique.
Britain aimed for a land link from the Cape to Cairo.
In 1896 Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa and remained independent.
German South West Africa corresponds to present-day Namibia.
Colonial rule brought great suffering to the people of Africa.

abschnitte.text: For a long time the Europeans held mainly bases on the coasts of Africa. France, however, conquered **Algeria** as early as **1830**. From about **1880** everything went very fast: several states wanted territory, raw materials and power. At the **Berlin Conference** of 1884 and 1885 the powers agreed on rules for how to divide Africa among themselves. Africans were not at the table. Around 1914 only **Ethiopia** and **Liberia** were still independent.

**Britain** wanted a land link **from the Cape to Cairo**, that is, from the south to the north. Britons such as **Cecil Rhodes** dreamed of a railway through British territories, but it was never completed. **France** wanted to cross Africa from west to east. In 1898 the two powers met at **Fashoda** in Sudan. France finally gave way, and a war was avoided.

Many African peoples resisted the conquest. Most successful was **Ethiopia**: in 1896 Emperor **Menelik II** defeated the Italian army at the **Battle of Adwa**. So Ethiopia remained independent. In **German South West Africa**, now Namibia, the **Herero and Nama** rose up against the German Empire in 1904. German warfare killed tens of thousands of people, and today we speak of genocide.

The settlers also fought one another. The **Boers** were descendants mainly of Dutch settlers in South Africa. From 1899 to 1902 Britain waged the **South African War** against them. The British defeated the Boer republics and so gained rich **gold and diamond deposits**. **Portugal** was one of the first colonial powers, and its colonies **Angola** and **Mozambique** became independent only in 1975.

Many borders in Africa were drawn then with a ruler on the map. They separated peoples or put hostile groups together. Most countries became independent only around **1960**, Algeria for example in 1962. **Switzerland** had no colonies. But Swiss traders, firms and missionaries were active in Africa, for example the **Basel Mission** on the Gold Coast, now Ghana.

gewusst: The Berlin Conference is also called the Congo Conference, because it was mainly about the territory on the Congo.
Liberia was co-founded by freed slaves from America and was never a European colony.

teile.einleitung: The Congress of Vienna was a great assembly of European princes and diplomats in Vienna in 1814 and 1815. After Napoleon's defeat they reorganised Europe and fixed borders that lasted for a long time. For Switzerland the Congress was especially important, because its neutrality was recognised and it received its present borders almost completely.
wichtigste: The Congress of Vienna met from 1814 to 1815.
The aim was to reorganise Europe after Napoleon's defeat.
The Congress was led by the Austrian statesman Klemens von Metternich.
A balance of power was meant to prevent any single state from dominating the whole of Europe.
In 1815 the great powers recognised the perpetual neutrality of Switzerland.
Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva joined the Confederation as new cantons.
Russia, Austria and Prussia formed the Holy Alliance in September 1815.

abschnitte.text: From September 1814 emperors, kings and envoys from almost the whole of Europe met in Vienna. The most important powers were Austria, Russia, Prussia and Britain, and later defeated France was also allowed a say. The host and chairman was the Austrian foreign minister **Klemens von Metternich**. France was represented by the skilful diplomat Talleyrand, and Russia by Tsar Alexander I himself.

Besides the negotiations there were countless balls, concerts, hunts and parties. People mocked this: “The Congress dances, but it does not advance.” The real work mostly took place in small meetings of the great powers. In March 1815 **Napoleon** escaped from his exile on Elba and returned to France. On 18 June 1815 he was finally defeated at **Waterloo**, shortly after the final act of the Congress had been signed on 9 June.

The most important aim was a **balance of power**, so that no state could dominate the whole of Europe again. Prussia received large territories on the Rhine, Russia a large part of Poland and Austria territories in northern Italy. Instead of the old Empire, the **German Confederation** was founded, a loose union of German states. Belgium was united with the Netherlands into one kingdom.

The period after the Congress is called the **Restoration**, that is, the restoring of the old order. Many princes whom Napoleon had driven out returned to their thrones. Ideas such as popular rule and freedom of the press were suppressed. In September 1815 Russia, Austria and Prussia formed the **Holy Alliance** to help one another against revolutions. Even so, uprisings came later, especially in 1830 and 1848.

For Switzerland, it was above all the Genevan **Charles Pictet de Rochemont** who campaigned in Vienna and Paris. In 1815 the great powers recognised Switzerland's **perpetual neutrality**. Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva joined as new cantons, so there were now 22 cantons. As compensation for the lost Vaud and Aargau, the canton of Bern received most of the former **Prince-Bishopric of Basel**, the Jura. Switzerland, on the other hand, finally lost the Valtellina, which had previously belonged to the Grisons.

The order of the Congress of Vienna brought a long period without a major European war. The borders of Switzerland of 1815 still apply today with small exceptions. Swiss neutrality too, recognised at that time, is still an important part of Swiss foreign policy. Many peoples, however, were dissatisfied, because their wishes for freedom and nation states of their own were ignored.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large assembly at which important questions are discussed.
The restoring of the old order with the power of the princes.
The idea that several states are about equally strong so that none dominates all the others.
A state keeps out of the wars of other states.

gewusst: The saying “The Congress dances” is attributed to the Austrian prince Charles Joseph de Ligne, who died during the Congress.
Napoleon returned from Elba while the Congress was still in session, and then ruled for about a hundred days.
Since 1815 Switzerland has not taken part in any war against other states.

teile.einleitung: The Space Shuttle was a spacecraft of NASA, the space agency of the USA. It flew from 1981 to 2011. The special thing: the orbiter could be used again and again.
wichtigste: The Space Shuttle was built by NASA.
The orbiter was reusable and flew many times.
It launched like a rocket and landed like an aircraft on a runway.
The first flight took place in April 1981 with Columbia.
The last flight was in 2011 with Atlantis.
In 30 years there were 135 flights in all.

abschnitte.text: In the past rockets were no longer needed after one flight. The **Space Shuttle** was meant to change that. Its **orbiter** could be used again after landing. That is why the individual shuttles flew into space many times. The English word “shuttle” means a service that goes back and forth.

At launch the Space Shuttle consisted of three parts: the orbiter with wings, two **solid rocket boosters** at the side and a large **external tank** for the fuel. The tank was orange because it was not painted. In this way weight was saved. The boosters and the tank were jettisoned during the ascent.

For the return the orbiter had **wings**. It glided back to Earth without an engine. Then it landed on a long **runway**, like an aircraft. A heat shield protected it from the great heat as it entered the Earth’s atmosphere.

The five shuttles that flew into space were called **Columbia**, **Challenger**, **Discovery**, **Atlantis** and **Endeavour**. They carried astronauts, satellites and parts of the International Space Station into space. The Hubble Space Telescope too was launched with a shuttle. With the shuttle Claude Nicollier also flew into space in 1992 as the first Swiss.

The first flight took place in April 1981 with **Columbia**. In 30 years there were **135 flights** in all. Two shuttles, Challenger and Columbia, were lost in accidents, and their crews died. In 2011 **Atlantis** flew for the last time. Today the remaining shuttles stand in museums.

gewusst: The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier flew into space four times with the Space Shuttle.
On the first flights the orange external tank was still painted white.

teile.einleitung: The Reformation was a great movement to renew the Church in the 16th century. Martin Luther and other reformers criticised abuses in the Catholic Church. From it the Protestant churches arose, and Europe was split into denominations.
wichtigste: The Latin word “reformation” means renewal or reshaping.
The beginning is taken to be the year 1517, when Martin Luther published his 95 Theses.
For Luther the Bible alone was the standard of faith, that is “sola scriptura”.
According to Luther a person is made righteous before God by faith and God’s grace alone.
The name “Protestants” comes from the protest at the Imperial Diet of Speyer in 1529.
The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 allowed the princes to decide the denomination of their land.
The Catholic Church answered with the Counter-Reformation and the Council of Trent.

abschnitte.text: Around 1500 the Catholic Church in Western Europe was very powerful and rich. Many people were angry about the **sale of indulgences**: one could buy letters of indulgence that promised a shortening of the punishments for sins. Even earlier critics such as John Wyclif in England and **Jan Hus** in Bohemia had demanded reforms. Hus was burned in 1415 at the Council of Constance.

The monk and professor **Martin Luther** published 95 Theses against indulgences in Wittenberg in 1517. In 1521 at the Imperial Diet of Worms he refused to recant his teachings. After that he hid in the **Wartburg** and translated the New Testament into German there. Thanks to printing, his writings spread very quickly.

The reformers said that the Holy Scripture alone was the standard of faith, in Latin **sola scriptura**. One became righteous before God not through good works or paid indulgences, but through faith and grace alone. Of the seven Catholic sacraments only **baptism and the Lord’s Supper** remained in most Protestant churches. Pastors were allowed to marry, and services were held in the national language.

Besides Luther, Huldrych Zwingli worked in Zurich and John Calvin in Geneva in Switzerland. In 1529 Protestant princes protested at the Imperial Diet of Speyer, and that is where the name **Protestants** comes from. In 1530 Philip Melanchthon wrote the **Augsburg Confession**, the basic confession of the Lutheran Church. The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 laid down: “cuius regio, eius religio”, that is, whose land, his religion.

The Catholic Church also renewed itself, which is called the **Counter-Reformation** or Catholic reform. The **Council of Trent** met from 1545 to 1563 and fixed Catholic doctrine. The Jesuit order, confirmed by the Pope in 1540, founded many schools and won back areas for the Catholic faith. The tensions later led to wars of religion such as the Thirty Years’ War from 1618 to 1648.

The Reformation changed religion, politics, language and education in Europe. Luther’s translation of the Bible strongly shaped the German written language. Because everyone was meant to read the Bible themselves, more schools were founded. Today Protestant churches recall the posting of the theses on 31 October with **Reformation Day**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A branch of Christianity, for example Catholic or Protestant.
A remission of punishments for sins, which at that time one could also buy.
A claim that one wants to have discussed.
A holy rite of the Church, such as baptism.
A great assembly of bishops of the Church.

gewusst: Whether Luther really nailed his theses to the door of the castle church in Wittenberg is disputed among historians.
Luther translated the whole New Testament in the Wartburg in only about eleven weeks.
The Jesuits were founded by the Spaniard Ignatius of Loyola.

teile.einleitung: The Meiji Restoration was a great turning point in the history of Japan. From 1868 the Emperor took power again, and in a few decades Japan turned into a modern industrial state. The models were European countries and the USA.
wichtigste: The Meiji Restoration began in 1868.
The shogun, who had ruled Japan for a long time, lost his power.
In 1853/54 the American Matthew Perry forced Japan to open its ports.
In the Boshin War of 1868/69 the supporters of the Emperor won.
The samurai lost their privileges.
The constitution of 1889 followed the model of Prussia.
In 1904/05 Japan defeated Russia in war.

abschnitte.text: For over 250 years Japan was ruled not by the Emperor, but by a military ruler, the **shogun**. The Emperor, the **Tennō**, had hardly any power. Japan had largely shut itself off from the world. In 1853 the American commodore **Matthew Perry** came with warships. In 1854 Japan had to sign a treaty and open ports to foreign ships.

Many Japanese were dissatisfied with the shogun, who had given way to the foreigners. In 1868 the rule of the Emperor was restored, which is what **restoration** means. In the **Boshin War** of 1868/69 supporters of the Emperor fought against the supporters of the shogunate and won. The young Emperor **Mutsuhito** chose the name **Meiji** for his reign. It means “enlightened rule”.

The new government wanted to make Japan strong. The old city of **Edo** became the capital in 1868 and was renamed **Tokyo**, which means “eastern capital”. Japan built factories, railways and a modern army. In 1872 the first railway ran between Tokyo and Yokohama. All children were to go to school. Envoys travelled through America and Europe to learn, including, in 1873, to Switzerland.

The **samurai** had long been a noble warrior class with many privileges. In the Meiji period they lost these. In place of the samurai there was now an army in which young men had to serve. From 1876 samurai were no longer allowed to carry swords in public. Some samurai resisted this, but were defeated.

In 1889 Japan got a **constitution** and a parliament. An important model was **Prussia**, where the Emperor likewise had a lot of power. Japan soon also became militarily strong. In the war of 1904/05 it defeated **Russia**. With that Japan was regarded as a new great power. Emperor Meiji died in 1912.

gewusst: Switzerland and Japan concluded a treaty of friendship and trade as early as 1864.
In 1873 Japan adopted the same calendar that is also used in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Russian Revolution of 1917 first overthrew the Tsar and then brought the Bolsheviks under Lenin to power. After a bloody civil war the Tsarist empire became the Soviet Union. The event changed the history of the whole 20th century.
wichtigste: The February Revolution of 1917 was triggered by hunger, war weariness and strikes.
Tsar Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917.
After that the Provisional Government and the soviets ruled side by side.
In the October Revolution the Bolsheviks overthrew the government of Alexander Kerensky.
At that time Russia still used the Julian calendar.
With the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk Russia left the First World War in 1918.
At the end of 1922 the Soviet Union was founded.

abschnitte.text: Russia was ruled by **Tsar Nicholas II**, who had almost unlimited power. Most people were poor peasants, and in the cities many worked in factories under hard conditions. In the **First World War** Russia suffered heavy defeats and millions of losses. Food became scarce, and discontent grew.

In February 1917 by the Russian calendar workers in **Petrograd**, today’s Saint Petersburg, went on strike because of hunger and war. The soldiers refused to shoot at the crowd and went over to it. In March 1917 Nicholas II abdicated, and Tsarist rule was at an end. Now there was a **dual power**: the Provisional Government and the councils of workers and soldiers, the soviets.

**Vladimir Lenin**, leader of the Bolsheviks, lived in exile in Zurich. In April 1917 he travelled back to Russia by train with German help. He demanded peace, land for the peasants and all power to the soviets. The Provisional Government under **Alexander Kerensky** carried on the war and lost support.

On 25 October 1917 by the Julian calendar, that is on 7 November by ours, armed Bolsheviks occupied important buildings in Petrograd. They stormed the **Winter Palace**, the seat of the government. The action was organised above all by Leon Trotsky. Because Russia still used the **Julian calendar**, it is still called the October Revolution today.

In January 1918 the Bolsheviks dissolved the freely elected **Constituent Assembly** as soon as it met. In March 1918 they concluded the **Treaty of Brest-Litovsk** with Germany and gave up large territories. After that the Reds fought the Whites in a civil war in which millions of people died. The Tsar’s family was murdered in Yekaterinburg in July 1918.

At the end of 1922 the **Soviet Union** was founded, a communist one-party state. The Communist Party suppressed dissenters with a secret police and camps. The revolution later divided the world into East and West and led to the Cold War. The Soviet Union lasted until 1991.

begriffe.erklaerung: The radical party under Lenin from which the Communist Party grew.
Russian for council, an assembly of workers and soldiers.
The title of the Russian emperor.
An old calendar that at that time ran 13 days behind our calendar.
An idea according to which all property is to be shared and there are no more classes.

gewusst: Before returning to Russia Lenin lived on the Spiegelgasse in Zurich’s old town.
Petrograd was later called Leningrad and is today called Saint Petersburg again.
Russia introduced the Gregorian calendar only in February 1918.

teile.einleitung: In the autumn of 1973 oil suddenly became scarce and very expensive. This first oil price crisis showed how strongly the rich industrial countries depended on oil from a few producing countries.
wichtigste: The trigger was the Yom Kippur War in October 1973.
Arab oil states cut production and imposed an embargo on supporters of Israel.
The oil price rose from around 3 to around 12 dollars a barrel, so it quadrupled.
In Switzerland the Federal Council ordered three car-free Sundays at the end of 1973.
Many industrial countries fell into stagflation: a stalled economy and rising prices at the same time.
In 1974 the industrial countries founded the International Energy Agency, and Switzerland was there from the start.
