abschnitte.text: In October 1973 Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. This war is called the **Yom Kippur War**, because it began on the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur. Arab oil states wanted to put pressure on the supporters of Israel. They produced less oil and delivered none at all to some countries such as the USA. Such a ban on deliveries is called an **embargo**.

Crude oil is measured in **barrels**, and one barrel holds about 159 litres. The price per barrel rose in 1973 and 1974 from about 3 to about 12 dollars. That is an increase of 300 per cent. An important role was played by **OPEC**, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. It was founded in Baghdad in 1960 and today has its seat in Vienna.

To save petrol the Federal Council banned driving on three Sundays in November and December 1973. The roads and even the motorways were suddenly empty. Many people walked on them, rode bicycles or roller-skated. Other countries such as Germany also had such driving bans. For many people the oil crisis became noticeable for the first time.

Expensive energy made almost all prices rise. At the same time firms produced less, and many people lost their jobs. This mixture is called **stagflation**, from stagnation and inflation. The usual tools of economic policy hardly helped. Switzerland too experienced a marked economic slump in the middle of the 1970s.

In 1974 the industrial countries founded the **International Energy Agency** (IEA). It is meant to secure supply, for example with joint emergency stocks of oil. Many states began to save energy and to look for other sources of energy. In 1979, after the revolution in Iran, a second oil price crisis followed.

gewusst: On the car-free Sundays of 1973 one could walk in the middle of the motorway in Switzerland.
Oil prices are still quoted in dollars per barrel today, although hardly any oil is now transported in barrels.

teile.einleitung: The Qing dynasty was the last imperial dynasty of China. It was founded by the Manchu people and ruled over a huge empire from 1644 to 1912.
wichtigste: The Manchus took Beijing in 1644 and founded the Qing dynasty.
Han Chinese men had to wear a pigtail with a shaved forehead.
Emperor Kangxi reigned for around 61 years.
From 1757 Europeans were only allowed to trade by sea in Canton.
In 1793 Emperor Qianlong rejected the British Macartney mission.
Dowager Empress Cixi largely determined policy from 1861 to 1908.
In 1912 the empire ended with the abdication of the last emperor.

abschnitte.text: The **Manchus** were a people from the north-east, from the region called Manchuria. In 1644 they took **Beijing** and thereby ended the Ming dynasty. They founded the **Qing dynasty**. Qing means roughly “clear” or “pure”. The Manchus were a small minority, while most people in China belonged to the **Han Chinese**.

As a sign of submission Han Chinese men had to adopt the hairstyle of the Manchus. They shaved their forehead and the front part of the head, and plaited the remaining hair into a long **pigtail**. Anyone who refused was severely punished. The pigtail thus became a mark of the Qing period. Only after the end of the dynasty did many men cut it off.

Under the first emperors the empire became large and powerful. Emperor **Kangxi** reigned for around **61 years**, from 1661 to 1722, longer than any other Qing emperor. His grandson **Qianlong** also reigned for a very long time. In this period China reached its greatest extent. The emperors promoted art, science and literature and had great books and dictionaries compiled.

From **1757** Europeans were only allowed to trade by sea in the port city of **Canton**, today Guangzhou. The British wanted more trade and in 1793 sent an embassy, the **Macartney mission**. Emperor Qianlong rejected their wishes, because China did not need their goods. Later British merchants brought opium to China. In the **Opium Wars** of the 19th century China lost and had to open ports and cede territories such as Hong Kong.

In the 19th century the Qing dynasty grew weaker. There were great uprisings, and foreign powers gained influence. From 1861 to 1908 the **Dowager Empress Cixi** largely determined policy at court. In 1898 Emperor **Guangxu** began the **Hundred Days’ Reform** in order to modernise China. Cixi had the reform stopped quickly. In 1911 a revolution broke out, and in 1912 the last emperor **Puyi** abdicated as a small child. China became a republic.

gewusst: Emperor Qianlong abdicated so as not to reign longer than his grandfather Kangxi.
The last emperor Puyi was only six years old at his abdication.

teile.einleitung: Robots are machines that move and carry out tasks on their own or following a program. Today they work in factories, in homes and even on other planets.
wichtigste: The word “robot” comes from the Czech word “robota”, which means work.
Many industrial robots work in car factories.
Small robots can vacuum on their own.
Robotic vehicles such as “Curiosity” drive around on Mars.
At ETH Zurich the four-legged walking robot ANYmal was developed.

abschnitte.text: The word **robot** comes from a play by the Czech writer **Karel Čapek** from the year 1920. In it humans build artificial workers. The word is derived from the Czech **“robota”**, which means **work**, especially hard forced labour. The idea of artificial helpers is much older, however. Even earlier, tinkerers built mechanical figures that could move.

Most robots work in **industry**. Many **industrial robots** stand in **car factories**. They are large gripping arms that weld, paint or lift heavy parts. They work very precisely and quickly and do not get tired. They are controlled by **computer programs**. Because they are often very strong, many of them work behind safety fences.

There are robots at home too. Small round robots can **vacuum** on their own. With **sensors** they recognise walls and furniture and steer around them. Other robots mow the lawn. Sensors are feelers that tell a robot what is happening around it. So it can react to its surroundings.

Robots can work where people cannot go. On **Mars** robotic vehicles such as **“Curiosity”** drive around. They are called **rovers**. They have cameras and small laboratories on board, examine rock and send pictures to Earth. Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012. Because radio signals take a long time to reach Earth, rovers have to decide some things themselves.

At **ETH Zurich** the four-legged walking robot **ANYmal** was developed. It looks a little like a dog and can climb stairs and walk over uneven ground. Such robots can, for example, inspect industrial plants where it is dangerous for people. From the research project a company of its own arose in Zurich. Switzerland is internationally known in robotics research.

gewusst: Karel Čapek said that his brother Josef had actually invented the word “robot”.
On Mars radio signals from Earth take several minutes to reach the rover, depending on the distance.

teile.einleitung: The Mediation period is the section of Swiss history from 1803 to 1813. During this time a constitution applied that Napoleon Bonaparte had given to Switzerland, the Act of Mediation. At that time several new cantons were created that still exist today.
wichtigste: Napoleon handed over the Act of Mediation on 19 February 1803 in Paris.
The name comes from the Latin word for intercession, because Napoleon acted as a go-between between the parties.
Switzerland now consisted of 19 cantons.
The cantons of St Gallen, Graubünden, Aargau, Thurgau, Ticino and Vaud were newly created.
Switzerland was once again a confederation of largely independent cantons.
The first Landammann of Switzerland was Louis d’Affry of Fribourg.
Switzerland had to make soldiers available to France.

abschnitte.text: From 1798 to 1803 Switzerland was the **Helvetic Republic**, a centrally governed unitary state on the French model. Many people rejected this order, and there was unrest. In the autumn of 1802 an uprising even broke out, called the Stick War. Napoleon then had French troops march into Switzerland and invited deputies to Paris.

From December 1802 Swiss deputies consulted with Napoleon in Paris about a new order. On 19 February 1803 he handed them the **Act of Mediation**. It contained a constitution for the whole of Switzerland and separate constitutions for each canton. Because Napoleon mediated between the supporters of the old and the new order, the period is called the Mediation period.

Switzerland now consisted of 19 cantons: the 13 old places and six new cantons. The new ones were **St Gallen, Graubünden, Aargau, Thurgau, Ticino and Vaud**, many of which had formerly been subject territories. The canton of Ticino emerged from the Helvetic cantons of Lugano and Bellinzona. To Aargau was added the formerly Further Austrian **Fricktal**, and Bern finally lost Vaud and Aargau.

Switzerland was once again a **confederation of states**, so the cantons were largely independent. Six directorial cantons, namely Fribourg, Bern, Solothurn, Basel, Zurich and Lucerne, took turns every year as the **Vorort** (leading canton). The head of government of the Vorort bore the title Landammann of Switzerland. The first Landammann in 1803 was Louis d’Affry of Fribourg, whom Napoleon had chosen.

In September 1803 Switzerland concluded a military alliance with France and had to supply Napoleon with soldiers. Swiss regiments therefore fought in Spain and in 1812 in Russia, where many fell at the **Berezina**. The Continental Blockade against Britain harmed the trade and the textile industry of eastern Switzerland. Valais was even taken over directly by France in 1810.

After Napoleon’s defeat at the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig, Allied troops marched through Switzerland at the end of 1813. At the end of December 1813 the Diet declared the Act of Mediation repealed. After that came the period of the **Federal Treaty** of 1815. The six new cantons remained, however, and in 1815 Valais, Geneva and Neuchâtel were added as further cantons.

begriffe.erklaerung: Intercession between parties in dispute.
A loose union of states that remain largely independent.
The title for the head of a canton, in the Mediation period also for the head of the whole of Switzerland.
The canton that led the common business of the Confederation for a year at a time.
The assembly of the envoys of all the cantons in the old Confederation.

gewusst: The cantons of Aargau, Thurgau, St Gallen, Graubünden, Ticino and Vaud celebrated their 200th anniversary together in 2003.
Napoleon said that Switzerland needed an order that suited its nature as a union of small states.
For the people of Vaud, Aargau and Ticino the Mediation period meant the final liberation from the rule of other cantons.

teile.einleitung: The Reign of Terror was the bloodiest time of the French Revolution, roughly from the middle of 1793 to July 1794. The government under Maximilien de Robespierre had thousands of alleged enemies of the Revolution executed. The period shows how a revolution for freedom can turn into violence.
wichtigste: The Reign of Terror lasted roughly from the middle of 1793 to July 1794.
The centre of power was the Committee of Public Safety.
Maximilien de Robespierre, “the Incorruptible”, shaped this period.
The Law of Suspects of 17 September 1793 allowed arrests on mere suspicion.
Around 16,600 death sentences were officially carried out, often with the guillotine.
Queen Marie-Antoinette and Georges Danton were also executed.
On 9 Thermidor (27 July 1794) the Convention overthrew Robespierre and had him executed.

abschnitte.text: In 1793 the young French Republic was threatened from all sides. Abroad Austria, Prussia and Britain were fighting against France. In the country itself there were uprisings, especially in the **Vendée** in the west. King Louis XVI had already been executed in January 1793. The radical **Jacobins** believed that they could save the Revolution only with harshness.

The parliament was called the **National Convention**. In 1793 it set up the **Committee of Public Safety**, which became the real centre of power. Its best-known member was **Maximilien de Robespierre**, a lawyer from Arras. Because of his strictness and because he was regarded as not open to bribes, he was called “the Incorruptible”.

The **Law of Suspects** of 17 September 1793 allowed arrests on mere suspicion. The **Revolutionary Tribunal** in Paris sentenced many people to death in short trials. Executions were carried out with the **guillotine**, a falling blade. According to the historian Donald Greer’s study around 16,600 death sentences were officially carried out, and many more people died without a verdict.

In July 1793 **Charlotte Corday** stabbed the radical journalist Jean-Paul Marat in his bath and was executed for it. In October 1793 Queen **Marie-Antoinette** died under the guillotine. Former revolutionaries also became victims. **Georges Danton**, who had demanded an end to the Terror, was executed on 5 April 1794.

On 8 June 1794 Robespierre had the **Festival of the Supreme Being** celebrated in Paris, a new kind of religion for the Republic. Two days later the **Law of 22 Prairial** tightened the Terror further. Defendants before the Revolutionary Tribunal could hardly defend themselves any more. In the following weeks executions in Paris rose sharply.

Many deputies feared that they themselves would be the next victims. On **9 Thermidor**, 27 July 1794, the Convention overthrew Robespierre. Already the next day he was executed with his supporters. With that the Reign of Terror ended, and a more moderate time began. The word **terror** for political violence comes from this time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device for execution with a heavy, falling blade.
A radical political group in the French Revolution.
A small body that governed France in 1793 and 1794.
A special court that sentenced alleged enemies of the Revolution.
A month in the French revolutionary calendar, in summer.

gewusst: During the Revolution France introduced a calendar of its own with new month names such as Thermidor or Prairial.
Many victims of the Reign of Terror were not nobles but ordinary peasants, craftsmen and workers.
The word “terrorism” goes back to the Reign of Terror of the French Revolution.

teile.einleitung: In 1994 hundreds of thousands of people were murdered in Rwanda in only about 100 days, mainly members of the Tutsi. The genocide is among the worst crimes of the 20th century.
wichtigste: The genocide in Rwanda lasted from April to July 1994.
It was triggered by the shooting down of President Juvénal Habyarimana's plane on 6 April 1994.
Hutu extremists deliberately murdered Tutsi and also moderate Hutu.
According to common estimates, about 800,000 to 1 million people were killed.
The radio station RTLM openly incited hatred against the Tutsi.
The Rwandan Patriotic Front ended the genocide in July 1994.
A UN criminal tribunal in Arusha convicted those responsible.

abschnitte.text: Rwanda is a small country in East Africa. The population consisted mainly of **Hutu** and **Tutsi**. In the past the border between these groups was not rigid. In the **colonial period** the division was fixed by identity cards that stated the group. After independence there was repeated violence, and many Tutsi fled to neighbouring countries. From there, from 1990, the rebel army **Rwandan Patriotic Front** fought against the government.

Extremists prepared the genocide. They formed militias, the **Interahamwe**, and distributed weapons. The radio station **Radio-Télévision Libre des Mille Collines**, RTLM for short, incited hatred against the Tutsi. It called them “cockroaches” and openly called for killing. Those responsible at the station were later convicted of incitement to genocide.

On **6 April 1994**, over the capital **Kigali**, the plane of President **Juvénal Habyarimana** was shot down. The president of Burundi also died. The killings began that very night. Hutu extremists deliberately killed **Tutsi** and also moderate Hutu who opposed them. In about **100 days**, according to common estimates, **800,000 to 1 million** people were killed.

A small UN force, the mission UNAMIR, was stationed in Rwanda. Its commander, the Canadian General **Roméo Dallaire**, had warned of planned massacres as early as January 1994. But he received no reinforcements, and the troops were even reduced. In **July 1994** the **Rwandan Patriotic Front** under **Paul Kagame** captured the capital Kigali and ended the genocide.

In 1994 the UN set up the **International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda**. It sat in **Arusha** in Tanzania. In 1998 it delivered the first verdict of an international court for genocide. In Rwanda itself, village courts, the **Gacaca**, later also ruled on very many cases. Every year from 7 April Rwanda remembers the victims.

gewusst: Because of its many hills, Rwanda is also called the “Land of a Thousand Hills”, and that is where the name of the radio station comes from too.
The Gacaca courts dealt with well over a million cases.

teile.einleitung: In autumn 1956 the people of Hungary rose up against the communist government and the influence of the Soviet Union. The uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks after a few weeks.
wichtigste: The Hungarian Uprising began on 23 October 1956 in Budapest.
On the first day demonstrators toppled a huge statue of Stalin.
From 4 November 1956 the Soviet army put down the uprising.
The Soviet Union installed János Kádár as the new leader.
Around 200,000 people fled from Hungary.
Switzerland took in about 14,000 Hungarian refugees.
At the same time the Suez Crisis distracted the attention of the West.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Hungary came under the influence of the **Soviet Union**. A communist party ruled alone, and there were no free elections. Anyone who criticised the government was persecuted. Many people suffered from poverty and fear. After the death of the Soviet dictator Stalin in 1953, many hoped for more freedom.

On **23 October 1956** students and many other people demonstrated in Budapest. They demanded freedom, free elections and the withdrawal of the Soviet troops. The same day they pulled a huge **statue of Stalin** off its plinth. It became the symbol of the uprising. The reformist politician **Imre Nagy** became head of government and declared that Hungary wanted to become neutral.

From **4 November 1956** the Soviet army moved into Budapest with tanks. The insurgents defended themselves but were much weaker. Thousands of people died. The Soviet Union installed **János Kádár** as the new leader, and he stayed at the head of the party until 1988. Imre Nagy was arrested and executed in 1958. The West did not help Hungary militarily, partly because at the same time the **Suez Crisis** at the Suez Canal in Egypt was taking up its attention.

Around 200,000 people fled from Hungary, most of them first to Austria. Switzerland took in about **14,000 refugees** without examining each individual case at length. The willingness of the population to help was very great: people donated clothes and money and offered flats. In protest against the crackdown, Switzerland, together with the Netherlands and Spain, stayed away from the **Summer Olympics in Melbourne**.

gewusst: 23 October is now a national holiday in Hungary in memory of the uprising.
The 1956 Summer Olympics in Melbourne took place only in November and December, because it is summer then in the Southern Hemisphere.

teile.einleitung: Neutrality means that a state does not take part in wars between other states and favours neither side. Switzerland has been neutral for over 200 years and is regarded worldwide as an example of it. Its perpetual neutrality was recognised by the European great powers in 1815.
wichtigste: On 20 November 1815 the great powers recognised the perpetual neutrality of Switzerland in the Second Peace of Paris.
At the same time they guaranteed the inviolability of Swiss territory.
The Geneva diplomat Charles Pictet de Rochemont worked especially hard for this recognition.
Perpetual neutrality means that a state remains neutral in all future wars.
Switzerland practises armed neutrality and must be able to defend its territory itself.
The law of neutrality was first set down comprehensively in 1907 in the Hague Convention.
Because of its neutrality Switzerland is not a member of a military alliance such as NATO.

abschnitte.text: A **neutral state** does not wage war against other states and does not support a party to a war with soldiers. It also may not make territory available to foreign troops. Switzerland has **perpetual neutrality**, which means it remains neutral in all future wars and not just in a single one. But being neutral does not mean having no opinion; Switzerland can still condemn wars.

For a long time the defeat at **Marignano in 1515** was seen as the beginning of Swiss neutrality, because the Confederates afterwards withdrew from the great wars of conquest. This view is strongly qualified by historians today. In the Thirty Years’ War from 1618 to 1648 the places largely stayed out all the same. At the end of 1813 the march of Allied troops through Switzerland showed that a merely declared neutrality without recognition was not respected.

After Napoleon’s fall the great powers reorganised Europe at the **Congress of Vienna**. The Geneva diplomat **Charles Pictet de Rochemont** worked in 1814 and 1815 to have neutrality recognised. During Napoleon’s Hundred Days the Confederate army under General Niklaus Franz von Bachmann briefly advanced into the Franche-Comté. On 20 November 1815 the great powers recognised in the Second Peace of Paris the perpetual neutrality and the inviolability of the territory, extended also to parts of Savoy.

A neutral Switzerland was in the interest of the great powers, for it separated France and Austria as a **buffer state**. Important Alpine passes such as the Simplon or the Gotthard were not to fall into the hands of a single power. The basis of the Confederation from 1815 to 1848 was the Federal Treaty. Later the law of neutrality was first set down comprehensively in the **Hague Convention** of 1907.

Switzerland practises **armed neutrality**: it must be able to defend its territory itself and therefore maintains an army. In both world wars the country was not attacked, although there was war all around. In 2002 Switzerland joined the UN, and since 2022 it has adopted sanctions against Russia, which triggered many discussions about neutrality. Because it is neutral, it often offers **good offices**, for example as a mediator or as host of peace talks in Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state does not take part in the wars of other states and does not help either side militarily.
A country between two great powers that separates them from each other.
Help from a neutral country so that parties in dispute talk to each other, for example as a mediator.
The agreement between the cantons that formed the basis of Switzerland from 1815 to 1848.

gewusst: As a so-called protecting power Switzerland represents the interests of other countries, for example those of the USA in Iran since 1980.
In 1815 neutrality even extended to parts of Savoy that did not belong to Switzerland at all.
In the Second World War General Henri Guisan became a symbol of Switzerland’s will to defend its neutrality.

teile.einleitung: Peter the Great was one of the best-known rulers of Russia. He wanted to modernise his huge country on the model of Western Europe and made Russia a great power.
wichtigste: Peter the Great lived from 1672 to 1725 and belonged to the ruling Romanov family.
From 1682 he was Tsar of Russia, at first still together with his half-brother.
On a great journey he learned shipbuilding in disguise in Holland.
He built up a Russian war fleet.
In 1703 he founded the city of Saint Petersburg.
In 1709 he defeated the Swedes at the Battle of Poltava.
Anyone who wanted to keep a beard had to pay a beard tax.

abschnitte.text: Peter was born in Moscow in 1672 and belonged to the **Romanov** family, which ruled Russia from 1613 to 1917. The rulers of Russia bore the title **Tsar**. Already in 1682, at about ten years old, Peter became Tsar, at first together with his half-brother Ivan. Later he ruled alone. Peter was about **2 metres** tall and so a real giant for his time.

In 1697 and 1698 Peter travelled with a large embassy through Western Europe. He travelled under a false name so as not to be treated as Tsar all the time. In Holland he worked in a **shipyard** and learned how to build ships. He also visited England. He brought many experts from the West to Russia, such as architects, officers and craftsmen.

A close friend and adviser of the young Tsar was **Franz Lefort** from **Geneva**. He lived in Moscow in a district where many foreigners lived. Lefort told Peter about life in Western Europe and helped him to build up a **war fleet**. Peter made him an admiral and the head of his great embassy to the West.

Peter wanted his country and his people to become more Western. Noble men were to shave and dress as in Western Europe. Anyone who absolutely wanted to keep his beard had to pay a **beard tax**. Peter also renewed the army, the administration and the schools. In 1703 he founded the new city of **Saint Petersburg** on the Baltic, which later became the capital.

In the **Great Northern War** Russia fought against Sweden for control of the Baltic. In 1709 Peter defeated the Swedish King Charles XII at the **Battle of Poltava** in what is now Ukraine. That was the turning point of the war. Afterwards Sweden lost its position as a great power. In 1721 Peter took the title of **Emperor**. He died in 1725.

gewusst: The hut in Holland in which Peter lived during his time at the shipyard can still be visited today.
Peter had himself trained in many crafts and is even said to have pulled teeth.

teile.einleitung: The Xinhai Revolution of 1911 ended the rule of the emperors in China. In 1912 the empire became the Republic of China.
wichtigste: The revolution began on 10 October 1911 with the Wuchang Uprising.
It is named after the year “Xinhai” in the traditional Chinese calendar.
On 1 January 1912 Sun Yat-sen became provisional president in Nanjing.
In February 1912 the six-year-old Emperor Puyi abdicated.
After that General Yuan Shikai took over the presidency.
In 1912 the Kuomintang party was formed.
Sun Yat-sen is regarded in China and Taiwan as the “Father of the Nation”.

abschnitte.text: Since 1644 the **Qing dynasty** had ruled China. Its emperors came from Manchuria. In the 19th century China grew weaker and weaker. Foreign powers forced rights in the country, and many people were dissatisfied. Revolutionaries wanted to overthrow the emperor and found a **republic**.

The most important revolutionary was **Sun Yat-sen**. For years he campaigned in **exile** for the overthrow of the monarchy. In 1905 he founded the revolutionary **Tongmenghui** in **Tokyo**, because many Chinese students lived in Japan at that time. He summed up his ideas in the **“Three Principles of the People”**: **nationalism, democracy and the people's livelihood**. These meant national independence, a government of the people and social justice.

On **10 October 1911** revolutionary-minded soldiers rose up in **Wuchang**, which is now part of Wuhan. Within a few weeks many provinces broke away from the Qing government. On **1 January 1912** Sun Yat-sen became provisional president of the **Republic of China** in **Nanjing**. Many men now cut off the long pigtail they had had to wear under the Qing.

In **February 1912** Emperor **Puyi** abdicated. He was only six years old. With that the more than 2,000 years of **imperial rule** in China came to an end. General **Yuan Shikai** had negotiated the abdication, because he controlled the strongest army in the north. In return he took over the presidency from Sun Yat-sen. Later he tried, without success, to make himself emperor.

In 1912 the **Kuomintang** party, also spelled Guomindang, emerged from the revolutionary movement. The name means National People's Party. Later, under **Chiang Kai-shek**, it ruled large parts of China. Sun Yat-sen is regarded today both in the People's Republic of China and in **Taiwan** as the “Father of the Nation”. In Taiwan 10 October is still the national holiday.

gewusst: In Taiwan 10 October is called “Double Ten”, because it is the tenth day of the tenth month.
There is the famous film “The Last Emperor” about the life of Puyi.

teile.einleitung: The Spanish flu was a worldwide wave of influenza in the years 1918 to 1920. It was one of the worst pandemics in history. In Switzerland too many people fell ill, and tens of thousands died.
wichtigste: The name comes from the fact that the Spanish press reported on it without censorship.
It was caused by an influenza A virus of type H1N1.
The second wave in the autumn of 1918 was the deadliest.
An unusually large number of young adults aged 20 to 40 died.
In Switzerland around 24,500 people died from July 1918 to June 1919.
Cantons closed schools and banned gatherings.

abschnitte.text: The flu did not begin in Spain. During the First World War the states at war censored their newspapers. **Neutral Spain** did not do this. That is why people read about the disease mainly from Spain. So it seemed especially widespread there, and it got the name **Spanish flu**.

A **pandemic** is a disease that spreads across the whole world. The Spanish flu was caused by an **influenza A virus of type H1N1**. Researchers were able to reconstruct the virus much later from tissue samples of victims. At that time viruses were hardly known, and there were neither vaccines nor antibiotics.

The first wave in the spring of 1918 was mostly mild. In the autumn of 1918 the virus returned much more dangerous. This **second wave** was the deadliest. Unusual was whom it hit: normally it is mainly old people and small children who die of flu. In 1918 particularly many **young adults** between 20 and 40 died.

In Switzerland around 2 million people fell ill. According to the Historical Dictionary of Switzerland **24,449 people** died between July 1918 and June 1919, about 0.6 per cent of the population. Many **cantons** closed schools, cinemas and churches and banned events. In this way people wanted to slow the infection.

In November 1918 the **General Strike** took place in Switzerland. Workers went on strike for better living conditions. The Federal Council deployed soldiers to keep order. Many of them fell ill with flu, and hundreds died. The middle class and the working class blamed each other for this.

gewusst: Because so many young adults died in 1918, the death curve has an unusual W shape.
Worldwide more people died of the Spanish flu than in the whole First World War.

teile.einleitung: Raphael was one of the most famous painters of the Italian Renaissance. His pictures are known for their harmony, their clear forms and their soft colours.
wichtigste: Raphael was born in 1483 in Urbino.
His father was a painter.
For the Pope he painted magnificent rooms in the Vatican.
His famous mural “The School of Athens” shows many scholars of the ancient Greeks.
He very often painted Mary with the child.
He was only 37 years old when he died.
With Leonardo and Michelangelo he is counted among the greatest painters of the High Renaissance.

abschnitte.text: Raphael’s real name was **Raffaello Santi**, and he was born in 1483 in **Urbino** in central Italy. His father **Giovanni Santi** was a **painter** and poet at the court of Urbino. So Raphael got to know painting even as a child. His parents died early. Later he worked with the well-known painter **Perugino** and learned a great deal from him.

Raphael painted **Mary with the child** especially often, and such pictures are called **Madonnas**. They look calm, friendly and harmonious. A famous example is the **“Sistine Madonna”**, which hangs today in Dresden. At the very bottom of this picture one sees **two little angels** who look thoughtfully upwards. These two angels are so popular that today they are found on postcards, mugs and much else.

In 1508 Raphael came to Rome. There, on the commission of the **Pope**, he painted magnificent rooms in the Vatican, which today are called the **Raphael Rooms**. The best-known mural is **“The School of Athens”**. It shows many scholars of the ancient Greeks, in the middle the philosophers Plato and Aristotle. Raphael painted the hall so that thanks to **perspective** it looks deep and spacious.

Raphael was very successful and ran a large workshop with many assistants. He also worked as an architect on **St Peter’s Basilica** in Rome. In 1520 he died unexpectedly, at only **37 years old**. He was buried in the Pantheon in Rome. Together with **Leonardo da Vinci** and **Michelangelo** he is counted among the greatest painters of the **High Renaissance**.

gewusst: Raphael’s tomb in the Pantheon in Rome can still be visited today.
Michelangelo was working in the Vatican at the same time as Raphael, on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

teile.einleitung: A wig is artificial hair that one wears on the head. In the 17th and 18th centuries large wigs were very fashionable among distinguished people in Europe. They showed how rich and important someone was.
wichtigste: At the court of Louis XIV distinguished men wore large curled wigs.
A large, expensive wig showed that someone was rich and distinguished.
Wigs were often made white with powder.
In the 18th century the wigmaker made the wigs.
After the French Revolution the large wigs went out of fashion.

abschnitte.text: In the 17th century King **Louis XIV** ruled in France. His court at Versailles set the fashion throughout Europe. Distinguished men there wore **large curled wigs** whose curls fell below the shoulders. Soon nobles and rich citizens in other countries also wanted to wear such wigs. A large, expensive wig showed everyone that someone was **rich and distinguished**.

Many wigs were dusted with **powder** so that they looked **white** or grey. The powder was usually made of starch or fine flour. When powdering, people held a cone in front of the face so that the dust did not get into the eyes and nose. In the 18th century wigs became smaller, often with a pigtail at the back of the neck.

Wigs were made by a craftsman of their own, the **wigmaker**. He used real human hair, horsehair or goat hair. The hairs were knotted one by one or in small tufts on to a net. That was a lot of work, and so good wigs were expensive. The wigmaker also looked after, curled and powdered the wigs regularly.

After the **French Revolution** the large wigs went out of fashion. Today wigs are worn above all in the **theatre**, in films or at carnival. People who have lost their hair because of an illness also sometimes wear a wig. In Britain some judges and barristers still wear traditional white wigs in court today.

gewusst: Even in ancient Egypt distinguished people wore wigs.
In many pictures the composer Johann Sebastian Bach also wears a wig.

teile.einleitung: Voltaire was a French writer and philosopher and one of the most famous thinkers of the Enlightenment. With a sharp pen he fought against injustice, superstition and religious intolerance. He spent his last years very close to the Swiss border near Geneva.
wichtigste: Voltaire was really called François-Marie Arouet and lived from 1694 to 1778.
After his stay in England he wrote the “Philosophical Letters”.
In his novel “Candide” of 1759 he mocks the belief that we live in the best of all possible worlds.
From 1750 to 1753 he lived as a chamberlain at the court of Frederick II of Prussia.
He spent most of the last 20 years of his life in Ferney near Geneva.
The execution of the Protestant Jean Calas moved him in 1763 to write his “Treatise on Tolerance”.
The famous quotation about freedom of speech is not by him but by his biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall.

abschnitte.text: Voltaire was born in Paris in 1694 as **François-Marie Arouet**. He was the son of a notary and attended a Jesuit school. Even as a young man he wrote mocking verses about the powerful and in 1717 ended up for eleven months in the **Bastille**, the notorious prison of Paris. After that he called himself Voltaire and became known for his plays. He wrote tragedies, poems, novels, history books and thousands of letters.

After a quarrel with a nobleman Voltaire had to go to **England** in 1726 and stayed until 1728. There he admired the freedom of the press, the tolerance between religions and the science of Isaac Newton. He wrote down his impressions in the **Philosophical Letters**, which appeared in 1734. In France the book was banned and publicly burned because it indirectly criticised conditions there.

abschnitte.titel: At the court of Frederick the Great
abschnitte.text: The Prussian king **Frederick II** admired Voltaire and brought him to his court in Potsdam. From 1750 to 1753 Voltaire lived there as a chamberlain and helped the king with his French texts. But the two had strong personalities and fell out. Voltaire left Prussia in anger, but later was in touch with Frederick by letter again.

From 1755 Voltaire lived first in Geneva on the country estate of Les Délices and then bought a château in **Ferney** on French soil just across the border. That way, if he ran into trouble with France, he could quickly flee to Switzerland and vice versa. He developed the village, had houses built and supported watchmakers. Visitors from all over Europe made pilgrimages to the “Patriarch of Ferney”. In his honour the village is now called **Ferney-Voltaire**.

abschnitte.titel: Candide and the fight for tolerance
abschnitte.text: The Lisbon earthquake of 1755, with tens of thousands of dead, made Voltaire doubt the belief in a good world order. In his novel **Candide** the young hero experiences one disaster after another while his teacher claims that everything is for the best. In the end Candide says: “We must cultivate our garden.” When the Protestant Jean Calas was wrongly executed in 1762, Voltaire fought for years for his honour and wrote the **Treatise on Tolerance**. The Calas family was rehabilitated in 1765.

Voltaire is regarded as a champion of **freedom of speech**, freedom of religion and fair trials. He attacked above all the power of the Church, but himself believed in a God as creator. He died on 30 May 1778 in Paris, shortly after a triumphant reception there. In 1791, during the French Revolution, his remains were ceremonially transferred to the **Panthéon**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement in the 18th century that relied on reason, knowledge and freedom instead of blind obedience.
Accepting other opinions and religions, even if you do not share them.
A text that exposes problems with mockery and exaggeration.
A pen name that someone uses instead of their real name.

gewusst: Voltaire is said to have drunk many cups of coffee a day, and some sources speak of up to 50.
Over the course of his life Voltaire wrote more than 20,000 letters.
Voltaire became rich through a clever share in a lottery and was therefore financially independent.

teile.einleitung: A games console is a device with which one plays video games. Some are connected at home to the television, others are carried in the hand. Since the 1970s there have been ever newer and better consoles.
wichtigste: A games console is a device just for video games.
At home it is usually connected to the television.
The first console for home use was the Magnavox Odyssey of 1972.
Nintendo brought out the Game Boy in 1989.
The first PlayStation from Sony appeared in 1994.

abschnitte.text: A **games console** is a small computer that is built mainly for playing. It is controlled with a **controller**, a device with buttons and sticks. The game appears on a screen. At home one usually uses the **television** for this. There are also **handheld consoles** with a built-in screen for on the move.

The first games console for home use was the **Magnavox Odyssey**. It came out in 1972 in the USA. It showed only simple dots and lines on the television. So that one could imagine the playing field better, one laid coloured sheets on the screen. There was no sound yet.

In 1989 the Japanese firm **Nintendo** brought out the **Game Boy**. It was a small console for on the move with game cartridges. Its screen showed only shades of grey. Even so it became very popular and sold in the millions worldwide. The game Tetris, which one could play on the Game Boy, became very well known.

The Japanese firm **Sony** brought out the first **PlayStation** in 1994. Its games were stored on CDs. Much more fitted on them than on cartridges, for example three-dimensional worlds and music. Since then there have been several new models. Other firms also build consoles.

Video games can be fun and train reaction time. Many games are also played together with friends. On game packaging in Switzerland and in Europe **age ratings** show from what age a game is suitable. It is important to take enough breaks and also to move around outdoors.

gewusst: With the Magnavox Odyssey one laid coloured sheets on the television in order to see the playing field.
The Game Boy showed no colours, only shades of grey, and was a huge success all the same.

t1gjt3mq.t: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child

teile.einleitung: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child is a treaty of the United Nations that sets out the rights of all children in the world. It was adopted in 1989 and has also applied in Switzerland since 1997.
wichtigste: The UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child on 20 November 1989.
Every person under 18 counts as a child.
The Convention has applied in Switzerland since 1997.
Every child has a right to education, health and protection.
Play, rest and leisure are expressly children's rights.
Every child has the right to a name and a nationality.
UNICEF is the UN children's fund and works for children's rights.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War the wish grew to protect children in a special way. On **20 November 1989** the General Assembly of the **UN** adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child. It came into force a year later. Almost all states in the world have since accepted it. No other human rights treaty has so many members.

According to the Convention, every person **under 18** is a child. The same rights apply to all children, no matter where they come from, what language they speak or whether they are poor or rich. This is called **non-discrimination**. Another principle is called the **best interests of the child**: in every decision that affects children, the first question should be what is good for the child. Children may also give their opinion, and they should be listened to.

Every child has the **right to education**, that is, the right to go to school. It has a right to **health**, to enough food and to a safe home. **Play, rest and leisure** are also part of it. Straight after birth every child should be given a **name** and be officially registered. Children should also be protected from violence and from hard labour.

Switzerland joined the Convention in **1997**. Since then it has had to make sure that children's rights are respected here too. The Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities are responsible for this, for example in schools, health and protection. At regular intervals Switzerland reports to a **UN committee** on how it puts children's rights into practice. The committee then makes recommendations.

**UNICEF** is the UN children's fund. It was founded in 1946, shortly after the Second World War. UNICEF helps children all over the world, for example with clean water, vaccinations, food and schools. It also makes people aware of the rights children have. In many countries, including Switzerland, there are separate UNICEF organisations for this.

gewusst: Every year 20 November is World Children's Day, the international day of children's rights.
The Convention on the Rights of the Child is the UN human rights treaty that most states have accepted.

teile.einleitung: The Salt March was a non-violent protest by Mahatma Gandhi against British rule in India. In 1930 he walked with followers to the sea in order to make salt there himself and so break an unjust law.
wichtigste: Gandhi set out on the Salt March in 1930 with 78 followers.
The route was about 385 km long and led to the sea.
The British had a monopoly on salt and levied a salt tax.
On the beach Gandhi picked up salt and so broke the British law.
In May 1930 about 2,500 volunteers wanted to occupy the Dharasana saltworks without violence.
The campaign ended in 1931 with the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.

abschnitte.text: India was then ruled by **Britain**. The British had a **monopoly** on salt. That means only they were allowed to make and sell salt, and they levied a **salt tax** on it. Every person needs salt to live, even the poorest. Gandhi therefore chose salt as a sign. Everyone understood that this law was unjust.

On **12 March 1930** **Mahatma Gandhi** set out with **78 followers** from his ashram near Ahmedabad. An ashram is a kind of community of living. They walked about **385 kilometres** to the coastal place of **Dandi** on the Arabian Sea. Along the way more and more people joined, and newspapers all over the world reported. On 6 April 1930 **Gandhi picked up salt on the beach**. In doing so he deliberately and publicly broke the British law.

Gandhi’s method is called **civil disobedience**. One breaks an unjust law openly and without violence and accepts the punishment for it. After the Salt March people all over India made salt themselves. Tens of thousands were arrested, Gandhi himself too. In May 1930 about **2,500 volunteers** wanted to occupy the **Dharasana** saltworks without violence. The police acted harshly against them, but the volunteers did not fight back.

In 1931 Gandhi and the British Viceroy **Lord Irwin** reached agreement in the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact**. The campaign of civil disobedience was ended, and many prisoners were released. Gandhi then travelled to a conference in London. On the way back at the end of 1931 he visited **Switzerland** and in Villeneuve on Lake Geneva met the writer Romain Rolland. India only became independent in 1947.

gewusst: The American magazine “Time” chose Gandhi as Man of the Year for 1930 after the Salt March.
The Salt March lasted 24 days.

teile.einleitung: During the First World War the government of the Ottoman Empire had a large part of the Armenian population deported and killed. These crimes are called the Armenian genocide.
wichtigste: The Armenian genocide took place from 1915, during the First World War.
On 24 April 1915 hundreds of Armenian intellectuals were arrested in Constantinople.
The Ottoman Empire was then ruled by the Committee of Union and Progress, the Young Turks.
Interior Minister Talât Pasha is regarded as chiefly responsible for the deportations.
Many death marches led into the Syrian desert to Deir ez-Zor.
The Swiss National Council recognised the genocide in 2003.
Turkey still denies today that it was a genocide.

abschnitte.titel: The Armenians in the Ottoman Empire
abschnitte.text: The **Armenians** are a people with a long history and their own language and script. Most of them were Christians. Many lived in the east of the **Ottoman Empire**, the predecessor of present-day Turkey. Since 1913 the **Committee of Union and Progress**, also called the **Young Turks**, had ruled there like a dictatorship. In the First World War the Ottoman Empire fought on the side of Germany.

On **24 April 1915** the government in **Constantinople**, today's Istanbul, had hundreds of Armenian politicians, clergy and scholars arrested. Most of them were murdered. This day is now observed as a **day of remembrance** for the genocide. Soon afterwards the **deportations** began, that is, the forced resettlement of the Armenian population. Interior Minister **Talât Pasha** ordered them.

Whole families had to leave their homes and cover long distances on foot. Many marches led into the **Syrian desert**, for example to the area around **Deir ez-Zor**. On the way and in the camps, very many people died of hunger, thirst, disease and violence. Estimates of the death toll range from several hundred thousand to over a million people. Some Armenians were able to save themselves, for example on **Musa Dagh**.

In 1944 the lawyer **Raphael Lemkin** coined the term **genocide**. He was also thinking of the fate of the Armenians. Lemkin afterwards campaigned for the UN **Genocide Convention** of 1948. As early as 1933 the writer **Franz Werfel** made the events known to a wide public with his novel “The Forty Days of Musa Dagh”.

Many states and parliaments have recognised the crimes as genocide. In Switzerland the cantons of **Vaud** and **Geneva** were the first to do so. In December 2003 the **National Council** also adopted a corresponding postulate. **Turkey** still denies today that it was a planned genocide. It speaks of victims on all sides during the war. The matter is still debated internationally.

gewusst: Raphael Lemkin formed the word “genocide” from the Greek “genos” for people and the Latin “caedere” for to kill.
Talât Pasha was shot in Berlin in 1921 by an Armenian survivor.

teile.einleitung: A World's Fair is a large international exhibition at which countries show their inventions, goods and ideas. The first took place in London in 1851.
wichtigste: The first World's Fair was in 1851 in Hyde Park in London.
Its building of glass and iron was called the Crystal Palace.
At World's Fairs countries showed new inventions and goods.
In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell showed his telephone in Philadelphia.
In 1893 Chicago had the first big Ferris wheel.
Since the World's Fair of 1958 the Atomium has stood in Brussels.
In 2025 a World's Fair took place in Osaka in Japan, with a Swiss pavilion.

abschnitte.text: The first World's Fair took place in **1851** in **Hyde Park** in London. Prince Albert, the husband of Queen Victoria, supported the idea. The gardener **Joseph Paxton** designed a huge building of **glass and iron**. It looked like a large greenhouse and was called the **Crystal Palace**. Many countries showed machines, raw materials and crafts there. Millions of people came to marvel.

At World's Fairs countries wanted to show what new things they could do. In 1876 in **Philadelphia**, **Alexander Graham Bell** showed his **telephone**. Visitors could hear a voice from far away. Machines, lamps and later cars were also demonstrated. This was how many people first heard of new technologies.

Some World's Fairs left behind famous buildings. In **Paris** the **Eiffel Tower** was built in 1889. In 1893 **George Ferris** built a large **Ferris wheel** in **Chicago**, about 80 metres high. Since 1958 the **Atomium** has stood in **Brussels**. It looks like an iron crystal magnified enormously, with nine spheres, and is now a museum.

Switzerland has long taken part in World's Fairs and builds its own **pavilions** for them. There it shows, for example, watches, technology, landscapes and ideas. At Expo 2000 in Hanover there was a pavilion of stacked wooden beams by the architect **Peter Zumthor**. Switzerland was also at **Expo 2025** in **Osaka** in Japan. Do not confuse them: the Swiss **national exhibitions** such as Expo.02 are national exhibitions.

World's Fairs today are often simply called **Expo**. An organisation based in Paris decides where they take place. Each Expo has a theme, such as food, the environment or the future of society. The countries try to stand out with special buildings and exhibitions. For the host city an Expo is a big task.

gewusst: After the exhibition the Crystal Palace was taken down, re-erected in another part of London and burned down in 1936.
The Eiffel Tower was actually supposed to be taken down again after a few years.

teile.einleitung: The Middle East conflict is a long-lasting dispute between Israel and the Palestinians as well as several Arab states. It is about land, borders, security and the city of Jerusalem. Both sides have their own views of history, and the conflict is still unresolved today.
wichtigste: Theodor Herzl published the work “The Jewish State” in 1896.
In 1917 Britain supported a “national home” for the Jewish people in the Balfour Declaration.
In 1947 the UN General Assembly decided on a partition plan for Palestine with Resolution 181.
Palestinians call the flight and expulsion in the war of 1948 the “Nakba”.
In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank, the Gaza Strip and East Jerusalem.
In 1979 Egypt was the first Arab state to make peace with Israel.
In 1993 Rabin and Arafat sealed the Oslo Accords.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 19th century Jews were persecuted in many countries of Europe. The journalist **Theodor Herzl** published the work **“The Jewish State”** in 1896. In it he demanded a state of their own for the Jewish people. This movement is called **Zionism**. In 1897 the first Zionist Congress took place in **Basel**. In Palestine at that time mainly Arabs lived, and many Jews immigrated little by little.

After the First World War **Britain** administered Palestine. As early as 1917 it had supported a “national home” for the Jewish people in the **Balfour Declaration**. Tensions arose between Jews and Arabs. After the Second World War and the Holocaust the UN General Assembly decided on **Resolution 181** in 1947. It provided for dividing the land into a Jewish and an Arab state.

abschnitte.titel: Founding of the state and wars
abschnitte.text: In 1948 the state of **Israel** was founded. A war with the neighbouring states followed. Around 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, which they call the **Nakba**, “catastrophe”. In the **Six-Day War** of 1967 Israel occupied the **West Bank**, the **Gaza Strip** and **East Jerusalem**. In October 1973 **Egypt** and **Syria** attacked Israel by surprise on the holiday of Yom Kippur.

In 1979 **Egypt** was the first Arab state to conclude a **peace treaty** with Israel. In 1993 Israel and the Palestinians agreed in the **Oslo Accords** on first steps towards a solution. The Israeli prime minister **Yitzhak Rabin** and Palestinian leader **Yasser Arafat** shook hands in front of the White House to mark it. In 1995 Rabin was murdered by an Israeli opponent of the agreement. A lasting peace has not come about so far.

To this day there is violence, attacks and war again and again. In October 2023, after an attack by Hamas on Israel, a severe war began in the Gaza Strip. Many people on both sides lost their lives. People often talk of a **two-state solution**, that is, a state of Israel and a state of Palestine side by side. Switzerland supports peace talks, and the Red Cross from Geneva helps people in the region.

gewusst: Jerusalem is a holy city for Jews, Christians and Muslims.
Rabin and Arafat received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 together with Shimon Peres.

teile.einleitung: Nicholas II was the last Tsar of Russia. He reigned from 1894 to 1917 and belonged to the Romanov family. In the February Revolution of 1917 he had to abdicate, and a year later he and his family were killed.
wichtigste: Nicholas II was the last Tsar of Russia.
The British King George V was his cousin.
On Bloody Sunday in St Petersburg in 1905 soldiers shot at peaceful demonstrators.
His son Alexei suffered from haemophilia.
The wandering preacher Grigori Rasputin had great influence at court.
In the February Revolution of 1917 Nicholas had to abdicate.
In 1918 the Tsar’s family was murdered in Yekaterinburg.

abschnitte.text: Nicholas was born in 1868 and was the eldest son of Tsar Alexander III. In 1894 he himself became **Tsar**, that is, emperor of Russia. He belonged to the **Romanov** family, which had ruled for over 280 years. Nicholas wanted to rule alone, without a parliament. He was related to many of the royal houses of Europe. The British King **George V** was his cousin, and the two even looked very alike.

Many workers and peasants in Russia were very poor. In January 1905 thousands of people walked peacefully in **Saint Petersburg** to the Winter Palace to ask the Tsar for help. Soldiers shot at the people and many died. This day is called **Bloody Sunday**. After that there was unrest throughout the country. Nicholas had to allow a parliament, the **Duma**, but kept a great deal of power.

Nicholas and his wife Alexandra had four daughters and one son, **Alexei**. The heir to the throne suffered from **haemophilia**. In this illness bleeding is hard to stop. The wandering preacher **Grigori Rasputin** seemed able to help Alexei. That is why he gained great **influence** at court. Many people in Russia distrusted him. At the end of 1916 Rasputin was killed by noblemen.

In the **First World War** Russia suffered heavy defeats, and in the cities bread was short. In February 1917 there were strikes and uprisings in Petrograd. In this **February Revolution** Nicholas had to **abdicate**. The family was taken prisoner. After the October Revolution the Bolsheviks brought them to **Yekaterinburg** in the Urals. There Nicholas, his wife and his children were murdered in July 1918.

gewusst: In 2000 the Russian Orthodox Church declared Nicholas II and his family saints.
Nicholas and George V had mothers who were sisters from Denmark.

teile.einleitung: A society of estates is a society in which every person belongs from birth to a particular estate. Rights, duties, taxes and even clothing depended on it. Best known is the order of estates in France before the Revolution of 1789, the Ancien Régime.
wichtigste: In the society of estates birth decided what place a person had in society.
The First Estate was formed by the clergy, that is, the churchmen.
The Second Estate was formed by the nobility, the Third Estate by all other people.
Before 1789 the Third Estate made up over 95 per cent of the population of France.
Clergy and nobility were largely exempt from the most important direct tax.
About four fifths of the French lived as peasants and had to give the tithe to the Church.
The political and social order of France before 1789 is called the Ancien Régime.
With the French Revolution the society of estates was abolished.

abschnitte.titel: What is a society of estates?
abschnitte.text: Already in the Middle Ages people were divided into three groups: some pray, others fight, the third work. People also spoke of the **estate of teaching**, the **estate of defence** and the **estate of feeding**. This order was regarded as willed by God and hardly changeable. Anyone born a peasant’s child mostly remained a peasant all his life.

In 18th-century France the **clergy** formed the First Estate, that is bishops, abbots, monks and priests. The Second Estate was formed by the **nobility**. The old warrior nobility was called Noblesse d’épée, the nobility that had gained its rank through high offices in justice and administration was called **Noblesse de robe**. To the Third Estate belonged everyone else, from the rich merchant to the poor day labourer.

Clergy and nobility had many **privileges**, that is, special rights. They were largely exempt from the most important direct tax, the taille. The peasants, by contrast, had to pay taxes to the king, dues to their landlord and the **tithe** to the Church. A peasant often had to hand over a large part of his harvest in this way. Many people felt this to be very unjust.

At the beginning of 1789 the clergyman **Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès** wrote the pamphlet “What Is the Third Estate?”. His answer was: Everything. Until then, however, it had been nothing politically. The pamphlet was read throughout France and encouraged many people to demand rights for the Third Estate.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the order of estates
abschnitte.text: In May 1789 the **Estates General** met in Versailles, an assembly of representatives of all three estates. The Third Estate demanded voting by head instead of by estate, because otherwise it could always be outvoted by clergy and nobility. On 17 June 1789 its deputies declared themselves the **National Assembly**. In the night of 4 August 1789 the privileges of nobility and clergy were abolished.

In the Old Confederacy too people were not equal. In cities such as Bern a few rich families ruled, the **patriciate**. Many areas were subject territories without any political say. Only the Helvetic Republic of 1798 brought equality before the law.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group in society to which one belonged by birth.
A special right that only certain people have.
All the churchmen of the Church, for example priests and bishops.
A levy of about a tenth of the harvest paid to the Church.
French for “old rule”, the order of France before 1789.

gewusst: At the Estates General of 1789 the deputies of the estates had to wear different clothing.
The First and Second Estates together made up only about two to three per cent of the population in France.
Sieyès, who defended the Third Estate, as a clergyman actually belonged to the First Estate himself.

teile.einleitung: A nautical chart is a map for shipping. It shows coasts, islands, harbours and dangerous places in the sea. For centuries nautical charts have helped sailors to reach their destination safely.
wichtigste: A nautical chart shows coasts and seas.
On it islands, harbours, shallows and rocks are drawn in.
Old nautical charts were often inaccurate, because many areas were still unknown.
Explorers drew in new coasts and islands on their journeys.
The compass rose is a star that shows the points of the compass.
Over time the charts became more and more accurate.

abschnitte.titel: What is on a nautical chart
abschnitte.text: A nautical chart shows above all the sea and the **coast**. On it one can see islands, harbours and lighthouses. Especially important are dangerous places such as **shallows**, that is, places with little water, and rocks beneath the surface. Often the depth of the water is also given. In this way the captain can choose a safe route.

On many old nautical charts a **compass rose** is painted. It is a star with points and shows north, south, east and west. Some compass roses were splendidly decorated. Together with the **compass** sailors could determine their direction. From the compass rose lines often ran across the whole chart.

In the past many parts of the world were still unknown. Some coasts no one had yet seen, so they were missing or drawn wrongly. Measuring distances at sea was also difficult. Empty areas were sometimes decorated with pictures of sea monsters. Such charts were therefore only a rough guide.

When **explorers** reached a new land they drew its coast. They brought these drawings home, where **cartographers**, that is, map makers, produced new charts. So the nautical charts got better journey by journey. Anyone who owned good charts had a great advantage in trade. That is why some countries even kept their charts secret.

Today the seas are measured accurately with sound soundings and satellites. Many ships use **electronic charts** on screens. Even so, paper nautical charts continue to exist as a safeguard. On large Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance or Lake Geneva too, ships use charts with depth information.

gewusst: On some old nautical charts sea monsters were painted in empty areas of the sea.
Nautical charts were once considered so valuable that some countries treated them like a state secret.

teile.einleitung: Otto von Bismarck was one of the most important politicians of the 19th century. He led Prussia and in 1871 founded the German Empire. As its first Chancellor he shaped Germany for almost twenty years.
wichtigste: Bismarck became Minister President of Prussia in 1862.
In a speech he said that the great questions would be decided by “iron and blood”.
In 1871 the German Empire came into being under his leadership.
He was called the “Iron Chancellor”.
In the 1870s he quarrelled with the Catholic Church, in what is called the culture struggle.
In 1878 he introduced a law against the Social Democrats.
In 1890 Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed him.

abschnitte.text: Otto von Bismarck was born in 1815 as the son of a noble family. In 1862 he became **Minister President** of **Prussia**, then one of the most powerful German states. In the same year he gave a famous speech. In it he said that the great questions of the time would not be decided by speeches, but **by iron and blood**. By that he meant weapons and war.

At that time there was not yet a united Germany, but many individual states. Bismarck wanted to unite them under the leadership of Prussia. After three wars, the last against France in 1870 and 1871, he succeeded. On 18 January 1871 the **German Empire** was proclaimed in the Palace of Versailles near Paris. The Prussian king became Kaiser Wilhelm I, and Bismarck became **Chancellor of the Empire**.

abschnitte.titel: The culture struggle and the Socialist Law
abschnitte.text: Bismarck did not want other powers to influence the state. In the 1870s he therefore quarrelled with the **Catholic Church**. This dispute is called the **culture struggle**. Since that time, for example, marriage before a registry office has been compulsory. In 1878 he had a law passed against the **Social Democrats**, the **Socialist Law**. It banned the clubs and newspapers of the labour movement.

At the same time Bismarck wanted to win the workers over to the state. So in the 1880s he introduced the first state **social insurance**: health insurance, accident insurance and insurance for old age and disability. Many countries later took over this idea. In Switzerland the AVS has existed since 1948.

Because of his toughness and endurance Bismarck was called the **Iron Chancellor**. In 1888 the young **Wilhelm II** became Kaiser. He wanted to rule himself and often held a different opinion from Bismarck. In 1890 he dismissed him. Bismarck spent his last years on his estate at **Friedrichsruh** near Hamburg. There he died in 1898.

gewusst: A British newspaper showed Bismarck’s dismissal in a drawing with the title “Dropping the Pilot”.
In Germany many lookout towers were built in Bismarck’s honour, which are called Bismarck towers.

teile.einleitung: Modern warfare means the way in which war has been waged since the First World War with machines, industry and new technology. In the First World War from 1914 to 1918 poison gas, tanks, submarines and aircraft were used on a large scale for the first time. This made war much more destructive than all wars before.
wichtigste: The First World War is seen as the first industrialised war.
On 22 April 1915 the German army used chlorine gas on a large scale for the first time, at Ypres.
The chemist Fritz Haber was a major driver of gas warfare.
On 15 September 1916 tanks were used for the first time on the Somme.
From 1 February 1917 Germany waged unrestricted submarine warfare.
At the start of the war aircraft were used mainly for reconnaissance.
“Big Bertha” was a heavy 42 cm mortar made by the firm Krupp.

abschnitte.text: In the First World War it was no longer only soldiers who decided things, but the **mass production** of weapons and ammunition. Factories made millions of shells, and women also worked in the armaments plants. The whole of society was mobilised for the war. That is why people speak of an **industrialised war**.

On the Western Front in France and Belgium the armies dug themselves into long **trenches** from the end of 1914. Machine guns and artillery made attacks across open ground almost impossible. In battles such as at Verdun or on the Somme in 1916 hundreds of thousands died without the front moving much. Giant guns such as **Big Bertha**, a 42 cm mortar from Krupp, shelled fortresses.

On 22 April 1915 the German army used chlorine gas on a large scale for the first time at **Ypres** in Belgium. The chemist **Fritz Haber** was a major driver of this development. Soon all sides used poison gas, and soldiers had to wear gas masks. After the war chemical warfare was banned in 1925 in the **Geneva Protocol**.

On 15 September 1916 the British used tanks for the first time on the **Somme**, to get across the trenches. The first tanks were slow and often broke down, but were quickly improved. Aircraft were used at first mainly for **reconnaissance** over enemy positions. Soon fighters and bombers were added, and airships even dropped bombs on London.

German **submarines** attacked ships in order to cut Britain off from supplies. In 1915 a German submarine sank the British passenger ship **Lusitania**, and many Americans died too. From 1 February 1917 Germany waged unrestricted submarine warfare and also sank neutral merchant ships without warning. Together with the **Zimmermann Telegram**, in which Germany proposed to Mexico an alliance against the USA with the prospect of Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, this led to the entry of the USA into the war in April 1917.

The First World War claimed about 17 million dead, soldiers and civilians together. Switzerland remained neutral, but under General Ulrich Wille guarded its borders with the army. Many of the new weapons were developed further in the Second World War, especially tanks and bomber aircraft. **International law** has since tried, with treaties such as the Geneva Conventions, to protect the civilian population.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, deep ditch in which soldiers sought protection from shelling.
Large guns that fire shells over long distances.
Scouting out where the enemy is and what he is planning.
A warship that can travel under water.
Rules that apply between states, in war too.

gewusst: The name “tank” for armoured vehicles arose because the British disguised the secret vehicles as water tanks.
Fritz Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918, however, for the production of ammonia and not for the poison gas.
Almost 1,200 people died when the Lusitania sank.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman. In his laboratory at Menlo Park many inventions arose. He contributed a great deal to bringing electric light and electricity into homes.
wichtigste: Edison worked as a telegraph operator as a young man.
From his youth he heard very badly.
His famous laboratory stood at Menlo Park in New Jersey.
In 1882 he opened a power station on Pearl Street in New York.
In the War of the Currents he backed direct current, but alternating current won through.
His firm developed the Kinetoscope at the beginning of the 1890s.

abschnitte.text: As a teenager Thomas Alva Edison worked in various places as a **telegraph operator**. So he transmitted messages with the telegraph. From his youth he **heard very badly**, he was almost deaf. Edison said that it helped him to concentrate better. His first invention was an electric vote-counting machine.

At **Menlo Park** in New Jersey Edison ran a large **inventor’s laboratory**. There he worked together with many assistants. Here many of his inventions arose, for example an improved **light bulb** and the phonograph, with which one could record and play back sounds. That is why Edison was called the “Wizard of Menlo Park”.

In 1882 Edison opened a **power station** on **Pearl Street** in New York. It supplied houses and offices in Manhattan with electricity. It was one of the first public power stations in the world. So people could use electric light instead of gas or candles.

Edison backed **direct current**. His competitors George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla backed **alternating current**. The dispute between them is called the **War of the Currents**. Alternating current could be transmitted more easily over long distances. In the end it won through for the power grids, and in Switzerland too alternating current comes from the socket.

At the beginning of the 1890s Edison’s firm developed the **Kinetoscope**. In it a person looked through a peephole at a moving strip of film. It was a forerunner of the cinema. Also well known is Edison’s saying that genius is one per cent **inspiration** and 99 per cent **perspiration**, that is, sweat. By that he meant that hard work is more important than a good idea.

gewusst: Edison was almost deaf and said that it helped him to concentrate.
In the course of his life Edison applied for over a thousand patents.

teile.einleitung: In the years 1848 and 1849 revolutions broke out in many countries of Europe. People demanded freedom, a say in government and in many areas a nation state of their own.
wichtigste: The revolutions of 1848 are also called the “Spring of Nations”.
In France King Louis-Philippe was overthrown in February 1848.
In Austria the State Chancellor Metternich had to resign and flee in March 1848.
In the German states they are called the March Revolution.
From May 1848 the Frankfurt National Assembly met in St Paul’s Church.
In 1849 the Prussian King Frederick William IV refused the imperial crown.
In 1848 Switzerland became a federal state with a new Federal Constitution.

abschnitte.text: The revolutions began in **February 1848** in France. In Paris many people took to the streets and put up barricades. King **Louis-Philippe** was overthrown and fled to England. France became a **republic** again. In December 1848 the men elected **Louis Napoleon Bonaparte**, a nephew of Napoleon, as president. A few years later he made himself emperor.

The news from Paris spread quickly. In Austria, Hungary, Italy and the German states too there were uprisings. This time is therefore called the **Spring of Nations**. In Vienna the powerful State Chancellor **Klemens von Metternich** had to resign and flee in March 1848. For decades he had suppressed all movements for freedom.

In the German states people speak of the **March Revolution**, because it broke out in March 1848. People wanted a united Germany with a constitution. From May 1848 the **National Assembly** met in Frankfurt am Main in **St Paul’s Church**. The deputies worked out a constitution. The revolutionaries wore the colours **black, red and gold**, which are today the colours of the German flag.

In 1849 the National Assembly offered the German imperial crown to the Prussian King **Frederick William IV**. He **refused**, because he did not want to receive his power from an elected parliament. After that the princes put down the revolution with soldiers. Many revolutionaries had to flee, some to Switzerland or to America. Even so, their ideas of freedom and a say in government stayed alive.

In Switzerland this time went differently. After the short **Sonderbund War** of 1847 the cantons gave themselves a new **Federal Constitution** in **1848**. From the loose confederation of states a **federal state** with a parliament and a Federal Council was made. Switzerland was thus one of the few countries in which a free order lastingly succeeded in 1848. This constitution is the basis of today’s Switzerland.

gewusst: The Frankfurt National Assembly was also called the “Parliament of Professors”, because many scholars sat in it.
The composer Richard Wagner took part in an uprising in Dresden in 1849 and afterwards fled to Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Social media are internet platforms on which people share texts, photos and videos and get in touch with one another. Well-known examples are Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Snapchat and Facebook. In the last twenty years they have changed how we communicate, inform ourselves and entertain ourselves.
wichtigste: Facebook started in February 2004 as “Thefacebook” at Harvard University.
The Facebook company has been called Meta Platforms since October 2021.
Google bought the video platform YouTube in 2006.
TikTok was developed by the Chinese company ByteDance.
Elon Musk took over Twitter, which is today called X, at the end of October 2022.
In the Cambridge Analytica scandal of 2018 the data of millions of Facebook users was misused.
Since 10 December 2025 Australia has banned children under 16 from having their own accounts on large platforms.

abschnitte.text: Social media are apps and websites on which users create and share content themselves. One can like posts, comment on them and follow other people. An **algorithm** decides which posts one gets to see in one’s own feed. Most platforms are free and make their money with advertising.

**Mark Zuckerberg** founded Facebook in February 2004 as “Thefacebook” at Harvard University. YouTube came into being in 2005 and was bought by **Google** in 2006. In 2010 Instagram was added, which Facebook took over in 2012, and in 2014 the purchase of WhatsApp followed. Since October 2021 the company has been called **Meta Platforms**.

**TikTok** was developed by the Chinese company **ByteDance** and is especially popular with young people. Short videos with music spread very quickly there. The short-message service Twitter was taken over by **Elon Musk** at the end of October 2022 and renamed X in 2023. Snapchat is known for pictures that disappear again after a short time.

Social media collect a lot of **personal data**. In the **Cambridge Analytica scandal** of 2018 the data of millions of Facebook users was analysed for political advertising without their knowledge. On the platforms false reports, hate messages and **cyberbullying** also spread. Many apps are built so that one stays on the screen as long as possible.

Most platforms allow their own accounts only from the age of 13. **Australia** is the first country since 10 December 2025 to ban by law children under 16 from having accounts on large social networks. In Europe and Switzerland too stricter rules are being discussed. In Switzerland the Data Protection Act protects personal data.

Think carefully about which photos and information you share, because the internet forgets little. Set your account to private and accept requests only from people you know. Do not believe everything you see, and check news with reliable sources. If something troubles you or you are being bullied, talk to someone you trust or in Switzerland call the number **147** of Pro Juventute.

begriffe.erklaerung: A set of calculation rules by which a program decides, for example, which videos you see.
A person with many followers who influences others with their posts and often advertises.
When someone is insulted, threatened or exposed on the internet deliberately and repeatedly.
False news that is spread deliberately.
The list of posts that an app shows you.

gewusst: The famous like symbol, the “thumbs up”, was introduced at Facebook only in 2009.
The first video on YouTube was uploaded in 2005 and shows one of the founders in front of elephants at the zoo.
In China the sister app of TikTok is called Douyin.

teile.einleitung: On 11 September 2001 terrorists in the USA hijacked four passenger aircraft and steered them into famous buildings. Around 3,000 people lost their lives. The attacks changed world politics and security in flying to this day.
wichtigste: On 11 September 2001 19 terrorists hijacked four aircraft in the USA.
The terrorist organisation al-Qaeda under Osama bin Laden was responsible.
Two aircraft destroyed the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York.
American Airlines Flight 77 hit the Pentagon near Washington.
United Airlines Flight 93 crashed near Shanksville in Pennsylvania after passengers had fought back.
