According to official figures around 3,000 people died in all.
NATO invoked the mutual assistance clause under Article 5 for the first time.
Osama bin Laden was killed on 2 May 2011 in Abbottabad in Pakistan.

abschnitte.text: On the morning of 11 September 2001 **19 attackers** took control of four passenger aircraft. At 8.46 local time the first aircraft flew into the north tower of the **World Trade Center** in New York. Shortly afterwards a second aircraft hit the south tower. Millions of people saw the burning towers live on television.

The two towers of the World Trade Center were over 400 metres tall and were among the best-known buildings in the world. Through the burning kerosene the steel beams became so hot that both towers **collapsed** after less than two hours. Among the dead were also over 400 firefighters, police officers and other **rescue workers**. Clearing the rubble took many months.

The third aircraft, American Airlines Flight 77, hit the **Pentagon**, the US Department of Defense near Washington. In the fourth aircraft, United Airlines Flight 93, passengers learned of the other attacks by telephone. They fought back against the hijackers, and the aircraft crashed into a field near **Shanksville** in Pennsylvania. Presumably it was meant to hit a target in Washington.

Behind the attacks stood the Islamist terrorist organisation **al-Qaeda** under its leader **Osama bin Laden**. Most of the attackers came from Saudi Arabia. Al-Qaeda misused religion to justify violence; the overwhelming majority of Muslims reject such acts. Bin Laden was killed on 2 May 2011 by a US special unit in Abbottabad in Pakistan.

**NATO** invoked the mutual assistance clause under Article 5 for the first time in its history. In October 2001 the USA and allies began the **war in Afghanistan**, where the Taliban gave al-Qaeda shelter. The USA proclaimed a “war on terror”, and in 2003 the Iraq War followed as well. At airports worldwide **security checks** were greatly tightened.

Where the Twin Towers stood, two large pools of water recall the victims today, edged with their names. Next to them since 2014 stands **One World Trade Center**, the tallest building in the USA. Every year on 11 September the names of all the dead are read out at a ceremony. In the USA the day is often simply called **“9/11”**, said “nine eleven”.

begriffe.erklaerung: Violence against people in order to spread fear and terror and to force political aims.
An Islamist terrorist organisation founded by Osama bin Laden.
The five-sided building of the US Department of Defense.
The rule that all NATO members help a member that is attacked.

gewusst: One World Trade Center is 1,776 feet tall, in memory of the year of American independence.
After the attacks the airspace of the USA stayed closed to almost all flights for several days.
In New York there is a pear tree that survived the attacks badly damaged and is today called the “Survivor Tree”.

teile.einleitung: Rosa Parks was a Black woman from the USA who in 1955 refused to give up her seat on the bus for a white passenger. Her brave behaviour became an important moment of the civil rights movement.
wichtigste: On 1 December 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on the bus.
This happened in Montgomery in the state of Alabama.
Rosa Parks worked as a seamstress.
After her arrest many Black people stopped taking the bus.
The Montgomery bus boycott lasted 381 days.
Rosa Parks is often called the “mother of the civil rights movement”.

abschnitte.text: In the southern states of the **USA** laws on **racial segregation** applied at that time. Black and white people had to use separate schools, toilets and seats. In the buses of **Montgomery** in the state of **Alabama** too there were separate areas. Black passengers had to give up their seat if white passengers could no longer find one. Many felt this to be a deep injustice.

**Rosa Parks** worked as a **seamstress** in a department store. On **1 December 1955** she was travelling home by bus after work. The driver demanded that she give up her **seat** for a white man. Rosa Parks stayed calmly seated and refused. She was then **arrested** by the police and had to pay a fine. She had for some time been campaigning for the rights of Black people.

After her arrest Black citizens called for a **boycott**. Boycott means that one deliberately stops using something. Many Black people **stopped taking the bus**. They walked, drove together in cars or took taxis. The boycott was led by the young pastor **Martin Luther King**. It lasted **381 days** and ended when the Supreme Court of the USA declared racial segregation on buses unconstitutional.

abschnitte.titel: Mother of the civil rights movement
abschnitte.text: The bus boycott made Martin Luther King well known and gave the **civil rights movement** great momentum. This movement fought without violence for equal rights for all people in the USA. Rosa Parks is therefore often called the **“mother of the civil rights movement”**. Later she received many honours. When she died in 2005 she lay in state in the Capitol in Washington, a very rare honour.

gewusst: The bus in which Rosa Parks sat stands today in a museum near Detroit.
Rosa Parks was the first woman to lie in state in the Capitol in Washington.

teile.einleitung: A video game is a game that you play on a screen with a computer, console or mobile phone. Since the 1970s video games have been popular all over the world.
wichtigste: Video games are played on game consoles, computers, mobile phones or arcade machines.
“Pong” from 1972 was one of the first successful video games.
In the game “Pac-Man” a yellow character eats dots and is chased by ghosts.
Tetris was invented in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow.
The well-known character Mario is a plumber.

abschnitte.text: As early as the 1950s and 1960s researchers built the first simple games on large computers. But video games became well known in the **1970s**. The game **“Pong”** from 1972 showed two bars and a dot, rather like table tennis. Soon **arcade machines** stood in restaurants and amusement arcades. Later **game consoles** came along for the home.

In 1980 **“Pac-Man”** appeared in Japan. The yellow character eats dots in a maze and is chased by four coloured **ghosts**. The company Nintendo invented the character **Mario**. Mario is a **plumber**, that is, someone who installs water pipes. That is why in his games he often runs through green pipes. **Tetris** comes from Russia, which was then part of the Soviet Union: Alexey Pajitnov invented it in Moscow in 1984.

Today people play on **consoles**, computers, tablets and **mobile phones**. Many games can be played over the internet together with other people. Age ratings such as **PEGI** show in Europe from what age a game is suitable. For games, as for other screen time, breaks and exercise do you good. By the way, the company Logitech, which makes game controllers among other things, comes from Switzerland.

gewusst: Tetris came with Nintendo's Game Boy from 1989 and became known all over the world as a result.

teile.einleitung: The textile industry makes yarns, fabrics and clothes. In the 18th century it became the engine of the Industrial Revolution in England, because there machines first replaced handwork. Switzerland too was for a long time an important textile country.
wichtigste: The textile industry was the first branch to be strongly mechanised.
John Kay invented the flying shuttle in 1733, which sped up weaving.
James Hargreaves invented the spinning machine the Spinning Jenny around 1764.
Richard Arkwright built a water-powered spinning mill at Cromford in 1771.
Samuel Crompton developed the Spinning Mule in 1779, Edmund Cartwright the power loom in 1784.
Eli Whitney’s cotton gin of 1793 made cotton growing and slave labour in the Southern states of the USA grow strongly.
The weavers’ uprising in Silesia in 1844 showed the hardship of the hand weavers.
In Switzerland the textile industry, especially in eastern Switzerland, was for a long time the most important branch of industry.

abschnitte.text: In the past threads were spun at home on the **spinning wheel** and woven into cloth on the hand loom. Often the whole family took part, which is called **home working**. In the 18th century the demand for cotton fabrics rose sharply in England. Because cotton fibres can be processed well by machine, the cotton industry became the pioneer of mechanisation.

In 1733 John Kay invented the **flying shuttle**, with which weavers could work much faster. Now yarn was lacking, so James Hargreaves around 1764 invented the **Spinning Jenny**, which spun several threads at the same time. Richard Arkwright used the power of water wheels for his Water Frame and opened a spinning mill at Cromford in 1771. Samuel Crompton combined both machines in 1779 into the **Spinning Mule**, and Edmund Cartwright invented the power loom in 1784.

Soon **steam engines** drove the machines in large factory halls. Cities such as Manchester grew rapidly and became the centre of the cotton industry. The workers often toiled 12 to 14 hours a day, and children also had to work. The halls were loud, dusty and dangerous. For the hand weavers the competition from machines was a catastrophe, as the **weavers’ uprising** in Silesia in 1844 showed.

The cotton came to a large extent from the Southern states of the USA. In 1793 Eli Whitney invented the **cotton gin**, a machine that quickly removed the seeds from the cotton. As a result growing it paid much better, and the plantations grew strongly. On them millions of enslaved people had to work. So the success of the textile factories was closely tied to **slavery**.

In 1802 the first mechanical spinning mill in Switzerland arose in the Hard near Winterthur. In the Zurich Oberland, in Glarus and in eastern Switzerland many textile factories arose on rivers. In 1832 desperate home weavers set fire to a factory in the **Uster fire**. Around 1910 **St Gallen embroidery** was Switzerland’s most important export branch.

Today most clothes are made in Asia, for example in China, Bangladesh or Vietnam. There seamstresses often work for very low wages. In 2013 the factory building **Rana Plaza** collapsed in Bangladesh, and over 1,100 people died. Since then more people have paid attention to **fair fashion** and quality labels.

begriffe.erklaerung: Twisting fibres into a thread or yarn.
Joining threads crosswise into a fabric.
When machines take over work that was previously done by hand.
Work that is done at home instead of in a factory.
The time from about 1760 in which machines and factories fundamentally changed life.

gewusst: The Spinning Jenny is said to be named after the daughter or wife of James Hargreaves.
The Jacquard loom of 1805 was controlled with punched cards, an early idea that later also became important for computers.
Arkwright’s mill at Cromford is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The Palace of Versailles near Paris is one of the largest and most magnificent palaces in the world. The French King Louis XIV, the Sun King, made it the centre of his power. With its golden halls and huge gardens it became a model for palaces throughout Europe.
wichtigste: Versailles lies about 20 kilometres south-west of Paris.
Originally there stood a hunting lodge of Louis XIII, the father of Louis XIV.
In 1682 Louis XIV officially moved his court to Versailles.
The most famous room is the Hall of Mirrors with around 350 mirrors.
André Le Nôtre designed the gardens in strict geometric forms.
In 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors.
In 1919 the Treaty of Versailles was signed there.

abschnitte.text: First King Louis XIII had a small **hunting lodge** built at Versailles. His son **Louis XIV** had it enormously enlarged from the 1660s. The architects Louis Le Vau and later Jules Hardouin-Mansart planned the buildings, and the painter Charles Le Brun the furnishings. In 1682 the king officially made Versailles the seat of his court and government.

The **Hall of Mirrors** is about 73 metres long and was completed in the 1680s. Opposite the 17 tall windows hang around 350 mirrors, which multiply the light. At that time large mirrors were very expensive and a sign of wealth. Chandeliers, gold and ceiling paintings show the glory of the king.

The gardens were designed by **André Le Nôtre** as a **French Baroque garden**. Typical are straight paths, geometrically cut hedges, ponds and fountains. A large canal in the shape of a cross is over one and a half kilometres long. In the park there are also smaller palaces such as the Grand Trianon and the Petit Trianon.

Louis XIV brought many nobles to Versailles in order to **control** them and keep them from uprisings. Thousands of people lived and worked at court. The king’s daily life followed strict rules: at the **lever** selected nobles watched the king get up and dress. Anyone who was allowed to be near the king counted as especially important.

Louis XV and Louis XVI with Queen Marie-Antoinette also lived at Versailles. In October 1789, during the French Revolution, a crowd forced the royal family to move to Paris. In 1871, after their victory over France, the Germans proclaimed the **German Empire** in the Hall of Mirrors. In 1919 the **Treaty of Versailles**, which formally ended the First World War, was signed in the same place.

Today the palace is a museum and since 1979 has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Every year several million people from all over the world visit it. Many rulers imitated Versailles. For example King Ludwig II of Bavaria had **Herrenchiemsee Palace** built on its model.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lavish style of art and building in the 17th and 18th centuries.
A form of rule in which a king has almost unlimited power.
All the people who live around a king and serve him.
French for rising, the king’s ceremonial morning ritual.

gewusst: Louis XIV was called the Sun King, and the sun can be found everywhere in the palace as a decoration.
For the fountains of Versailles elaborate pumping systems were built that pumped water up from the Seine.
In the park Marie-Antoinette had a little farming village built, the Hameau de la Reine.

teile.einleitung: The Warsaw Pact was a military alliance of the Soviet Union with the communist states of Eastern Europe. It was founded in Warsaw in 1955 and was the counterpart of the Western NATO in the Cold War. Its troops, however, were used mainly against its own member states that wanted to break away from Moscow.
wichtigste: The Warsaw Pact was founded on 14 May 1955.
The direct occasion was the admission of the Federal Republic of Germany into NATO.
The Soviet Union led the alliance, and the commander-in-chief was always a Soviet general.
In 1956 Hungary's prime minister Imre Nagy declared withdrawal, but Soviet troops crushed the uprising.
In August 1968 troops of the Pact ended the Prague Spring.
Albania left in 1968, and socialist Yugoslavia never belonged to it.
On 1 July 1991 the Warsaw Pact was formally dissolved.

abschnitte.text: On 14 May 1955 eight states signed the “Treaty of Friendship, Co-operation and Mutual Assistance” in Warsaw. The members were the **Soviet Union**, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Albania and East Germany. Shortly before, the Federal Republic of Germany had joined **NATO**. The Soviet Union wanted to answer with an alliance of its own.

The high command sat in Moscow, and the commander-in-chief was always a Soviet marshal. The armies of the members largely used Soviet weapons, tanks and aircraft. In several countries Soviet troops were stationed permanently, particularly many in East Germany. Officially all members had equal rights, but in reality the **Soviet Union** decided policy.

In autumn 1956 many people in Hungary rose up against the communist dictatorship. Prime Minister **Imre Nagy** declared Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact and its neutrality on 1 November 1956. A few days later Soviet tanks moved into Budapest and put down the **popular uprising** bloodily. Nagy was executed in 1958. Around 200,000 people fled from Hungary at that time, and over 10,000 of them were taken in by Switzerland.

In Czechoslovakia the party leader Alexander Dubček wanted “socialism with a human face”, with more freedom of speech. In the night of 21 August 1968 troops from the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria marched in and ended the **Prague Spring**. Romania did not take part. After that the **Brezhnev Doctrine** applied: the sovereignty of socialist states was limited, and intervening to protect socialism was allowed. At that time too, many refugees came to Switzerland.

Not all socialist states followed Moscow. **Yugoslavia** under Josip Broz Tito had already broken with Stalin in 1948 and never joined the Pact. From 1961 Albania moved away from the Soviet Union and turned to China. After the invasion of Czechoslovakia Albania formally left in 1968. Romania remained a member but often went its own way.

At the end of the 1980s the Soviet leader **Mikhail Gorbachev** gave the countries of Eastern Europe more freedom. In 1989 the communist governments fell, and the Berlin Wall opened. With German reunification in 1990 East Germany left. In spring 1991 the military co-operation ended, and on 1 July 1991 the Pact was formally dissolved in Prague. Later many former members such as Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary joined NATO.

begriffe.erklaerung: A treaty in which states promise to help one another militarily if one is attacked.
The Western defence alliance to which the USA and many states of Western Europe belong.
The rule that the Soviet Union may intervene in socialist states to protect socialism.
The right of a state to decide its own affairs.

gewusst: The only war fought jointly by troops of the Warsaw Pact was the invasion of one of its own member countries, Czechoslovakia.
In 1968 the East German army was actually supposed to march in too, but stayed almost entirely at the border.
The Pact existed for exactly 36 years, from 1955 to 1991.

teile.einleitung: The putting-out system was a form of home work before the factories. An entrepreneur supplied raw materials, and families in the countryside processed them at home for pay.
wichtigste: In the putting-out system a merchant supplied raw materials and often equipment.
Home workers spun and wove in their living rooms and were paid wages for it.
The merchant took the finished goods and sold them on.
In Switzerland, middlemen called Fergger distributed the material and collected the goods.
For farming families, home work was an important extra income.
In 1972 the historian Franklin Mendels coined the term “proto-industrialisation”.
In the watch industry of the Jura the system was called Etablissage.

abschnitte.text: The German name comes from the word for “advance”: the **merchant** advanced the money for raw materials. He supplied cotton, yarn or linen, for example, and often also spinning wheels or looms. The **home workers** processed the material in their houses. The merchant took the finished goods, paid a wage and sold them at distant markets. So the workers owned neither the material nor the finished goods.

In areas such as the **Zurich Oberland**, the Toggenburg or eastern Switzerland, the farms were small and the soil was often poor. The yield was often not enough to live on. **Spinning and weaving** at home brought in extra money. Often the whole family helped, including the children. In Switzerland the **Fergger** stood between the merchant and the home workers. They distributed the raw materials and collected the finished goods again.

abschnitte.titel: The Poor Man of the Toggenburg
abschnitte.text: **Ulrich Bräker** from the Toggenburg gives us a special insight. In the 18th century he lived as a smallholder, yarn dealer and weaver. He described his life in his famous autobiography, “The Life Story and Natural Adventures of the Poor Man of Toggenburg”. The book shows how hard and uncertain home work was. If business went badly, families quickly fell into hardship.

The **watch industry** in the Swiss Jura was also organised as home work for a long time. This system was called **Etablissage**. An **établisseur** bought individual parts from specialised home workers and had them assembled into watches. Each craftsman was an expert in one stage of the work. Only later did large **watch factories** take over.

In 1972 the historian **Franklin Mendels** coined the term **proto-industrialisation**. He saw rural home industry as a forerunner of the factories. When machines took over spinning and weaving, the wages of home workers fell sharply. In 1844 the **weavers in Silesia** protested against their misery. The poet Gerhart Hauptmann later wrote the play “The Weavers” about it.

gewusst: The German word “Verleger” for someone who publishes books has the same origin: he too advances the money for production.
Ulrich Bräker's life story appeared in 1789 and is still read today.

teile.einleitung: The Napoleonic Wars were a series of wars that the French Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte waged between about 1803 and 1815 against many states of Europe. For a time France controlled almost the whole continent. The wars changed the map of Europe and also affected Switzerland.
wichtigste: In 1805 Napoleon defeated Austria and Russia at Austerlitz.
In the same year the British fleet under Nelson defeated the French at Trafalgar.
In 1806 the Holy Roman Empire ended as a result of Napoleon’s successes.
With the Continental Blockade Napoleon banned trade with Britain.
In 1812 Napoleon marched against Russia with the Grande Armée and captured Moscow, but Russia did not give up.
At the Berezina Swiss regiments covered the retreat in November 1812.
On 18 June 1815 Napoleon was finally defeated at Waterloo in present-day Belgium.

abschnitte.text: Napoleon Bonaparte was a general of the French Revolution who seized power in 1799 and crowned himself **emperor** in 1804. Britain, Austria, Russia and Prussia allied against him again and again in so-called **coalitions**. Napoleon was a skilful commander who attacked quickly and by surprise. His army, the **Grande Armée**, was long regarded as unbeatable.

abschnitte.titel: Victories on land, defeat at sea
abschnitte.text: On 2 December 1805 Napoleon defeated Austria and Russia at **Austerlitz**, which is also called the Battle of the Three Emperors. At sea the British fleet under Admiral Horatio Nelson defeated the French fleet at **Trafalgar** in the same year, and Nelson fell. In 1806 the Holy Roman Empire dissolved, and many German states joined Napoleon in the Confederation of the Rhine. In the same year he also defeated Prussia.

Because Napoleon could not defeat Britain at sea, he wanted to hit it economically. With the **Continental Blockade** he banned all countries under his influence from trading with Britain from 1806. But that also harmed many European countries, Switzerland too. In Spain from 1808 insurgents fought a long guerrilla war against the French troops.

In 1812 Napoleon marched against Russia with the Grande Armée, more than half a million soldiers. In September 1812 he captured **Moscow**, but the city burned and Russia did not give up. On the retreat in the icy winter the vast majority of the soldiers died or were taken prisoner. At the **Berezina** in November 1812 Swiss regiments fought to cover the retreat, and only a few of them survived.

In October 1813 Napoleon lost the **Battle of the Nations** at Leipzig against Russia, Prussia, Austria and Sweden. In 1814 he had to abdicate and was banished to the island of Elba. In 1815 he returned for the “Hundred Days”. On 18 June 1815 he was finally defeated at **Waterloo** in present-day Belgium by the British and Prussians and died in 1821 in exile on St Helena.

In this period Switzerland was under French influence and had to supply Napoleon with soldiers. With the **Berezina Song** the Swiss soldiers in Russia are still remembered in Switzerland today. After the wars the Congress of Vienna reorganised Europe in 1814 and 1815. In this the perpetual neutrality of Switzerland was also recognised.

begriffe.erklaerung: An alliance of several states against a common enemy.
French for “Great Army”, Napoleon’s main army.
Napoleon’s ban on trade with Britain from 1806.
When a ruler gives up his office, voluntarily or under compulsion.
A punishment in which someone is sent to a distant place and may not return.

gewusst: Of Napoleon’s huge army in Russia only a small fraction of the soldiers returned.
The word “Waterloo” still stands in English today for a final defeat.
Nelson’s flagship HMS Victory still lies today in the harbour of Portsmouth and can be visited.

teile.einleitung: A pocket watch is a small watch that one carries in the pocket. It was invented around 1510 in Nuremberg. Later Switzerland, especially the Jura, became a centre of watchmaking.
wichtigste: Peter Henlein is regarded as the inventor of the pocket watch.
Early watches from Nuremberg are called “Nuremberg eggs”.
A tensioned spring drives the mechanical watch.
One had to wind the watch regularly.
A chain connected the watch to the clothing.
In the Jura there have long been especially many watchmakers.
In the 20th century the wristwatch pushed out the pocket watch.

abschnitte.text: The Nuremberg locksmith **Peter Henlein** built small watches around 1510 that one could take along. That is why he is regarded as the **inventor of the pocket watch**. Before that there were almost only large clocks on church towers or heavy standing clocks. Early small watches from Nuremberg are called **“Nuremberg eggs”**. The name probably comes from an old word for a small clock.

In a mechanical pocket watch there is a **spring** that one tensions. As it relaxes it moves the hands through many small gear wheels. That is why one had to **wind** the watch regularly. For this one turns a small wheel, the **crown**. Otherwise the watch stops after some time.

A pocket watch was usually kept in the **waistcoat pocket**. So that it was not lost or did not fall out, it was fastened to a **chain**. The chain connected the watch to the clothing. Many pocket watches had a cover that protected the glass. A valuable pocket watch was long regarded as a sign of prosperity.

In the **Jura Arc** from Geneva to Basel many watchmaking workshops arose. Swiss watches became world famous. The towns of **La Chaux-de-Fonds** and **Le Locle** in the canton of Neuchâtel were built entirely for the watchmakers. Wide streets and many windows gave good light for the fine work. Since 2009 the two towns have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

In the 20th century more and more people wore the watch on the **wrist**. That was more practical than pulling the watch out of the pocket. So the **wristwatch** pushed out the pocket watch. Today pocket watches are mainly collectors’ items or heirlooms.

gewusst: La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are World Heritage because their streets were planned entirely according to the needs of the watchmakers.
To this day many of the best-known watch brands in the world come from Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Mughal Empire was a large empire in India that existed from 1526. Its rulers, the Great Mughals, were Muslims and ruled over a country with many religions. Famous buildings such as the Taj Mahal date from this time.
wichtigste: Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526 after the Battle of Panipat.
The Great Mughal Akbar abolished the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims, in 1564.
Akbar promoted the teaching Din-i Ilahi and had Fatehpur Sikri built.
Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built in Agra for Mumtaz Mahal.
Under Aurangzeb the empire was at its largest.
After Aurangzeb’s death in 1707 the empire fell apart.
In 1858 the British deposed the last Great Mughal.

abschnitte.text: **Babur** came from Central Asia and was a descendant of the famous conqueror Timur. In 1526 he defeated the Sultan of Delhi in the **Battle of Panipat** in northern India. With that the **Mughal Empire** began. The word Mughal comes from “Mongol”, for Babur also had Mongol ancestors. His successors extended the empire further and further.

The Great Mughal **Akbar** ruled from 1556 to 1605. He wanted Muslims and Hindus to live together in peace. In 1564 he abolished the **jizya**, a tax that non-Muslims had to pay. Akbar invited scholars of different religions to talks. He promoted a teaching of his own called **Din-i Ilahi**, which combined elements of several religions. In the second half of the 16th century he had the residential city of **Fatehpur Sikri** newly built.

The Great Mughal **Shah Jahan** had a tomb built for his dead wife **Mumtaz Mahal**. This is how the **Taj Mahal** of white marble came to be in the city of **Agra**. Thousands of craftsmen worked on it for over twenty years. Shah Jahan also built the Red Fort in Delhi. The Mughal rulers promoted art, painting and poetry, and the language at court was Persian.

Under the Great Mughal **Aurangzeb** the empire reached its **greatest extent**. Almost the whole of India belonged to it. But Aurangzeb fought many expensive wars and reintroduced the jizya. After his death in 1707 the empire fell apart. Local princes became independent, and the British **East India Company** gained more and more power.

In 1857 many people in India rose up against British rule. This **Indian Rebellion** was put down by the British. The old Great Mughal **Bahadur Shah II** had joined the rebels. In 1858 the British deposed him and sent him into exile. After that the British Crown ruled India directly.

gewusst: The Taj Mahal has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
Fatehpur Sikri was used as a capital for only a few years and was then largely abandoned.

teile.einleitung: A mobile phone is a telephone without a cable that you can take anywhere. In Switzerland it is often called a Natel, in Germany a Handy. The first devices were heavy and expensive; today the smartphone is a small computer in your pocket.
wichtigste: Martin Cooper made the first call with a portable mobile phone in 1973.
This first device weighed about 1 kilogram.
In Switzerland the first mobile phones were installed in cars from 1978.
The word Natel means “national car telephone”.
The first mobile phones could mainly make calls.
The first SMS in 1992 read “Merry Christmas”.
With 112 you can reach the emergency services all over Europe.

abschnitte.text: On 3 April 1973 the American **Martin Cooper** made a call on a street in New York with a portable mobile phone. He worked for the company Motorola. His device weighed about **1 kilogram** and was as big as a brick. The battery lasted only for a short talk time. Such devices only went on sale a few years later, and they were very expensive.

In Switzerland mobile telephoning began in the **car**. From 1978 the then PTT offered the **Natel**. The word is an abbreviation for **Nationales Autotelefon** (national car telephone). The devices were big and heavy and were built permanently into the car. Later the telephones became smaller and smaller, and you could carry them in your hand. The name Natel has stayed in use in Switzerland to this day.

With the first mobile phones you could do almost nothing but **make calls**. In the 1990s a new mobile network came that could send messages made of letters. These short texts are called **SMS**. The first SMS was sent in 1992 in Britain from a computer to a mobile phone. It read “Merry Christmas”. Soon millions of people were sending SMS every day.

From 2007 phones with a large **touchscreen** became popular, that is, a screen that you operate with your finger. They are called **smartphones**. With them you can take photos, listen to music, search the internet and play games. Small programs for this are called **apps**. Today most adults and many young people in Switzerland own a smartphone.

With a mobile phone you can quickly get help anywhere. The number **112** works all over Europe and connects you to the emergency services. In Switzerland there are also numbers of their own: **117** for the police, **118** for the fire brigade and **144** for the ambulance. Anyone who calls in an emergency should say calmly where they are and what has happened.

gewusst: The first portable mobile phone had to be charged for hours after a short call.
The word “Handy” sounds English, but is not used in English for the telephone at all.

teile.einleitung: The Reformation in Switzerland began around 1520 in Zurich with Huldrych Zwingli and then spread in many towns. Other places stayed Catholic, and so the Confederation was split into two religious camps. This division shaped Switzerland for centuries.
wichtigste: Huldrych Zwingli began the Reformation in Zurich from 1519.
Bern introduced the Reformation in 1528, Basel in 1529 under Johannes Oekolampad.
In St Gallen the physician and mayor Joachim Vadian carried through the Reformation.
The places of Central Switzerland, Fribourg and Solothurn stayed Catholic.
The Second War of Kappel in 1531 ended with a victory of the Catholic places.
After the Second Peace of Kappel each place was allowed to keep its denomination.
Geneva became a centre of the Reformation with John Calvin.

abschnitte.text: From 1519 **Huldrych Zwingli** preached at the Grossmünster in Zurich and relied entirely on the Bible. In 1522 followers publicly broke the fasting rule at the so-called sausage meal. After debates, the **disputations** of 1523, the Zurich council supported the Reformation. Pictures were removed from the churches, and in 1525 the Mass was replaced by a plain Lord’s Supper.

**Bern** introduced the Reformation in 1528, **Basel** in 1529 under the reformer Johannes Oekolampad. Schaffhausen too became Reformed in 1529. In St Gallen the physician and mayor **Joachim Vadian** carried through the new doctrine. Bern brought the Reformation to the Vaud in 1536 after conquering it, and in Neuchâtel Guillaume Farel won people for it around 1530.

The places of Central Switzerland, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne and Zug, kept the old faith. The towns of **Fribourg** and **Solothurn** also stayed Catholic. In Glarus and Appenzell there were followers of both denominations. The territories administered jointly became a point of dispute between the camps.

In 1529 the armies faced each other in the First War of Kappel, but a peaceful agreement was reached. In 1531 the Catholic places attacked, and in the **Second War of Kappel** they won. Zwingli fell in the battle at Kappel am Albis. The **Second Peace of Kappel** laid down that each place was allowed to keep its denomination.

Some followers of Zwingli went further than he did and rejected infant baptism, and they were called **Anabaptists**. They wanted to baptise only adults who had consciously decided for the faith. The Zurich council persecuted them harshly, and in 1527 **Felix Manz** was drowned in the Limmat. Descendants of the Anabaptists live today, for example, as Mennonites and Amish, also in North America.

Zwingli’s successor in Zurich was **Heinrich Bullinger**, who wrote the Second Helvetic Confession in 1566. It was recognised in many Reformed churches of Europe. In Geneva from 1536 the Frenchman **John Calvin** worked, whose teaching spread as far as France, Scotland and the Netherlands. So Switzerland became a starting point of the Reformed churches worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Protestant Christians who follow the teaching of Zwingli and Calvin.
A public debate about questions of faith.
Christians who wanted to baptise only adults and were therefore persecuted.
A peace treaty between the places of the Confederation.
What the members of the Confederation were then called, much like the cantons today.

gewusst: At the Zurich sausage meal of 1522 Zwingli was present, but did not eat any sausage himself.
The Zurich Bible, which Froschauer printed in 1531, was one of the first complete Bibles in German.
In Geneva the great Reformation Monument recalls Calvin, Farel and other reformers.

teile.einleitung: Anaesthesia makes sure that you feel no pain during an operation. Under a general anaesthetic you sleep deeply and notice nothing. The invention of anaesthesia in the 19th century was a huge advance for medicine.
wichtigste: Anaesthesia prevents pain during an operation.
A general anaesthetic feels like a deep sleep.
The doctor for the anaesthetic is called an anaesthetist.
Before anaesthesia operations were very painful.
In 1844 a dentist made laughing gas known against pain.
In 1846 a famous anaesthetic with ether succeeded in Boston.
Before an anaesthetic you usually must not eat anything, so that nothing gets into the lungs.

abschnitte.text: In the past operations were **very painful**. Patients were held down, and some were given alcohol to drink. Surgeons therefore had to work as fast as possible. Many people were very afraid of an operation and preferred to wait, even if it was dangerous. Longer and difficult procedures were hardly possible.

In 1844 the American dentist Horace Wells made **laughing gas** known to ease pain when pulling teeth. On 16 October 1846 the dentist William Morton in **Boston** put a patient to sleep with **ether**. After that a surgeon removed a tumour on the neck without pain. This demonstration became world famous. Soon afterwards doctors in many countries used anaesthesia.

In a **general anaesthetic** you are given drugs through a vein or breathe in a gas. You fall asleep quickly and notice nothing of the operation. For the patient it feels like a **deep sleep**. The **anaesthetist** is a doctor who looks after the anaesthetic. During the operation he constantly monitors heart, breathing and blood pressure and wakes the patient up again afterwards.

A general anaesthetic is not always needed. At the dentist you often get a **local anaesthetic**. Then only a part of the mouth feels nothing, but you stay awake. Afterwards the lip feels thick and numb for a while. Even in small procedures on the skin, hands or feet, often only one spot is numbed.

abschnitte.titel: Why you must have an empty stomach
abschnitte.text: Before a general anaesthetic you usually must **not eat** for several hours. You must have an **empty stomach**. During the anaesthetic the protective reflexes in the throat do not work as usual. If the stomach were full, stomach contents could get into the **lungs**. That would be dangerous. That is why doctors explain exactly before the operation from when you may no longer eat and drink.

gewusst: The word narcosis comes from Greek and means roughly “numbness” or “stupor”.
16 October is celebrated in the USA as “Ether Day”.

teile.einleitung: The Sykes-Picot Agreement was a secret treaty between Britain and France from the year 1916. In it the two powers planned to divide the Middle East between themselves after the First World War. The agreement still influences the region today.
wichtigste: The agreement was concluded in May 1916 in the middle of the First World War.
Britain and France divided the Middle East into zones of influence.
It is named after the Briton Mark Sykes and the Frenchman François Georges-Picot.
France was to receive Syria and Lebanon.
At the end of 1917 the Bolsheviks in Russia made the agreement public.
It contradicted British promises to the Arabs.
In 1920 the San Remo Conference distributed the mandates.

abschnitte.titel: The Middle East in the war
abschnitte.text: Before the First World War large parts of the Middle East belonged to the **Ottoman Empire**. In the war the Ottoman Empire fought on the side of Germany. Britain and France reckoned that it would lose the war. So they considered early on who should control which territories afterwards.

In May 1916 the Briton **Mark Sykes** and the Frenchman **François Georges-Picot** agreed the plan. It divided the region into **zones of influence**. France was to receive the coast of Syria and Lebanon as well as influence in the interior. Britain was to get territories in what is now Iraq and Jordan. Russia agreed to the division.

For a large part of **Palestine** the agreement provided for an **international administration**. The reason was the holy sites of Jews, Christians and Muslims. In fact Britain later took over rule there as the mandatory power.

In letters of 1915 and 1916 the British High Commissioner McMahon had held out to the Sharif **Hussein of Mecca** the prospect of an independent Arab empire. These letters are called the **Hussein-McMahon Correspondence**. At the end of 1917 the **Bolsheviks**, after the October Revolution, published secret treaties of the Tsarist empire. So the Arabs learned of the plans for division. This is regarded as one of the reasons for Arab mistrust of the West.

After the war the victorious powers met in April 1920 at **San Remo** in Italy. There they distributed the **League of Nations mandates** over Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Mesopotamia. France received Syria and Lebanon, Britain Palestine and Mesopotamia. A mandate meant that a great power administered a territory on behalf of the League of Nations. So the ideas of Sykes-Picot were put into effect in altered form.

gewusst: The secret agreement became known only because the Russian revolutionaries published the Tsar’s secret treaties.
Mesopotamia is the old name for the area of present-day Iraq.

teile.einleitung: Cinnamon is a spice made from the dried bark of the cinnamon tree. In the past it was very precious in Europe, because it had to be brought from far away.
wichtigste: Cinnamon is the dried bark of the cinnamon tree.
When drying, the bark rolls up into tubes, the cinnamon sticks.
True cinnamon, Ceylon cinnamon, comes from Sri Lanka.
Sri Lanka used to be called Ceylon.
In the past cinnamon was rare and expensive in Europe because it travelled a long way.

abschnitte.text: Cinnamon is made from the **bark** of the **cinnamon tree**. The thin inner bark is peeled from young twigs. When **drying**, it rolls up by itself. That is how the brown **cinnamon sticks** come about, which look like rolled-up tubes. If you grind them you get cinnamon powder.

**True cinnamon**, also called **Ceylon cinnamon**, comes from the island of **Sri Lanka**. The island used to be called **Ceylon**. There is also **cassia cinnamon**, which comes mainly from China and other countries of Asia. It has a stronger flavour and is usually cheaper. Ceylon cinnamon has finer, thinner sticks with many layers.

In the past cinnamon was **rare and expensive** in Europe. It had to be brought over a very long route from Asia, over land and sea. Many traders took a share of the profit along the way. That is why European sailors looked for a route of their own to the spice lands. Later the Portuguese, then the Dutch and finally the British controlled the cinnamon trade from Ceylon.

Today cinnamon can be found in every shop. In Switzerland it is part of many **Christmas biscuits**, for example **cinnamon stars**. It is also sprinkled on rice pudding or apple sauce. In other countries it is also used to season meat dishes. Cassia cinnamon contains a substance that in large amounts can harm the liver, so it should be eaten only in moderation.

gewusst: The Greek historian Herodotus told the legend that great birds built their nests from cinnamon sticks.

teile.einleitung: At the Nuremberg Trials after the Second World War leading National Socialists stood in court. The victorious powers wanted to show that even the powerful are punished for serious crimes. The trials are regarded as the beginning of international criminal law.
wichtigste: The main trial in Nuremberg began in November 1945.
The judges came from the USA, Britain, France and the Soviet Union.
Nuremberg was chosen because the Palace of Justice was hardly destroyed.
On 1 October 1946 the court announced twelve death sentences.
Hermann Göring took his own life before his execution.
Albert Speer received 20 years in prison.
For the first time charges of crimes against humanity were brought before an international court.

abschnitte.text: After the end of the Second World War in 1945 the four victorious powers wanted to bring those mainly responsible to court. These were the **USA**, **Britain**, **France** and the **Soviet Union**. They formed the **International Military Tribunal**. As the place they chose **Nuremberg**, because the **Palace of Justice** was hardly destroyed and a prison lay right next to it. In addition the NSDAP had held its great party rallies in Nuremberg.

On 20 November 1945 the **main trial** began. Those accused were leading politicians, military men and officials of National Socialist Germany. Hitler himself was no longer alive. The highest-ranking defendant was **Hermann Göring**. The defendants had defence lawyers, and witnesses were questioned. So that everyone could follow, interpreting into four languages took place at the same time.

The charges were, among others, **crimes against peace**, that is, waging a war of aggression, and **war crimes**. New was the charge of **crimes against humanity**. By this were meant serious crimes against whole groups of people, such as the murder of the Jews of Europe. For the first time such an accusation was brought before an international court.

On 1 October 1946 the court announced its verdicts. There were **twelve death sentences**, several prison sentences and three acquittals. Hitler’s armaments minister **Albert Speer** received **20 years in prison**. Hermann Göring took his own life in prison shortly before his execution. After the main trial twelve further trials followed in Nuremberg, for example against doctors and lawyers.

The Nuremberg Trials showed that anyone who orders serious crimes cannot hide behind his office. This idea is taken up today by the **International Criminal Court** in **The Hague**. It began its work in 2002. Switzerland is among the states that support this court. The courtroom in which the main trial took place can be visited today.

gewusst: In Nuremberg simultaneous interpreting was used for the first time on a large scale, that is, translating at the same time as the speaking.
The courtroom is called “Room 600” and is part of a memorial site.

teile.einleitung: The Wild West is the name for the territories in the west of the USA that were opened up by settlers in the 19th century. For Native Americans this period meant expulsion and the loss of their homeland.
wichtigste: From the 1840s hundreds of thousands of settlers travelled west with covered wagons on the Oregon Trail.
The Homestead Act of 1862 gave settlers land if they farmed it for five years.
In 1869 the first transcontinental railroad in the USA was completed.
In the forced removal of the Cherokee in 1838, the Trail of Tears, thousands died.
The bison was almost wiped out, which took away the livelihood of the prairie peoples.
Many Native Americans were forced onto reservations.
The Wounded Knee massacre of 1890 is regarded as the end of the Indian Wars.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many people from the east of the USA and from Europe moved west. They hoped for land of their own and a better life. From the 1840s the **Oregon Trail** ran about 3,500 kilometres from Missouri to the Pacific coast in the north-west. The journey by **covered wagon** usually took four to six months. From 1848 the **gold rush** in California attracted tens of thousands more.

The **Homestead Act** of 1862 promised settlers about **65 hectares** of land. In return they had to farm it for five years. The gold rush in California began on the land of the **Swiss emigrant Johann August Sutter**. Gold was found there in 1848. For Sutter it brought no luck: gold seekers occupied his land, and he lost much of his property.

On **10 May 1869** the tracks from east and west met at **Promontory Summit** in Utah. The first **transcontinental railroad** was complete. Now you could travel across the USA in a few days. The railway brought still more settlers, traders and hunters to the west. For the peoples of the prairie, life became harder and harder as a result.

As early as **1838** the US government drove the **Cherokee** from the south-east to what is now Oklahoma. On this **Trail of Tears** thousands died of cold, hunger and disease. For the prairie peoples the **bison** was food, clothing and material. Hunters killed millions of bison until only a few hundred were left around 1890. Many peoples were forced onto **reservations**, which were often on poor land.

Many Native Americans fought back. In 1876 the Sioux and Cheyenne under **Sitting Bull** and **Crazy Horse** defeated the troops of General **George Custer** at the **Little Bighorn**. But in the end the US army was much stronger. In 1890 US soldiers killed hundreds of Lakota at **Wounded Knee** in South Dakota, among them many women and children. After that there was no more large armed resistance.

gewusst: Johann August Sutter was a citizen of Rünenberg in what is now the canton of Basel-Landschaft.
Many Western films show the Wild West quite differently from how it really was.

teile.einleitung: The Constitution of the United States is the most important law of the USA. It was signed in Philadelphia in 1787 and is still in force today.
wichtigste: The US Constitution was signed in Philadelphia on 17 September 1787 and came into force in 1789.
James Madison is regarded as the “Father of the Constitution”.
The first ten amendments are together called the “Bill of Rights”.
State power is divided into three branches that check one another.
Congress consists of the Senate and the House of Representatives.
The president is elected for four years, at most twice.
The Swiss Federal Constitution of 1848 took over the idea of two chambers.

abschnitte.text: After independence from Britain, the American states were only loosely connected. In 1787 delegates met in **Philadelphia** to create a new order. On **17 September 1787** they signed the Constitution, and in 1789 it came into force. **James Madison** had contributed many ideas and drafts, which is why he is called the “Father of the Constitution”. Later he became the fourth president of the USA.

The Constitution divides state power into **three branches**. **Congress** makes the laws, the **president** leads the government, and the **courts** administer justice. The three branches check one another so that nobody gets too much power. The highest court is the **Supreme Court**. It can declare laws unconstitutional.

Congress has two chambers: the **Senate** and the **House of Representatives**. In the Senate every state has two seats, no matter how big it is. In the House of Representatives the number of seats depends on the population. The **president** is elected for **four years**. Since an amendment of 1951 he may serve at most two terms.

Many people wanted the Constitution to protect their freedoms as well. So **amendments** were soon added. The first ten are together called the **Bill of Rights** and came into force in 1791. They protect basic rights such as **freedom of speech**, **freedom of the press** and **freedom of religion**. The Constitution has been changed only rarely up to the present day.

When Switzerland became a federal state in 1848, its authors also looked to the USA. They took over the idea of a **two-chamber system** with two chambers of equal standing. The **National Council** represents the people, much like the House of Representatives. The **Council of States** represents the cantons, much as the Senate represents the states. The seats in the National Council are distributed according to population, while in the Council of States most cantons have two seats.

gewusst: The US Constitution is regarded as the oldest written constitution of a state still in force.
It begins with the famous words “We the People”.

teile.einleitung: In the October Revolution of 1917 the Bolsheviks under Lenin took power in Russia. They overthrew the Provisional Government, which had governed after the end of Tsarist rule. From the revolution the Soviet Union later emerged.
wichtigste: The October Revolution took place in 1917 in Russia.
The Bolshevik party seized power in it.
Lenin travelled back to Russia from exile in Zurich in April 1917.
Leon Trotsky organised the armed uprising.
The cruiser Aurora gave the signal for the storming of the Winter Palace.
The slogan “Peace, land and bread” won many supporters.
A civil war between Reds and Whites followed.

abschnitte.text: Russia was fighting in the **First World War** and suffering heavy losses. In the cities bread was short and many people went hungry. In February 1917 Tsar Nicholas II had to abdicate. After that a **Provisional Government** ruled, that is, a government for a transitional period. But it carried on the war. At the same time workers and soldiers formed their own councils, the **soviets**.

The revolutionary **Vladimir Lenin** was then living in **exile** in **Zurich**. In April 1917 he travelled by train through Germany back to Russia. Germany allowed the journey because it hoped that Lenin would weaken Russia. Lenin led the party of the **Bolsheviks**. With the slogan **“Peace, land and bread”** it won many supporters among workers, soldiers and peasants.

abschnitte.titel: The storming of the Winter Palace
abschnitte.text: **Leon Trotsky** was chairman of the soviet in **Petrograd**, as Saint Petersburg was then called. He organised the armed uprising. On 25 October 1917 by the old Russian calendar the revolutionaries occupied important buildings. In the evening the **cruiser Aurora** gave the signal with a shot. During the night they stormed the **Winter Palace**, where the Provisional Government was meeting.

In 1917 Russia still used an older calendar than Western Europe. By this calendar the revolution took place in **October**. By our present calendar it was the beginning of **November**. That is why the anniversary was later celebrated in the Soviet Union on 7 November. The name October Revolution was kept all the same.

abschnitte.titel: Civil war and the Soviet Union
abschnitte.text: After the revolution the new government made peace with Germany in 1918. But many opponents did not want to recognise the Bolsheviks. A bloody **civil war** followed between the **Reds**, the supporters of Lenin, and the **Whites**, their opponents. The Reds won. At the end of 1922 the **Soviet Union** came into being, in which the Communist Party ruled alone.

gewusst: In Zurich Lenin lived on the Spiegelgasse in the old town, where a plaque recalls him today.
The cruiser Aurora still lies in Saint Petersburg today and is a museum ship.

teile.einleitung: The storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 in Paris is regarded as the beginning of the French Revolution. On that day an angry crowd captured an old fortress that served as a state prison. To this day France celebrates this day as its national holiday.
wichtigste: The Bastille was stormed on 14 July 1789 in Paris.
The Bastille was above all a state prison of the king.
The insurgents were looking there mainly for gunpowder and ammunition.
At the storming only seven prisoners were still in the Bastille.
About 100 attackers died, and the commander Bernard-René de Launay was killed.
The fortress was demolished afterwards.
14 July is today the national holiday of France.

abschnitte.text: The Bastille was built in the 14th century as a **fortress** on the eastern edge of Paris. It had eight mighty towers and thick walls. Later the kings used it as a **state prison**. Anyone who ended up there had often been locked up without a court verdict, only on the king’s order. That is why the Bastille was for many a symbol of arbitrary rule.

In the summer of 1789 bread was very expensive, and many people went hungry. In Versailles the **Estates General** were arguing about reforms, and the Third Estate had declared itself the National Assembly. The king drew troops together around Paris. On 11 July he dismissed the popular finance minister **Jacques Necker**, which greatly angered the Parisians.

In the morning the crowd took tens of thousands of rifles from the **Hôtel des Invalides**. But there was no powder for the rifles, and that was stored in the Bastille. After hours of fighting, in which about 100 attackers died, the commander **Bernard-René de Launay** gave up. He was afterwards killed by the crowd.

In the Bastille on that day there were only **seven prisoners** left. They were four forgers, two mentally ill men and a nobleman. The famous writer the Marquis de Sade had been transferred only a few days earlier. Even so the people celebrated the liberation as a great victory over the king’s **arbitrary rule**.

Soon after the storming people began to **demolish** the Bastille. Stones of the fortress were sold as souvenirs, and some were used for a bridge over the Seine. Today in its place is the **Place de la Bastille** with a tall column. In the ground paving stones mark where the walls once stood.

Since 1880 14 July has been the **national holiday** of France. In Paris a great military parade takes place on the Champs-Élysées, and in the evening there are fireworks. The day stands for the ideas of the Revolution: **liberty, equality, fraternity**. Many French speakers in Switzerland also know and celebrate this day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A heavily secured building for defence.
A prison in which the king could have people locked up without a trial.
A rapid, fundamental overthrow of the existing order.
When someone acts as they please, without keeping to rules or laws.

gewusst: The key of the Bastille was given by the Marquis de Lafayette to the American president George Washington, and it can still be seen in the USA today.
Stones of the Bastille were made into little models of the fortress and distributed throughout France.
The French national anthem, the Marseillaise, came into being only three years after the storming of the Bastille.

teile.einleitung: The Treaty of Versailles is the peace treaty with which the victorious powers laid down the terms for Germany after the First World War. It was signed on 28 June 1919 in the magnificent Hall of Mirrors of the Palace of Versailles near Paris. The treaty was meant to bring peace, but in Germany it caused great anger and put a heavy burden on the young Weimar Republic.
wichtigste: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
Germany was not allowed to take part in the negotiations and could only comment in writing.
Article 231 made Germany and its allies responsible for the damage caused by the war.
Germany lost territory and all its colonies and had to pay high reparations.
The German army was allowed to have at most 100,000 men.
The treaty founded the League of Nations, based in Geneva.
Many Germans called the treaty a “dictated peace”, which the Nazis later exploited.

abschnitte.text: After the armistice of 11 November 1918 the victorious powers met from January 1919 at the **Paris Peace Conference**. The most important men were US President Woodrow Wilson, the British prime minister David Lloyd George, the French head of government Georges Clemenceau and the Italian Vittorio Orlando. The treaty was signed on 28 June 1919 in the **Hall of Mirrors** at Versailles. The date was no coincidence: exactly five years earlier the Austrian heir to the throne had been murdered in Sarajevo. The treaty came into force on 10 January 1920.

Germany lost about an eighth of its territory. **Alsace-Lorraine** went back to France, and large parts of Posen and West Prussia went to the newly founded Poland. Danzig became a Free City under the supervision of the League of Nations. The Saar region was placed under League of Nations administration for 15 years, after which the population was to vote. All German **colonies** in Africa and in the Pacific were distributed to other states as mandates.

The German army was limited to 100,000 men, and general conscription was banned. Germany was not allowed to have an air force, tanks or submarines. The Rhineland was **demilitarised** and occupied by Allied troops. Germany also had to pay **reparations**, that is, compensation for the damage caused by the war. The amount was only fixed in 1921 and came to 132 billion gold marks.

The German delegation was not allowed to take part in the negotiations, which is why many spoke of a **dictated peace**. Article 231 in particular, the so-called **war guilt clause**, outraged people. At the same time the stab-in-the-back myth spread: the army, it was claimed, had been undefeated in the field and betrayed by the home front. This lie harmed democracy, because its politicians were denounced as traitors.

Versailles was only one of several peace treaties near Paris. With Austria the victorious powers concluded the **Treaty of Saint-Germain** in 1919, and with Bulgaria the Treaty of Neuilly. Hungary signed the Treaty of Trianon in 1920 and the Ottoman Empire the Treaty of Sèvres. Together these treaties completely redrew the map of Europe, and many new states such as Poland and Czechoslovakia came into being.

The first part of the treaty was the charter of the **League of Nations**, the first worldwide peace organisation, based in Geneva. Switzerland joined it in 1920. Adolf Hitler stirred up hatred against the “Versailles Diktat” and broke the treaty step by step from 1935, for example by rearming and by occupying the Rhineland in 1936. Many historians today think the treaty was too harsh to bring reconciliation, but too weak to restrain Germany permanently.

begriffe.erklaerung: Payments made by a country as compensation for damage it caused in a war.
A peace whose terms the losing side was not allowed to negotiate.
The false claim that the German army was betrayed by its own home front in 1918.
A former colony that was administered by another state on behalf of the League of Nations.

gewusst: The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles was already a historic place in 1871, because that was where the German Empire was proclaimed.
The USA did sign the treaty, but its Senate rejected it, so the USA never joined the League of Nations.
In 1935, after the 15 years had passed, the Saar region voted by a large majority to return to Germany.

teile.einleitung: Physiocracy was a school of economics in 18th-century France. Its followers, the physiocrats, were convinced that all the wealth of a country comes from the soil and from agriculture.
wichtigste: Physiocracy arose around 1750 in France.
The physician François Quesnay is regarded as its founder.
In 1758 Quesnay in the “Tableau économique” showed the economic cycle for the first time in a diagram.
According to this doctrine only agriculture produces a real surplus.
The physiocrats called craftsmen and merchants the “sterile class”.
The physiocrats demanded a single tax on the yield of the land.

abschnitte.text: The word **physiocracy** comes from Greek. **Physis** means nature, **kratos** means rule or power. What is meant, then, is a rule of nature. The physiocrats believed that in the economy there are natural laws, similar to those in nature. The state was to disturb this order as little as possible. They are regarded as one of the first scientific schools of economics.

The founder of physiocracy was the French physician **François Quesnay**. He was personal physician at the court of the French King Louis XV. Besides medicine he concerned himself with the economy. In 1758 he published the **“Tableau économique”**, in English roughly “economic table”. In it he showed for the first time in a diagram how goods and money flow between the groups of a society, rather like blood in the body.

Quesnay divided society into three groups. The **productive class** were the farmers. Only they, in his opinion, produced a real surplus, for from one seed many new grains grow. The second group were the **landowners**, to whom the land belonged. Craftsmen and merchants he called the **sterile class**. Sterile here means unfruitful: they process or sell things, but according to this doctrine produce no additional value.

Because only the land brings a surplus, the physiocrats demanded a **single tax on the yield of the land**. Many other duties and tariffs were to disappear, and trade in grain was to be free. The physiocrat **Anne Robert Jacques Turgot** tried from 1774 to 1776, as Controller General of Finances, to carry out such reforms in France. He met strong resistance and was dismissed. The ideas of the physiocrats later influenced the Scottish economist **Adam Smith**.

gewusst: Quesnay was already over 60 years old when he published his famous “Tableau économique”.
Today we know that crafts, trade and services also create value. But the idea of an economic cycle is still important today.

teile.einleitung: The Taiping Rebellion was a huge uprising in China from 1850 to 1864. It was directed against the ruling Qing dynasty. It is regarded as one of the costliest conflicts of the 19th century.
wichtigste: The rebellion lasted from 1850 to 1864.
The leader was Hong Xiuquan, who believed himself to be the younger brother of Jesus.
“Taiping Tianguo” means Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace.
In 1853 the Taiping made Nanjing their capital.
Zeng Guofan put down the rebellion with the Xiang Army.
According to estimates around 20 to 30 million people died.

abschnitte.text: The leader of the rebellion was **Hong Xiuquan**. He had failed several times in the difficult Chinese **civil service examinations**. Afterwards he had visions, which he interpreted in a Christian way. He believed himself to be the younger brother of Jesus. From his followers a religious and political mass movement arose.

The movement called its state **“Taiping Tianguo”**, which means Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace. The Taiping wanted to create a kingdom according to their religious ideas. These included **equality** and **common ownership of land**: the land was to belong to everyone together. Many poor peasants joined them.

The rebellion began in 1850 in the province of **Guangxi** in the south of China. The Taiping moved north and conquered many cities. In 1853 they made **Nanjing** their capital. They called it the “Heavenly Capital”, in Chinese Tianjing. For eleven years they ruled large areas from there.

The regular troops of the Qing failed against the Taiping. So the official **Zeng Guofan** built up an army of his own in the province of Hunan, the **Xiang Army**. Near Shanghai the “Ever Victorious Army”, led by foreigners under the Briton **Charles Gordon**, helped. In 1864 the Xiang Army captured Nanjing, and the rebellion was over.

Fighting, hunger and epidemics claimed enormous numbers of victims. According to common estimates **around 20 to 30 million people** died. Whole regions were laid waste. The rebellion greatly weakened the Qing dynasty. It is regarded as one of the costliest conflicts of the 19th century.

gewusst: After his service in China Charles Gordon received the nickname “Chinese Gordon”.
The Taiping ruled a state of their own in the middle of China for eleven years.

teile.einleitung: Vasco da Gama was a sailor from Portugal. He was the first European to find the sea route to India and reached the city of Calicut in 1498.
wichtigste: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese sailor who sailed on behalf of the king.
In July 1497 he set out from Lisbon with a small fleet of sailing ships.
He sailed along the coast of Africa and round the southern tip of the continent.
In May 1498 he reached Calicut in India.
Above all he brought spices such as pepper back to Europe.
With the sea route, traders no longer needed the long land route.

abschnitte.text: Spices such as **pepper**, cinnamon and cloves were very valuable in Europe. They came from Asia and travelled a long way over land and sea. On this **land route** many middlemen took a share of the profit, which is why the spices were expensive. Portugal wanted to find its own **sea route** to India. That way the Portuguese could fetch the goods directly.

In **July 1497** Vasco da Gama set out from **Lisbon**, the capital of Portugal. He commanded a small fleet of four **sailing ships**. The ships sailed south along the coast of **Africa**. As early as 1488 the Portuguese Bartolomeu Dias had rounded the southern tip of Africa. Vasco da Gama now sailed round the **Cape of Good Hope** and on northwards along the east coast of Africa.

In East Africa Vasco da Gama found an experienced pilot who knew the way across the **Indian Ocean**. In **May 1498** the fleet reached the city of **Calicut** on the west coast of India. There he bought spices and other goods. The negotiations with the ruler were difficult, however. Even so, the way to India had now been found.

The return journey was very hard. Many sailors died on the way of **scurvy**, an illness caused by a lack of vitamin C. In 1499 Vasco da Gama returned to Portugal and was celebrated. His cargo was worth far more than the cost of the voyage. Portugal then built up a large **sea trade** with Asia. Vasco da Gama later travelled to India twice more and died there in 1524.

gewusst: For the sea route to India, Vasco da Gama had to sail all the way round Africa, a journey of many thousands of kilometres.
One of the longest bridges in Europe, in Lisbon, is named after Vasco da Gama.

teile.einleitung: Urbanisation means that cities grow and more and more people live in cities instead of in the countryside. This happened especially strongly in the 19th century, when factories appeared everywhere with industrialisation. Today more than half of all people in the world live in cities.
wichtigste: Urban growth means the growth of cities, while urbanisation also covers the spread of urban ways of life.
A main cause in the 19th century was people leaving the land because of population growth and factory work.
In the cramped working-class districts, families often lived in dark and overcrowded tenement blocks.
Polluted drinking water spread dangerous diseases such as cholera.
Sewers and central water supplies made the cities healthier.
According to the United Nations, since about 2008 more than half of the world's population has lived in cities.
Zurich was greatly enlarged in 1893 when eleven suburbs were incorporated.

abschnitte.text: Experts use **urban growth** to mean that cities grow in area and population and the share of the urban population rises. The term **urbanisation** goes further: it also describes how urban ways of life spread, for example in housing, work and leisure. The Latin word “urbs” means city. Today even many people in the countryside live much like city dwellers.

In the 19th century the population of Europe grew strongly, but there was not enough work on the farms. At the same time the new **factories** in the cities needed many workers. So millions of people moved from the countryside into the city, which is called **rural flight**. The railway made it easier to travel long distances and to bring goods into the cities. Cities such as London, Paris, Berlin and Manchester grew enormously within a few decades.

Working-class families often lived crowded together in **tenement blocks**, which were densely built, multi-storey houses with dark back courtyards. Often many people shared one toilet and one tap. In 1845 Friedrich Engels described the wretched working-class districts of the English industrial city of **Manchester**. Children often had to help earn money from an early age, and diseases spread quickly.

In the cities, waste water often flowed into the same rivers and wells from which drinking water was fetched. This is how **cholera**, a dangerous diarrhoeal illness, spread. In 1854 the London doctor John Snow showed that a contaminated water pump caused the disease. After that many cities built a **sewer system** and a central water supply. Street lighting, trams and rubbish collection were also among the innovations of this time.

In Switzerland, too, the cities grew with industrialisation, above all Zurich, Basel, Geneva and Winterthur. In 1893 Zurich was greatly enlarged by the **incorporation** of eleven suburbs such as Aussersihl, Enge and Wiedikon. Later the cities spread into the surrounding countryside, and **agglomerations** with commuters came into being. Today the great majority of people in Switzerland live in cities and agglomerations.

According to the United Nations, since about 2008 more than half of the world's population has lived in cities. Cities are growing particularly fast today in Africa and Asia. Huge **megacities** such as Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai and Lagos each have well over ten million inhabitants. Many newcomers there, however, find room only in **slums**, that is, poor districts without clean water or safe houses.

begriffe.erklaerung: When many people leave the countryside to look for work and a better life in the city.
The spread of cities and of the urban way of life.
A large, densely built block of rented flats for many working-class families.
A city together with the surrounding municipalities that are closely linked to it.
A huge city with more than ten million inhabitants.

gewusst: Around 1800 only about one in twelve people in the world lived in a city.
Because many people in Berlin lived in back courtyards, there were buildings with up to five courtyards one behind the other.
Zurich's District 4 is still called Aussersihl today, after the former working-class municipality.

teile.einleitung: Scurvy is a disease that arises when the body gets too little vitamin C. In the past it was mainly sailors on long voyages who suffered from it. Many of them died of it until the remedy for it was found.
wichtigste: Scurvy arises from a lack of vitamin C.
Sailors often got scurvy on long voyages.
On board there was no fresh fruit and vegetables.
In scurvy the gums bleed, and teeth can fall out.
Lemons and limes protect against scurvy.
James Cook took sauerkraut on board his ships.

abschnitte.text: At the time of the great voyages of discovery ships were often away for months. The sailors ate mainly ship’s biscuit, salted meat and dried peas. There was hardly any fresh fruit and vegetables. That is why many got **scurvy**. On some voyages more sailors died of this disease than through storms or fighting.

Scurvy arises when the body gets too little **vitamin C**. The body needs this vitamin, among other things, for firm skin, blood vessels and gums. Humans cannot make vitamin C themselves. They have to take it in with food, for example from fruit, vegetables or potatoes.

At the start the sick feel tired and weak. Later the **gums** become soft and bleed. Bruises appear, and wounds heal badly. With time even teeth can fall out. Without vitamin C scurvy can be fatal, but with food rich in vitamins the sick usually recover quickly.

It was discovered that **lemons** and limes help against scurvy. They contain a lot of vitamin C. The British navigator **James Cook** had a great deal of **sauerkraut** brought on board on his voyages. It keeps for a long time and contains some vitamin C. Later British sailors regularly received lemon or lime juice.

Today scurvy is very rare in countries such as Switzerland. Anyone who eats a varied diet gets enough vitamin C. A lot of it is found in peppers, kiwis, oranges, berries and cabbage. Vitamin C is partly destroyed by long cooking, so raw fruit and vegetables are also valuable.

gewusst: British sailors got the nickname “Limeys” because they drank lime juice against scurvy.
Most animals can make vitamin C themselves, but humans cannot.

teile.einleitung: The Prague Spring was an attempt to make communism in Czechoslovakia freer and more humane. In 1968 the country experienced a short time full of hope, which was ended by force in August.
wichtigste: The Prague Spring took place in 1968 in Czechoslovakia.
It was led by the party chief Alexander Dubček.
The aim was called “socialism with a human face”.
Censorship was largely abolished.
In August 1968 troops of the Warsaw Pact marched in.
Romania did not take part in the invasion.
Switzerland took in thousands of refugees.

abschnitte.titel: A country in the Eastern Bloc
abschnitte.text: After the Second World War **Czechoslovakia** belonged to the so-called Eastern Bloc. The Communist Party decided everything, and the **Soviet Union** had great influence. People were not allowed to say their opinion freely, and newspapers were controlled. Many were dissatisfied, also because the economy was doing badly. The capital was Prague, which is today the capital of Czechia.

In January 1968 **Alexander Dubček** became head of the Communist Party. He wanted to keep socialism, but make it freer. For this the slogan **“socialism with a human face”** was coined. **Censorship** was largely abolished, so that newspapers, radio and television could report openly. People discussed freely, and many took great hope.

The leadership of the Soviet Union found the reforms went too far. It feared that other countries could follow the example. In the night of **21 August 1968** troops of the **Warsaw Pact** marched into Czechoslovakia. The Warsaw Pact was the military alliance of the Eastern Bloc states. **Romania** did not take part in the invasion and criticised it. The population mostly offered non-violent resistance, for example by removing street signs.

After the invasion many people left the country. **Switzerland** took in **thousands of refugees** from Czechoslovakia. Many Swiss people showed great helpfulness. The refugees found work here and built a new life. Some of them later became well known in Switzerland, for example in sport, art or science.

Dubček was removed in 1969. The new leadership reversed most of the reforms, and this time was called **normalisation**. Censorship returned, and many reformers lost their jobs. Only in 1989, with the peaceful **Velvet Revolution**, did communist rule end. Dubček afterwards became president of the parliament.

gewusst: The troops of East Germany stayed almost entirely at the border during the invasion.
Many people in Prague tried to talk to the invading soldiers instead of fighting.

teile.einleitung: Suleiman I, called the Magnificent, was Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. He reigned from 1520 to 1566, longer than any other Ottoman sultan. Under him the empire experienced one of its greatest golden ages.
wichtigste: Suleiman ruled the Ottoman Empire from 1520 to 1566.
In Turkey he is called “Kanuni”, the Lawgiver.
In 1521 he conquered Belgrade, in 1522 the island of Rhodes.
In 1526 he defeated Hungary at the Battle of Mohács.
In 1529 he besieged Vienna without success.
The architect Mimar Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque for him.
His wife Hürrem, called Roxelana in Europe, had great influence.

abschnitte.text: Suleiman became **sultan**, that is ruler of the Ottoman Empire, in 1520. He ruled for 46 years. In Europe he was called **the Magnificent**, because his court was so splendid. In Turkey he is called **“Kanuni”**, the Lawgiver. He had many laws collected and put in order.

Shortly after taking office Suleiman conquered the fortress city of **Belgrade** on the Danube in 1521. It was regarded as the key to Hungary. In 1522 he besieged the island of **Rhodes**. After a siege lasting months the **Knights of St John**, a Christian order of knights, had to leave the island. They later settled on Malta.
