In 1526 Suleiman defeated the Kingdom of Hungary at the **Battle of Mohács**. King Louis II died in it. After that a large part of Hungary came under Ottoman rule. In 1529 Suleiman besieged **Vienna**. He could not take the city and withdrew because of the approaching winter.

Under Suleiman magnificent buildings arose. The famous architect **Mimar Sinan** built in Istanbul the **Süleymaniye Mosque**, which is named after the sultan. Sinan is regarded as the most important architect of the Ottoman Empire. The mosque with its great dome still shapes the cityscape today.

Suleiman’s influential wife was called **Hürrem**, and in Europe she was called **Roxelana**. She came from Ruthenia, today the west of Ukraine, and came to the court as a slave. That the sultan married her was a break with tradition. She had great influence at court. Suleiman died in 1566 during a campaign in Hungary.

gewusst: Suleiman ruled for 46 years, longer than any other Ottoman sultan.
The Knights of St John, who had to leave Rhodes, are also called the Knights of Malta after their new island.

teile.einleitung: The Vietnam War was a long war in South-East Asia in which communist North Vietnam and South Vietnam, supported by the USA, fought against each other. From the mid-1960s the USA intervened with hundreds of thousands of soldiers. The war ended in 1975 with the victory of the North and is regarded as one of the most important events of the Cold War.
wichtigste: After the Geneva Conference on Indochina in 1954, Vietnam was provisionally divided at the 17th parallel.
Before that France had lost the Battle of Dien Bien Phu and withdrawn from Indochina.
The USA justified its intervention with the domino theory.
The Gulf of Tonkin incident of 1964 gave the US president far-reaching war powers.
The Tet Offensive of 1968 shook Americans' confidence in a quick victory.
After the Paris Agreement of 1973 the US troops withdrew.
With the capture of Saigon on 30 April 1975 the war ended.

abschnitte.text: Vietnam long belonged to the French colony of **Indochina**. After the Second World War the independence movement Viet Minh under Ho Chi Minh fought against France. In 1954 the French lost the Battle of **Dien Bien Phu** and withdrew. At the Indochina Conference in Geneva, Vietnam was provisionally divided at the 17th parallel. The planned elections for the whole of Vietnam never took place.

abschnitte.titel: The Cold War and the domino theory
abschnitte.text: In the north the communists ruled with the capital Hanoi, and in the south a Western-oriented government ruled in Saigon. According to the **domino theory**, the USA feared that after Vietnam the neighbouring states would also become communist. So they supported South Vietnam with money, weapons and advisers. Guerrillas known as the **Vietcong** fought against the government in the south. North Vietnam supplied them via the Ho Chi Minh Trail, a network of jungle paths through Laos and Cambodia.

After the **Gulf of Tonkin incident** in August 1964, President Lyndon B. Johnson received far-reaching war powers from Congress. From 1965 the USA bombed North Vietnam and sent ground troops. At the end of the 1960s over half a million US soldiers were in Vietnam. The army used helicopters, napalm and the defoliant **Agent Orange**, which was contaminated with toxic dioxin. It still damages the health of many people today.

At the beginning of 1968 the Vietcong and North Vietnamese troops launched the **Tet Offensive**, attacking many cities by surprise at the same time. Militarily the attack failed, but the pictures on television shocked the American public. In the same year US soldiers killed hundreds of civilians in the village of My Lai. In the USA and in Europe, including Switzerland, many young people demonstrated against the war. In this way the Vietnam War became the first “television war”.

President Richard Nixon wanted to leave the fighting more and more to the South Vietnamese army. In the **Paris Agreement** of January 1973 a ceasefire and the withdrawal of US troops were agreed. After that the war between North and South went on. On 30 April 1975 North Vietnamese tanks took Saigon, which was later renamed **Ho Chi Minh City**. In 1976 Vietnam was officially reunified.

Millions of Vietnamese people and about 58,000 US soldiers died in the war. Large parts of the country were devastated by bombs and poison. After the war many people fled across the sea in small boats, and they were called **boat people**. Switzerland, too, took in refugees from Vietnam at that time. In the USA the defeat still shapes thinking about wars abroad today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The idea that states become communist one after another, like falling dominoes.
Communist fighters in South Vietnam who fought against the government there and against the USA.
Warfare with small, mobile groups who attack from hiding.
A toxic weedkiller with which the US army stripped forests of their leaves.

gewusst: The conference that divided Vietnam in 1954 took place in Geneva.
A photograph from 1972 showing a crying girl burned by napalm became world famous and changed many people's view of the war.
The Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington bears the names of over 58,000 fallen US soldiers.

teile.einleitung: Telegraphy means sending messages over long distances. With the electric telegraph the message travelled as current through wires. For it Samuel Morse developed the famous Morse code of dots and dashes.
wichtigste: Samuel Morse developed a telegraph and the Morse code from 1837.
Before that Morse was a well-known painter.
The Morse code consists of dots and dashes.
The E is just a single dot.
The distress signal SOS is 3 short, 3 long, 3 short.
In 1844 Morse sent his first official message from Washington to Baltimore.
In 1866 a telegraph cable through the Atlantic linked Europe and America.

abschnitte.text: **Samuel Morse** was a well-known American **painter**. Only later did he turn to electricity. From 1837 he developed a **telegraph**. This included a code that bears his name: the **Morse code**. In 1844 he sent his first official message over a line of around 60 kilometres from **Washington to Baltimore**. It read “What hath God wrought”.

With the electric telegraph the message travelled as **current through wires**. The current flowed through long lines in seconds. So a message arrived much faster than a letter that travelled by stagecoach. Soon telegraph lines were built everywhere, often along the railway lines.

The Morse code consists of **dots and dashes**. A dot is a short signal, a dash a long one. Together they form letters and numbers. The **E** is just a single dot, because it is the most common letter in English. The famous distress signal **SOS** is three short, three long and three short signals. It is easy to send and easy to recognise.

A message sent with the telegraph is called a **telegram**. A telegram was usually short, because every word cost money. So unimportant words were left out. At the destination a telegraph operator wrote down the message, and a messenger took it to the home.

In 1866 a **telegraph cable** was successfully laid through the Atlantic. It lay on the sea floor and linked Europe with America. Messages now arrived in minutes instead of days or weeks. For laying the cable a huge ship was needed.

gewusst: The letter E in Morse code is just a single short dot.
Thomas Edison also worked as a telegraph operator as a young man.

teile.einleitung: A zeppelin is a huge airship with a rigid frame. It is named after Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, whose first airship rose over Lake Constance in 1900.
wichtigste: A zeppelin is a large airship with a rigid frame.
It is named after Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin.
On 2 July 1900 the first airship, LZ 1, rose over Lake Constance.
The old zeppelins were filled with light but flammable hydrogen.
Many zeppelins were built in Friedrichshafen.
In 1937 the airship Hindenburg burned while landing in the USA.

abschnitte.text: A zeppelin has a rigid **frame** of light metal covered with fabric. Inside there are large bags of **gas**. The gas is lighter than air, which is why the airship floats. Engines with propellers drive it forwards. Gondolas for the crew and passengers hang underneath.

**Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin** had long dreamed of building large airships. On **2 July 1900** his first airship, **LZ 1**, rose over **Lake Constance**. That was even before the first powered aeroplane. Lake Constance borders Germany, Austria and **Switzerland**. In **Friedrichshafen** on the northern shore, the great halls of the Zeppelin works later stood.

In the 1920s and 1930s people travelled by zeppelin across the **Atlantic**. The journey was much faster than by ship. On board there were dining rooms and cabins. The airship **“Graf Zeppelin”** even went once round the whole world in 1929. For many people it was a great experience to see a zeppelin in the sky.

The old zeppelins were filled with **hydrogen**. This gas is very light but can catch fire easily. In 1937 the huge airship **Hindenburg** caught fire while landing at **Lakehurst** in the USA. Many people lost their lives. After that the era of the large **passenger zeppelins** came to an end.

Today there are modern airships again, the **Zeppelin NT**. They are filled with **helium**, which does not burn. In Friedrichshafen you can take sightseeing flights over Lake Constance with them, sometimes also over Switzerland. There is also a large **Zeppelin Museum** there. It shows the history of airships.

gewusst: The Hindenburg was about 245 metres long, longer than two football pitches end to end.
Count Zeppelin was already over 60 years old when his first airship rose into the air.

teile.einleitung: Nazi propaganda is the name for the advertising and influencing with which the National Socialists steered the thinking of people in Germany from 1933 to 1945. Radio, newspapers, films, posters and large celebrations were meant to convince everyone of the ideology. Anyone who knows the tricks of propaganda can also recognise manipulation better today.
wichtigste: The Reich Ministry for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda was set up on 13 March 1933 and led by Joseph Goebbels.
From 1933 the Reich Chamber of Culture controlled people working in culture in the press, film, theatre and broadcasting.
The cheap People’s Receiver was meant to let as many people as possible hear the propaganda on the radio.
On 10 May 1933 books by unwanted authors were burned in many university towns.
Leni Riefenstahl made the propaganda film “Triumph of the Will” about the Reich Party Rally of 1934.
The 1936 Summer Olympics in Berlin were meant to give a false picture of a peaceful and open-minded country.
Photos and films from the Nazi period must be looked at critically as sources, because many were deliberately staged.

abschnitte.text: **Propaganda** is the deliberate attempt to steer the opinion of many people, often with exaggerations, lies and strong feelings. The National Socialists made it a central tool of their rule. They glorified Adolf Hitler as the “Führer” and portrayed Jews and political opponents as enemies. Simple slogans were repeated again and again until many believed them.

On 13 March 1933 the **Reich Ministry for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda** was set up. Its head was **Joseph Goebbels**, one of the most important men of the regime. The **Reich Chamber of Culture**, founded in 1933, controlled everyone working in culture in the press, film, theatre and broadcasting. Anyone who was not a member, for example because he was a Jew or counted as an opponent, was no longer allowed to practise his profession.

The regime promoted the cheap **People’s Receiver** so that as many people as possible heard the propaganda on the radio. Before every cinema film the newsreel ran with its glossed-over news. Leni Riefenstahl made the film “Triumph of the Will” about the Reich Party Rally of 1934, which was meant to impress with mass marches. Newspapers were only allowed to write what the government permitted, which is called **Gleichschaltung**, or forced coordination.

On 10 May 1933 books by unwanted authors were publicly burned in Berlin and many other university towns. Works by Erich Kästner, Heinrich Heine and Sigmund Freud, for example, were affected. In 1937 the exhibition **“Degenerate Art”** in Munich was meant to mock and condemn modern art. Many artists fled abroad, some also to Switzerland.

The regime used the 1936 Summer Olympics in Berlin to give the world a false picture of a peaceful and open-minded country. Anti-Jewish signs were even removed for that time. After the defeat at Stalingrad Goebbels asked on 18 February 1943 in the Berlin Sportpalast: “Do you want total war?” The carefully selected audience cheered, and the speech was broadcast throughout the Reich.

Many photos and films from the Nazi period were deliberately staged and selected for propaganda, so they must be looked at **critically as sources**. One asks, then: who made this, with what aim, and what is not shown? At that time Switzerland set its own values such as democracy and diversity against it with **Spiritual National Defence**. Today too these questions help us see through fake news on the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: Deliberate influencing of many people, often with lies and feelings instead of facts.
The forcing of newspapers, clubs and organisations under the control of the NSDAP.
A cheap radio set that almost every family could afford in the Nazi period.
Checking carefully who made a source and with what intention.

gewusst: The People’s Receiver had such weak reception that with it one could usually only hear German stations well.
Listening to foreign radio stations was forbidden in Germany during the Second World War and was severely punished.
On Bebelplatz in Berlin an underground room with empty bookshelves today recalls the book burning.

teile.einleitung: Resistance to Nazism covers all the people and groups who stood against Hitler's rule between 1933 and 1945. Some distributed leaflets, others hid people who were being persecuted, and a few even tried to kill Hitler. Many paid for their courage with their lives.
wichtigste: On 8 November 1939 Georg Elser carried out a bomb attack on Hitler on his own, in the Bürgerbräukeller in Munich.
Elser was arrested the same evening in Konstanz, just before the Swiss border.
The student group “White Rose” distributed leaflets against the regime in Munich.
Hans Scholl, Sophie Scholl and Christoph Probst were executed on 22 February 1943.
On 20 July 1944 Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg detonated a bomb in the Wolf's Lair.
In 1941 Bishop Clemens August Graf von Galen denounced the murders of sick and disabled people.
In the protest in Berlin's Rosenstrasse in 1943, wives secured the release of their Jewish husbands.

abschnitte.text: Resistance came from very different groups. From 1933 **communists** and Social Democrats fought underground, and many ended up in concentration camps. Christians of both denominations, students, workers, artists and later also officers stood against the regime. Others offered quiet resistance by hiding Jewish people or helping them to flee. Overall, though, the resistance was small, because most Germans went along with it or stayed silent.

The carpenter **Georg Elser** acted entirely alone. For months he built a bomb into a pillar of the Bürgerbräukeller in Munich at night, where Hitler gave a speech every year on 8 November. In 1939, however, Hitler left the hall 13 minutes earlier than planned, and the bomb killed other people. Elser was arrested the same evening in **Konstanz** while trying to get into Switzerland. Shortly before the end of the war, in April 1945, he was murdered in Dachau concentration camp.

The **White Rose** was a group of students and one professor in Munich. It included the siblings Hans and Sophie Scholl, Christoph Probst, Alexander Schmorell, Willi Graf and Kurt Huber. They wrote six **leaflets** in which they called for resistance against Hitler and the war. On 18 February 1943 the Scholl siblings were discovered in the university as they threw leaflets into the atrium. Only four days later they were executed together with Christoph Probst.

A group of officers and civilians wanted to kill Hitler and end the war. On 20 July 1944 Colonel **Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg** placed a briefcase containing a bomb in the Wolf's Lair headquarters in East Prussia. After that, **Operation Valkyrie**, a plan for dealing with internal unrest, was to be used for a coup. Hitler, however, survived with only slight injuries. Stauffenberg and other conspirators were shot in Berlin that same night, and hundreds of people were later arrested and many executed.

The Catholic Bishop of Münster, **Clemens August Graf von Galen**, publicly denounced the murder of sick and disabled people in sermons in 1941. The Protestant pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer supported the resistance and was executed in April 1945. In 1943 non-Jewish wives protested for days in Berlin's **Rosenstrasse** until their arrested Jewish husbands were released. Young people such as the Edelweiss Pirates also defied the Hitler Youth.

Swiss people, too, acted courageously against persecution. The St Gallen police commander **Paul Grüninger** allowed hundreds of Jewish refugees into Switzerland in 1938 despite a ban, and was dismissed for it. The Swiss diplomat **Carl Lutz** saved tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest with letters of protection. In Germany 20 July is now a day of remembrance. In the Bendlerblock in Berlin, where Stauffenberg was shot, there is the German Resistance Memorial.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fighting back against unjust rule, for example through protest, help for the persecuted or sabotage.
A printed sheet of paper with a message that is distributed secretly or openly.
An attempt to murder an important person, often for political reasons.
An attempt to remove the government suddenly and by force.

gewusst: If Hitler had stayed just 13 minutes longer in the Bürgerbräukeller on 8 November 1939, Elser's bomb would probably have hit him.
Sophie Scholl was only 21 years old when she was executed.
Paul Grüninger was fully rehabilitated by a court only in 1995, long after his death.

teile.einleitung: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was one of the most famous composers in the world. Even as a small child he played wonderfully and wrote music of his own.
wichtigste: Mozart was born in 1756 in Salzburg, which is now in Austria.
At about the age of 5 he was already writing little pieces of music.
His father Leopold Mozart was his first music teacher.
His older sister Maria Anna was called Nannerl.
As children Wolfgang and Nannerl travelled through Europe and played before kings.
In 1766 the family also visited Switzerland, for example Zurich.
His best-known pieces include “Eine kleine Nachtmusik”.

abschnitte.text: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in **1756** in **Salzburg**. The city is now in **Austria**. His father **Leopold Mozart** was a musician himself and taught his children. Wolfgang learned incredibly fast. At about **5 years old** he was already writing little pieces of music. That is why he is called a **child prodigy**.

Mozart had an older sister, **Maria Anna**, who was called **Nannerl**. She too played the piano superbly. Their father travelled through Europe with the two children, for example to Munich, Paris and London. They played before **kings and princes** and were marvelled at. The journeys by coach were long and tiring.

On the way home from a long tour, the Mozart family travelled through **Switzerland** in **1766**. They visited Geneva, Lausanne, Bern and **Zurich**, among other places. In Zurich the children gave **concerts**. After that the family travelled on towards Salzburg. Wolfgang was ten years old at the time.

As an adult Mozart lived in **Vienna**. He wrote over 600 works: **symphonies**, piano concertos, chamber music and **operas**. In 1787 he wrote **“Eine kleine Nachtmusik”**, whose cheerful melody many people know. The opera **“The Magic Flute”** of 1791 is also famous. In the same year Mozart died in Vienna, aged only 35.

gewusst: Mozart's works are arranged in the “Köchel catalogue”, which is why his pieces often have “K.” or “KV” followed by a number.
His birthplace in the Getreidegasse in Salzburg is now a museum.

teile.einleitung: An arms race is a race in which states build more and more and ever stronger weapons because they distrust one another. The best-known example is the nuclear arms race between the USA and the Soviet Union in the Cold War. In the end both sides had enough nuclear weapons to destroy the world several times over.
wichtigste: The USA built the first atomic bomb in 1945, and the Soviet Union followed in 1949.
The strategy MAD stands for mutually assured destruction.
Second-strike capability means being able to strike back devastatingly even after a nuclear attack.
In 1972 Nixon and Brezhnev signed the treaties SALT I and ABM.
The NATO Double-Track Decision of 1979 set off large peace demonstrations.
With the INF Treaty of 1987 whole categories of weapons were abolished for the first time.
Important summit meetings on disarmament took place in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: In an **arms race** one state feels threatened by another's weapons and arms itself. The opponent responds again with new weapons, and so the spiral keeps turning. Even before the First World War, Germany and Britain were competing to build up their war fleets. In the **Cold War** from 1945 it was mainly about nuclear weapons and missiles.

In 1945 the USA used atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and in 1949 the Soviet Union tested one too. Soon much more powerful hydrogen bombs followed. When the Soviet Union launched the satellite Sputnik into space in 1957, the Americans feared a **missile gap**, a Soviet superiority in missiles, which was in fact overestimated. Both sides built **intercontinental missiles** that can reach another continent in half an hour. In the mid-1980s there were at times over 60,000 nuclear warheads worldwide.

The strategy was called **MAD**, mutual assured destruction. What mattered was **second-strike capability**: even after a surprise attack, the attacked side could still have struck back devastatingly, for example with missiles on submarines. So nobody could have won a nuclear war. This state of affairs was called the balance of terror. In the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 the world was nevertheless close to nuclear war.

After the Cuban Missile Crisis negotiations began to limit the arms race. On 26 May 1972 Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev signed **SALT I** and the ABM Treaty on missile defence in Moscow. The SALT II treaty, signed in Vienna in 1979, never formally came into force because the US Senate did not ratify it after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. In the same year NATO adopted the **Double-Track Decision**: new intermediate-range missiles in Western Europe, combined with an offer to negotiate. Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated against it.

In 1983 US President Ronald Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative, a missile defence system in space that critics called **Star Wars**. From 1985 the new Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev sought understanding. In November 1985 Reagan and Gorbachev met for a famous summit in **Geneva**. With the **INF Treaty** of 8 December 1987, land-based nuclear missiles with a range of 500 to 5,500 kilometres were abolished.

In the 1950s and 1960s Switzerland also considered building nuclear weapons of its own, but gave up the idea. In 1969 it signed the **Non-Proliferation Treaty**. Out of fear of a nuclear war, Switzerland built **shelters** for almost the whole population. Geneva is still an important place for disarmament negotiations. Worldwide there are still about 12,000 nuclear warheads (as of 2025).

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of a missile or bomb that sets off the nuclear explosion.
Making an opponent so afraid of a counter-strike that he does not attack in the first place.
Reducing or abolishing weapons.
To make a signed treaty officially valid through parliament.

gewusst: Switzerland has so many shelters that almost all its inhabitants have a place in them, which is unique in the world.
After the Reagan-Gorbachev summit in Geneva in 1985, both declared that a nuclear war could not be won and must never be fought.
The most powerful bomb ever detonated, the Soviet “Tsar Bomba” of 1961, was about 3,000 times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb.

teile.einleitung: The Nuremberg Laws were racist laws that National Socialist Germany passed in September 1935. They made Jews into people with fewer rights and separated them from the rest of the population. With them the exclusion of the Jews had become law, an important step on the road to the Holocaust.
wichtigste: The Nuremberg Laws were passed on 15 September 1935.
They were announced at the NSDAP’s “Reich Party Rally of Freedom” in Nuremberg.
The Reich Citizenship Law gave full political rights only to people “of German or related blood”.
The “Law for the Protection of German Blood” banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews.
The Reich Flag Law is also often counted among the Nuremberg Laws.
Who counted as a “Jew” was decided by the religion of the grandparents.
The laws were repealed by Control Council Law No. 1 of 20 September 1945.

abschnitte.text: On 15 September 1935 the NSDAP’s Reich Party Rally took place in **Nuremberg**, which the party called the “Reich Party Rally of Freedom”. For this occasion the Reichstag was specially summoned to Nuremberg. There the deputies, all of whom belonged to the NSDAP, passed three laws without a single vote against. Since then these laws have been called the **Nuremberg Laws**.

The **Reich Citizenship Law** laid down that only people “of German or related blood” should have full political rights. The “Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour” banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews. In addition the **Reich Flag Law** made the swastika flag the flag of the Reich. The language of the laws was based on the false racial doctrine of the National Socialists.

The First Regulation to the Reich Citizenship Law of 14 November 1935 determined who counted as a “Jew”. Because there is no “Jewish race”, the authorities fell back on the **religious affiliation of the grandparents**. Anyone with three or four Jewish grandparents counted as a “Jew”, even if he himself was a Christian. People with two Jewish grandparents were called by the authorities persons of “**mixed descent** of the first degree”, and with one Jewish grandparent of “mixed descent of the second degree”.

Jews in Germany lost the right to vote and were no longer allowed to hold public office. They became second-class citizens and were pushed step by step out of working life, schools and clubs. Many tried to emigrate, but numerous countries, Switzerland among them, took in only a few refugees. The laws were followed by the November pogrom of 1938 and finally the **Holocaust**, in which around six million Jews were murdered.

After the Second World War the victorious powers repealed the laws with **Control Council Law No. 1** of 20 September 1945. Of all places, it was in Nuremberg that the trials of the main war criminals took place from November 1945. Today in Nuremberg the Documentation Centre on the former Reich Party Rally grounds recalls this time. The Nuremberg Laws show how injustice can also come in the form of law.

begriffe.erklaerung: The false idea that people can be divided into superior and inferior groups.
Hatred of and prejudice against Jews.
Under the Nuremberg Laws, a person with full political rights; Jews were excluded from this.
The joint government of the four victorious powers over Germany after 1945.

gewusst: The Nuremberg Laws were drafted in great haste; officials worked on them partly during the night before the vote.
Although the National Socialists spoke of “race”, to divide people they had to fall back on baptism certificates and religious entries.
In Nuremberg first the Reich Party Rallies and after the war the trials of the main Nazi war criminals took place.

teile.einleitung: The Moon landing was one of the greatest adventures of humankind: on 20 July 1969, with the Apollo 11 mission, humans landed on the Moon for the first time. Hundreds of millions of people around the world followed the event on television. Even an experiment from Switzerland was on board.
wichtigste: On 25 May 1961 President John F. Kennedy announced that a man would be put on the Moon and brought back safely before the end of the decade.
The lunar module Eagle of Apollo 11 landed in the Sea of Tranquility on 20 July 1969.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin set foot on the Moon, while Michael Collins stayed in the command module in lunar orbit.
The astronauts set up a solar wind sail from the University of Bern.
With the Moon landing the USA overtook the Soviet Union in the space race.
By 1972 a total of twelve astronauts had set foot on the Moon.

abschnitte.text: In the **Cold War** the USA and the Soviet Union also competed in space. In 1957 the Soviet Union sent the first satellite into space with Sputnik, and in 1961 the first human with Yuri Gagarin. The USA wanted to catch up. On 25 May 1961 President **John F. Kennedy** announced to Congress that a man would be put on the Moon and brought back safely before the end of the decade.

The crew of **Apollo 11** consisted of three astronauts. **Neil Armstrong** was the commander, and Buzz Aldrin flew with him in the lunar module. Michael Collins stayed in the command module Columbia and orbited the Moon. So he never set foot on the Moon, although he was so close.

On 16 July 1969 Apollo 11 launched with the huge **Saturn V rocket** in Florida. On 20 July the lunar module **Eagle** touched down in the **Sea of Tranquility**, a flat, dark plain. Armstrong had to steer the module by hand shortly before landing, because the planned landing site was full of boulders. A few hours later he stepped onto the surface of the Moon as the first human; in Europe it was already the morning of 21 July.

As the first experiment the astronauts set up a **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern. It consisted of a thin aluminium foil that caught particles of the solar wind. After about 77 minutes the foil was packed up again and brought to Earth. The experiment, led by the Bernese physicist Johannes Geiss, was the only non-American experiment of Apollo 11.

Armstrong and Aldrin stayed outside the module for about two and a half hours. They set up an American flag and measuring instruments, including a **laser reflector** that is still used today. They also collected around 21 kilograms of Moon rock. On 24 July 1969 the capsule landed safely in the Pacific.

With the Moon landing the USA had overtaken the **Soviet Union** in the space race, which never managed a crewed Moon landing. Up to the Apollo 17 mission in December 1972 five more Apollo missions landed, and in all twelve people set foot on the Moon. The Moon rock still helps researchers today to understand how the Moon came about. With the Artemis programme the USA now wants to bring people to the Moon again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who flies into space.
A small spacecraft with which astronauts landed on the Moon and took off again.
The path on which a spacecraft circles the Moon.
A stream of tiny particles that the Sun constantly hurls into space.

gewusst: The astronauts’ footprints can probably still be seen today, because there is no wind on the Moon.
The computers of Apollo 11 were far less powerful than a present-day smartphone.
The Bernese solar wind sail was set up before the American flag.

teile.einleitung: The Great Depression was the most severe economic collapse of the 20th century. It began in October 1929 with a stock market crash in New York and spread quickly across the whole world. Millions of people lost their jobs, and in Germany the hardship contributed to the rise of the Nazis.
wichtigste: On “Black Thursday”, 24 October 1929, prices collapsed on the New York stock exchange.
Germany was hit especially hard by the crisis because it depended heavily on short-term US loans.
In February 1932 there were around 6.1 million unemployed in Germany.
Reich Chancellor Heinrich Brüning pursued a strict policy of cutting spending.
Britain gave up the gold standard for the pound on 21 September 1931.
US President Franklin D. Roosevelt responded from 1933 with the New Deal.
Switzerland devalued the franc only in September 1936.

abschnitte.text: In the 1920s many people in the USA bought shares, often with borrowed money, because prices kept rising. On **Black Thursday**, 24 October 1929, everyone suddenly sold at the same time, and prices plunged. On the following Tuesday the crash continued. Many investors lost everything, banks went bankrupt and companies had to close. In Europe, because of the time difference, people often speak of “Black Friday”.

The American banks took their money back from abroad. Many countries raised their **tariffs** to protect their own economies, which made world trade shrink sharply. In the USA around 1933 about one worker in four was unemployed. Britain gave up the **gold standard** for the pound on 21 September 1931 so that it could manage its money more freely. Many other states followed.

After the First World War Germany had received many short-term **loans** from the USA, which were now called in. In July 1931 the Danatbank collapsed, all banks stopped payments and stayed closed for a few days. Reich Chancellor **Heinrich Brüning** cut wages and public spending, which made the hardship even worse. In February 1932 around 6.1 million people were unemployed. At the Lausanne Conference in 1932 the German reparations were practically ended, but by then it was politically already very late.

Many families had hardly enough to eat and queued at soup kitchens. Unemployed people travelled from town to town looking in vain for work. In the USA farmers lost their farms, and at the same time drought and dust storms in the Midwest turned whole regions into the **Dust Bowl**. Despair made many people open to radical parties that promised simple solutions.

From 1933 US President **Franklin D. Roosevelt** launched the **New Deal**. The state had roads, dams and schools built and so created work. Unemployment insurance and old-age pensions were new. The British economist John Maynard Keynes demanded that in crises the state should spend more money instead of saving. In Germany, by contrast, the Nazis used the crisis to come to power.

The Swiss export industry, for example watches, machinery and embroidery, lost many customers abroad. Unemployment rose, particularly in eastern Switzerland and in the Jura. For a long time Switzerland held on to the strong franc tied to gold. Only in September 1936 did the Federal Council devalue the **franc** by about 30 per cent. After that the economy slowly recovered.

begriffe.erklaerung: A marketplace where shares and other securities are traded.
A stake in a company whose price can rise or fall.
When a currency is deliberately made worth less so that exports become cheaper.
President Roosevelt's programme against unemployment and poverty in the USA.

gewusst: Because the crash in New York on Thursday only began in the evening European time, the news reached Europe on Friday, which is why it is called “Black Friday”.
The term “Great Depression”, meaning great low spirits, is still the name of this crisis in English.
The Great Depression is regarded as one of the reasons why the International Monetary Fund was later founded.

teile.einleitung: NATO is a military alliance of states from North America and Europe. It was founded in 1949 in order to protect its members together. Its most important promise is: if one member is attacked, all the others help.
wichtigste: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed on 4 April 1949 in Washington.
Twelve states were among the founding members.
Under Article 5 an attack on one member counts as an attack on all.
The Federal Republic of Germany joined in 1955.
Since 1967 NATO has had its headquarters in Brussels.
The mutual defence clause was invoked for the first time after the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001.
Switzerland is not a member, because a military alliance is incompatible with its neutrality.

abschnitte.text: NATO is the abbreviation for **North Atlantic Treaty Organization**. It is a **defence alliance**, that is, a union of states that protect one another. The members keep their own armies, but work closely together and train together. Decisions are taken unanimously in the North Atlantic Council, so every member has a say.

After the Second World War the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other as opponents, a time called the **Cold War**. Many Western European countries feared the power of the Soviet Union. On 4 April 1949 twelve states therefore signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, among them the USA, Canada, Britain, France, Italy and the Netherlands. As a counterpart the Soviet Union and its allies founded the **Warsaw Pact** in 1955.

abschnitte.titel: Article 5 and the mutual defence clause
abschnitte.text: The heart of the treaty is **Article 5**. It says that an armed attack on one member counts as an attack on all and that the others give assistance. How they help is decided by each country itself. This **mutual defence clause** has been invoked only once so far, after the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001 in the USA. After that many NATO states took part in the operation in Afghanistan.

The Federal Republic of Germany joined in 1955, and reunified Germany has been a member since 1990. France withdrew from military cooperation in 1966 and only returned fully in 2009. That is why the headquarters had to move from Paris to **Brussels**, where it has been since 1967. After the end of the Cold War many Eastern European states joined, most recently Finland in 2023 and Sweden in 2024, so that NATO has about 32 members (as of 2026).

Switzerland is not a member of NATO, because joining a military alliance would be incompatible with its **neutrality**. But since 1996 it has taken part in the **Partnership for Peace**, a programme of cooperation without an obligation of assistance. This involves, for example, training, disaster relief and promoting peace. Swiss soldiers serve, for example, in the Swisscoy in Kosovo on a peace mission under NATO leadership.

begriffe.erklaerung: States promise to help one another if attacked.
NATO’s mutual assistance clause: an attack on one counts as an attack on all.
The time from about 1947 to 1991 in which East and West stood in hostile opposition without waging war directly.
The military alliance of the Soviet Union and its allies from 1955 to 1991.

gewusst: During the whole Cold War the mutual defence clause was never invoked; it happened for the first time because of a terrorist attack in 2001.
Iceland is among the founding members of NATO, although it has no army of its own.
The Warsaw Pact dissolved in 1991, whereas NATO grew strongly afterwards.

teile.einleitung: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist. In 1895 he discovered invisible rays that pass through the body and with which you can see the bones.
wichtigste: In November 1895 Röntgen discovered invisible rays in Würzburg.
He called them “X-rays”; in German they are called Röntgen rays.
On an X-ray picture you can see mainly the bones clearly.
One of the first X-ray pictures shows the hand of his wife Anna Bertha.
Röntgen studied mechanical engineering in Zurich.
In 1901 he was the first person to receive the Nobel Prize in Physics.
He did not take out a patent so that everyone could use his discovery.

abschnitte.text: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was born in 1845 in Lennep, which is now part of Remscheid in Germany. He studied **mechanical engineering** in **Zurich** at the Polytechnic, today's ETH. He also earned his **doctorate** in Zurich. After that he did research and taught at various universities. Later he became professor of physics at the University of **Würzburg**.

In **November 1895** Röntgen was experimenting with glass tubes and electricity in his laboratory in Würzburg. He noticed that a screen nearby was glowing even though the tube was covered. So there had to be **invisible rays**. Because they were unknown, he called them **X-rays**. In English they are still called “X-rays” today, and in German we say **Röntgenstrahlen**.

Röntgen noticed that the rays pass easily through **skin and muscle** but poorly through **bone**. He X-rayed the hand of his wife **Anna Bertha**. In the picture you can see her bones and her **ring**. The picture quickly became known all over the world. People were amazed that you could see inside the body.

In 1901 the **Nobel Prizes** were awarded for the first time. Röntgen received the Nobel Prize in Physics. He took out **no patent** and earned no money from his discovery. So hospitals all over the world could quickly start using the rays. Röntgen died in Munich in 1923.

At the doctor's you often need an **X-ray**, for example for a **broken bone**. It shows whether and where a bone is broken. Dentists also take X-rays, to find holes in the teeth. X-rays can do harm in large amounts. So the body is protected during an X-ray, and people are X-rayed only when necessary.

gewusst: At the airport too, suitcases are scanned with X-rays.
The chemical element roentgenium is named after Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen.

t5ajgtl.t: Switzerland in the First World War

teile.einleitung: In the First World War from 1914 to 1918 Switzerland remained neutral and was not attacked. Even so they were difficult years: the army guarded the borders, people suffered from rising prices and hardship, and the country was divided within. At the same time Switzerland helped many victims of the war.
wichtigste: On 3 August 1914 the Federal Assembly elected Ulrich Wille as General.
At the mobilisation around 250,000 men reported for duty.
The “ditch” separated the German-friendly German-speaking part from the French-friendly French-speaking part.
In 1915 the war tax introduced the first direct federal tax.
From 1916 Switzerland took in around 68,000 wounded and sick prisoners of war.
The ICRC received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1917.
Many soldiers’ families fell into hardship because there was no compensation for loss of pay.

abschnitte.text: At the outbreak of war in August 1914 the Federal Council called up the army, and around **250,000 men** reported for duty. On 3 August 1914 the Federal Assembly elected **Ulrich Wille** as General. The soldiers guarded above all the borders in the Jura, where the Western Front reached very close to Switzerland. Over the war years many men served hundreds of days of active service.

Switzerland was divided within: many German-speaking Swiss sided with Germany, many French-speaking Swiss with France. This division was called the **ditch**. The **Colonels’ Affair** of 1915 and 1916 sharpened the dispute: two General Staff officers had passed secret reports on to Germany and Austria-Hungary. The writer Carl Spitteler warned in 1914 in a famous speech against the division of the country.

Switzerland wanted to remain neutral towards all the parties to the war. In 1917 Federal Councillor **Arthur Hoffmann** tried to broker a separate peace between Germany and Russia. This was seen as a **violation of neutrality**, because it would have benefited Germany, and Hoffmann had to resign. His successor was Gustave Ador of Geneva, who was at the same time president of the ICRC.

Because there was no **compensation for loss of pay** during military service, many soldiers’ families fell into hardship. The prices of food rose sharply, but wages hardly at all. From 1917 bread and other foods were rationed. To pay for the war the Confederation levied a **war tax** in 1915, the first direct federal tax.

From 1916 Switzerland took in around 68,000 wounded and sick **prisoners of war** from both sides to recover. They were housed, for example, in hotels in the mountains. The **International Committee of the Red Cross** ran a central agency in Geneva that searched for prisoners and passed news to families. For this it received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1917.

abschnitte.titel: End of the war and the General Strike
abschnitte.text: The hardship and the inequality led to great tensions between the working class and the middle class. In November 1918 trade unions and Social Democrats called the **General Strike**, in which around 250,000 people took part. The army was deployed, and the strike was called off after three days. At the same time thousands of people in Switzerland died of the Spanish flu.

begriffe.erklaerung: A country keeps out of the wars of other countries and supports neither side.
Calling up the army so that the soldiers are ready for action.
The military service that Swiss soldiers performed in wartime to protect the country.
Housing foreign soldiers or prisoners in a neutral country.
Each person receives only a fixed amount of a scarce good, for example bread.

gewusst: In the middle of the war artists founded the Dada art movement in 1916 in Zurich at the Cabaret Voltaire.
Lenin also lived in Zurich during the war before he returned to Russia in 1917.
Only in the Second World War did Switzerland introduce a system of compensation for loss of pay for soldiers.

teile.einleitung: Wherever European powers conquered colonies, the people resisted foreign rule. The resistance ranged from great battles and uprisings to non-violent protest such as that of Mahatma Gandhi in India. After the Second World War most colonies achieved independence.
wichtigste: Under Emperor Menelik II, Ethiopia defeated the Italian army at Adwa on 1 March 1896.
On 10 May 1857 the great uprising of Indian soldiers against British rule began in Meerut.
The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885.
Gandhi's Salt March of 1930 was directed against the British salt tax and salt monopoly.
Gandhi's method of non-violent resistance is called Satyagraha.
In the Maji Maji Rebellion in German East Africa many people died of a famine that was deliberately caused.
Abd el-Kader in Algeria, Abd el-Krim in Morocco and Yaa Asantewaa in Ghana became symbols of resistance.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century European states divided up almost the whole of Africa and large parts of Asia among themselves. The colonial rulers took land from the people, demanded taxes and often forced them to work. **Resistance** stirred everywhere against this. Sometimes armies fought, sometimes villages rose up, and later educated people organised themselves in parties. The colonial powers put down most uprisings with great harshness.

Italy wanted to make **Ethiopia** a colony. Emperor **Menelik II** gathered a large army equipped with modern rifles. On 1 March 1896 the Ethiopians defeated the Italians crushingly in the **Battle of Adwa**. Ethiopia then remained independent as one of only very few African countries. The victory gave courage to many people in Africa and worldwide.

abschnitte.titel: India: from the uprising to Gandhi
abschnitte.text: On 10 May 1857 Indian soldiers of the British army, the sepoys, rose up in **Meerut**. One trigger was the rumour that their rifle cartridges were greased with beef and pork fat, which offended Hindus and Muslims. The British put down the uprising and afterwards ruled India directly. In 1885 the **Indian National Congress** was founded, which later demanded independence. Under Mahatma Gandhi, India achieved independence in 1947.

**Mahatma Gandhi** developed the method of **Satyagraha**, which means roughly “holding on to truth”. Instead of violence he used boycotts, strikes and civil disobedience. In 1930 he marched with many followers about 390 kilometres to the sea in order to produce salt there himself. The **Salt March** was directed against the British salt tax and salt monopoly. Gandhi's ideas later also influenced Martin Luther King and Nelson Mandela.

In German East Africa, now Tanzania, many peoples fought from 1905 in the **Maji Maji Rebellion**. They believed that a holy water, “maji” in Swahili, would protect them from bullets. The German troops burned down villages and fields, which caused a famine with very many deaths. In German South West Africa, from 1904 Herero and Nama were killed in a **genocide**. In what is now Ghana, in 1900 the queen mother Yaa Asantewaa led the Ashanti fight against the British over the sacred Golden Stool.

The scholar and warrior **Abd el-Kader** led the resistance to the French conquest of Algeria from 1832 to 1847. In Morocco Abd el-Krim defeated the Spanish army in 1921 in the Battle of Annual. After the Second World War the colonial powers grew weaker, and **decolonisation** began. In 1960 especially many African states became independent. Algeria won its freedom in a bloody war from 1954 to 1962, and the peace agreements were signed in Évian on Lake Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area that is conquered and ruled by a foreign state.
Gandhi's method of resisting injustice without violence.
Deliberately and peacefully breaking an unjust law in order to protest against it.
The process in which colonies become independent states.

gewusst: In Ethiopia the anniversary of the Battle of Adwa on 1 March is still a national holiday today.
After the Salt March tens of thousands of people were arrested in India, including Gandhi himself.
In 2021 Germany officially recognised the murder of the Herero and Nama as genocide.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland all children have to go to school. This compulsory schooling has existed at federal level since 1874. The public primary school is free and is organised by the cantons.
wichtigste: Since 1874 the Federal Constitution has required all cantons to provide compulsory schooling.
Article 27 demanded compulsory and free primary teaching.
The cantons are mainly responsible for schools.
Attending the public primary school costs nothing.
Today compulsory schooling lasts 11 years in most cantons.
In 1882 the voters rejected the so-called “school bailiff”.
Compulsory schooling helped against child labour.

abschnitte.text: Even at the time of the **Helvetic Republic** people wanted to improve the schools. In 1799 the Helvetic minister of education **Philipp Albert Stapfer** had a great survey carried out of all the schools of Switzerland. It is called the **Stapfer Survey**. Teachers answered questions about their school, their pupils and their pay. So today we know a great deal about what the schools of that time looked like.

In the Federal Constitution of **1874** **Article 27** demanded that all cantons offer **compulsory** and **free** primary teaching. Compulsory means obligatory, free means without charge. Since then **compulsory schooling** has applied throughout Switzerland. The school was also to be under state direction and open to children of all denominations. In 1882 the Confederation wanted to supervise the schools more strongly with an official. The voters rejected this **“school bailiff”**, because they feared federal supervision of the schools.

In the 19th century many children had to work, for example in factories or on the farm. Compulsory schooling helped against **child labour**, because children had to be at school during the day. In addition the federal Factory Act of 1877 banned factory work for children under 14. The classrooms were plain at that time. The children often wrote on a **slate** with a stylus, because paper was expensive.

In Switzerland the **cantons** are mainly responsible for schools. That is why schools are not the same everywhere. The public **primary school** is **free** for all children. After **kindergarten** the children attend **primary school** and then lower secondary school. In most cantons compulsory schooling today lasts **11 years**, kindergarten included. Many cantons have agreed to regulate important things such as starting school and its length in the same way.

gewusst: The answers of the Stapfer Survey have survived and can be read on the internet today.
Some cantons had compulsory schooling long before 1874.

teile.einleitung: Winston Churchill was prime minister of Britain in the Second World War. With his speeches he gave people the courage to hold out against Hitler.
wichtigste: Churchill became British prime minister on 10 May 1940.
In his first speech he offered “blood, toil, tears and sweat”.
He made the V sign for “victory” famous.
In February 1945 he met Roosevelt and Stalin in Yalta.
In the election of July 1945 he lost to the Labour Party.
In 1946 he called at the University of Zurich for a United States of Europe.
In 1953 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature.

abschnitte.text: Winston Churchill was born in England in 1874. As a young man he was a soldier and war correspondent. After that he became a **politician** and held many important offices even before the Second World War. In the 1930s he warned early of the danger from **Hitler**. At that time, however, few people listened to him.

On **10 May 1940** Churchill became **prime minister**. On the same day Germany attacked France, Belgium and the Netherlands. Churchill never wanted to negotiate with Hitler. In his first speech he said honestly that he could offer only **“blood, toil, tears and sweat”**. His radio speeches gave people the courage to **hold out**, especially when German aircraft bombed British cities.

Churchill liked to hold up his **index and middle finger** in a V. The **V sign** stands for the English word **“victory”**. It became his trademark. He was also known for his **cigars** and his hats. To this day the V sign is widespread all over the world.

Britain fought against Hitler together with the **USA** and the **Soviet Union**. In **February 1945** Churchill, US President **Roosevelt** and **Stalin** met in **Yalta** in Crimea. They were called the “Big Three”. They discussed the future of Europe and the division of Germany after the war. In May 1945 the war in Europe was over.

Despite the victory Churchill lost the election in **July 1945**. The **Labour Party** under Clement Attlee won, because many people wanted social reforms. On **19 September 1946** Churchill gave a famous speech at the **University of Zurich**. He called for a kind of **“United States of Europe”**, and said that Germany and France should be reconciled. From 1951 to 1955 he was prime minister once more.

gewusst: Churchill received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953 for his historical works and speeches; he never received a Nobel Peace Prize.
In his free time Churchill liked to paint landscapes.

teile.einleitung: Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite to orbit the Earth. The Soviet Union shot it into space on 4 October 1957 and with it began the age of space travel. The little beeping metal ball caused a great shock in the West.
wichtigste: Sputnik 1 launched on 4 October 1957 as the first artificial Earth satellite.
It was a metal sphere and weighed about 84 kilograms.
The “Sputnik shock” describes the dismay in the West at the Soviet lead.
The launch rocket showed that the Soviet Union could bring nuclear warheads as far as the USA.
In reaction the USA founded NASA in 1958.
On 3 November 1957 the dog Laika flew into space with Sputnik 2.
On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin flew into space as the first human.

abschnitte.text: Sputnik 1 was a shiny sphere of metal with a diameter of about 58 centimetres. It weighed about **84 kilograms** and had four long **antennas**. Inside were batteries and a radio transmitter. The Russian word sputnik means companion or fellow traveller.

Sputnik 1 launched on 4 October 1957 from the **Baikonur** space centre in what is now Kazakhstan. An **R-7 rocket** brought it into an orbit in which it circled the Earth once in about 96 minutes. Its radio signal, a regular beeping, could be received by radio amateurs all over the world. After about three weeks the batteries were empty, and at the beginning of 1958 it burned up in the atmosphere.

In the Cold War the USA and the **Soviet Union** were rivals. The Americans had believed they were far ahead technically. The Soviet Union’s success caused the **Sputnik shock**. Especially worrying was that such a rocket could also carry nuclear warheads as far as the USA.

The USA launched its first satellite, Explorer 1, on 31 January 1958. In the same year they founded the space agency **NASA**. They spent much more money on schools, natural sciences and research. With that the **space race** between the two superpowers began.

Already on 3 November 1957 Sputnik 2 brought the dog **Laika** into Earth orbit, though she did not survive the flight. On 12 April 1961 **Yuri Gagarin** flew into space as the first human. Behind the successes stood the chief designer Sergei Korolev, whose name was kept secret at the time. The USA caught up and in 1969 were the first to land people on the Moon.

With Sputnik 1 the **age of space travel** began. Today thousands of satellites orbit the Earth. They help with weather forecasts, navigation, television and the internet. Without satellites, for example, the navigation systems in mobile phones would not work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body that orbits a planet, for example an artificial craft around the Earth.
The path on which a satellite circles the Earth.
The long hostility between the USA and the Soviet Union after 1945 without direct war.
A rocket that brings a satellite or a spacecraft into space.

gewusst: The beeping of Sputnik 1 could be heard with a simple radio receiver.
Sputnik 1 orbited the Earth about 1,400 times before it burned up.
The dog Laika was a stray from Moscow.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Verdun was one of the longest and worst battles of the First World War. Germans and French fought in 1916 for almost the whole year over the fortress town of Verdun in north-eastern France.
wichtigste: The Battle of Verdun began in February 1916.
Mainly Germans and French fought against each other.
Verdun lies on the Meuse.
In February 1916 German soldiers captured Fort Douaumont.
General Philippe Pétain led the French defence.
The French called the only supply road the “Sacred Way”.
In 1984 Helmut Kohl and François Mitterrand shook hands at Verdun.

abschnitte.text: **Verdun** is a town on the **Meuse** in the north-east of France. Around the town there was a ring of strong **forts**, that is, fortifications. On **21 February 1916** the German army attacked. The German leadership wanted to weaken the French army. The fighting lasted until December 1916, so almost the whole year.

Only a few days after the start of the attack German soldiers captured the important **Fort Douaumont**. After that General **Philippe Pétain** took over the leadership of the French defence. He saw to it that the troops were relieved regularly. So in the course of the battle very many French soldiers fought at Verdun. Later in the year the French recaptured Fort Douaumont.

To Verdun there led only a single usable road, over which supplies came. On it lorries drove day and night with soldiers, ammunition and food. Workers kept the road constantly in repair. The French called it the **“Sacred Way”**, in French Voie Sacrée. Without it Verdun could not have been held.

Because of the constant shelling and the many dead the battle was called the **“hell of Verdun”**. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers on both sides lost their lives. The landscape was strewn with shell craters, and whole villages disappeared. In the end the front had hardly shifted. Verdun became a symbol of the senselessness of war.

Today Verdun is a place of remembrance and **reconciliation**. In 1984 the German Chancellor **Helmut Kohl** and the French President **François Mitterrand** shook hands at Verdun. The picture went around the world. It showed that the former enemies Germany and France had become friends. Many school classes visit the memorials today.

gewusst: Some of the destroyed villages near Verdun were never rebuilt, but officially still have a mayor.
In the forest near Verdun one can still find traces of the shell craters today.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Jefferson was the third President of the United States. He wrote the Declaration of Independence of 1776 and governed from 1801 to 1809. He was a many-sided person, but also a man of contradictions.
wichtigste: Jefferson was the third President of the USA from 1801 to 1809.
In 1803 he bought the huge territory of Louisiana from France.
He sent the Lewis and Clark Expedition as far as the Pacific.
His self-designed country house is called Monticello.
In 1819 he founded the University of Virginia.
He wrote about freedom but owned hundreds of enslaved people.
He died on 4 July 1826, the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.

abschnitte.text: Thomas Jefferson was the main author of the **Declaration of Independence** of 1776. In it it says that all men are created equal. From 1801 to 1809 he governed as the **third president** of the USA. Before him George Washington and John Adams had held office.

In 1803 the USA under Jefferson bought a huge territory west of the Mississippi from **France**. The seller was Napoleon. This territory was called **Louisiana** and was much larger than the present-day state of that name. With the purchase the area of the USA roughly doubled.

Jefferson wanted to know what the West looked like. So he sent **Meriwether Lewis** and **William Clark** on an **expedition**. From 1804 to 1806 they travelled to the Pacific and back. They explored the land, the plants, the animals and the peoples who lived there.

Jefferson was very interested in **architecture**. He designed his country house **Monticello** in Virginia himself. In 1819 he founded the **University of Virginia** and even planned its buildings. He was prouder of that than of his presidency. Monticello and the university are today **UNESCO World Heritage**.

Jefferson wrote that all men are created equal. Even so he held **hundreds of enslaved people** all his life. This contradiction is often held against him to this day. Jefferson died on **4 July 1826**, exactly 50 years after the Declaration of Independence. On the same day John Adams also died.

gewusst: Jefferson and John Adams both died on 4 July 1826, the 50th birthday of the USA.
Jefferson’s face is carved in stone on Mount Rushmore, together with three other presidents.

teile.einleitung: Tulip mania was a period in the Netherlands when the prices of tulip bulbs rose sharply. At the beginning of 1637 they suddenly collapsed. It is often seen as one of the first speculative bubbles in history.
wichtigste: The tulip came to Europe from the Ottoman Empire.
From 1593 Carolus Clusius planted tulips in the garden in Leiden.
The most famous variety was the Semper Augustus.
Flamed patterns were caused by a virus spread by aphids.
In the wind trade, promises of delivery were traded instead of bulbs.
In February 1637 suddenly no buyers could be found in Haarlem.
More recent research holds that the consequences were much smaller than long claimed.

abschnitte.text: The tulip reached Europe from the **Ottoman Empire**. From 1593 the botanist **Carolus Clusius** planted tulips in the **Hortus botanicus**, the plant garden of Leiden University. From there the flower spread across the Netherlands. Soon many rich people wanted special tulips in their gardens.

Tulips with **flamed patterns** were especially sought after. The most famous variety was the **Semper Augustus**, with white petals and red flames. Prices of several thousand guilders were quoted for a single bulb. Today we know that the patterns were caused by a **virus** that is spread by **aphids**. This made the bulbs weaker and they multiplied more slowly, which made them even rarer.

Often the bulbs traded were still in the ground and were to be delivered only later. So people were buying only a **promise of delivery**. This trade was called the **wind trade**. Such deals were often made in taverns and hardly checked. Many hoped to be able to sell the bulbs on later at a higher price. This hope of rising prices is called **speculation**.

At the beginning of February 1637, at an auction in **Haarlem**, suddenly no buyers could be found. After that the prices of tulip bulbs fell quickly. Many promises of delivery were no longer kept. A situation in which prices rise sharply and then suddenly collapse is called a **speculative bubble**.

Tulip mania was made world famous by the author **Charles Mackay** in a book about mass delusions from 1841. He described it as a great disaster. More recent historians such as **Anne Goldgar** see it differently. Their studies of the sources show that only a small circle of traders took part. There was no general collapse of the Dutch economy.

gewusst: The most beautiful tulips of the tulip mania were actually ill, because their patterns came from a virus.
The Netherlands is still the most important country for growing tulip bulbs today.

teile.einleitung: The “economic miracle” is the name for the rapid economic upswing in West Germany after the Second World War. Other countries of Western Europe, including Switzerland, also experienced a long boom lasting into the 1970s.
wichtigste: The currency reform of June 1948 with the Deutsche Mark is regarded as the starting signal for the economic miracle.
Economics Minister Ludwig Erhard is regarded as the father of the social market economy.
From 1948 the US Marshall Plan supported the reconstruction of Western Europe.
The VW Beetle became the symbol of the economic miracle.
In France the boom years are called “Les Trente Glorieuses”.
Switzerland too experienced a long period of high economic activity.
The oil crisis of 1973 ended the long boom.

abschnitte.text: After the war Germany lay in ruins. The old money, the Reichsmark, was worth hardly anything any more. Many people exchanged goods directly with one another. On **20 June 1948** the **Deutsche Mark** was introduced in West Germany. Almost overnight the shop windows filled with goods again. This **currency reform** is regarded as the starting signal for the economic miracle.

In 1948 **Ludwig Erhard** abolished many price controls and relied on competition. He combined free markets with social balance, which is called the **social market economy**. From 1949 to 1963 he was economics minister. From 1948 the USA supported Western Europe with the **Marshall Plan**. It went back to a speech by Secretary of State George C. Marshall and supplied loans, raw materials and food.

In the 1950s and 1960s the economy grew very fast. Almost everyone found work, and wages rose. Many families could now afford a fridge, a television or a car. The **VW Beetle** was built in its millions and became the symbol of this time. In East Germany, by contrast, the **Trabant** was the best-known car.

Not only West Germany enjoyed an upswing. In **France** the years from 1945 to about 1975 are called **“Les Trente Glorieuses”**, the thirty glorious years. The term was coined by the economist Jean Fourastié in 1979. **Switzerland**, which had been spared the war, also enjoyed a long period of **high economic activity**. Many workers came from abroad, above all from **Italy**, to work in factories and on building sites.

In **1973** Arab oil-producing countries cut back oil production. The **oil price** rose sharply. This **oil crisis** ended the long period of the post-war boom. In Switzerland a **recession**, that is, a decline in the economy, followed in the mid-1970s. Hundreds of thousands of jobs were lost, and many foreign workers had to return to their home countries.

gewusst: Because of the oil crisis there were car-free Sundays in Switzerland and Germany in 1973.
The VW Beetle was built more than 21 million times.

teile.einleitung: William Shakespeare was an English poet and playwright. His plays such as “Romeo and Juliet” and “Hamlet” have been performed all over the world for over 400 years.
wichtigste: William Shakespeare was born in 1564 in Stratford-upon-Avon in England.
He lived and worked mainly in London.
He wrote mainly plays, and also poems.
Many of his plays were performed in the round Globe Theatre.
His best-known works include “Romeo and Juliet”, “Hamlet” and “A Midsummer Night's Dream”.
In his time young men and boys played the female roles.
Shakespeare died in 1616.

abschnitte.text: William Shakespeare was born in **1564** in the little town of **Stratford-upon-Avon** in England. You can visit his birthplace today. As a young man he went to **London**. There he worked as an **actor** and wrote plays. He belonged to a successful theatre company. Towards the end of his life he returned to Stratford, where he died in 1616.

Many of Shakespeare's plays were performed in the **Globe Theatre**. It was a round **wooden theatre** with no roof over the middle. Ordinary people stood in front of the stage, while richer spectators sat in the galleries. The Globe burned down in 1613. A **reconstruction** now stands again in London, near the old site.

Shakespeare wrote **tragedies**, that is, sad plays, and **comedies**, that is, funny plays. In **“Romeo and Juliet”** two young people fall in love in **Verona**, but their families are enemies. In **“Hamlet”** the prince says the famous line “To be or not to be”. In **“A Midsummer Night's Dream”** fairies and the sprite **Puck** play tricks in an enchanted wood. He also wrote many poems, the **sonnets**.

At that time **women** were not allowed to act on stage in England. So **young men and boys** took the female roles. There was hardly any scenery, and the audience had to imagine a lot. Instead, the characters described in their words where they were and what they saw. Performances took place in the afternoon in daylight.

Shakespeare's plays are performed all over the world and translated into many languages. They are often on the programme on Swiss stages too. Many films, operas and musicals are based on his stories. He is regarded as one of the most important poets in world literature. Many words and expressions of the English language go back to him.

gewusst: More than 150 sonnets by Shakespeare survive.
The musical “West Side Story” retells the story of Romeo and Juliet in New York.

teile.einleitung: On 11 September 1973 the military in Chile overthrew the elected government of President Salvador Allende. After that General Augusto Pinochet ruled the country for many years as a dictator.
wichtigste: The coup took place on 11 September 1973.
Salvador Allende had been elected in 1970 and led the Unidad Popular alliance.
Allende’s government nationalised copper, Chile’s most important export commodity, in 1971.
During the coup the presidential palace La Moneda was bombed.
General Augusto Pinochet remained head of state until 1990.
In 1998 Pinochet was arrested in London.

abschnitte.text: In 1970 **Salvador Allende** was elected President of Chile. He led the left-wing alliance of parties **Unidad Popular**, which means popular unity. Allende wanted to turn the country socialist by democratic means. Large estates were divided up, and many businesses came into the ownership of the state. In 1971 **copper**, Chile’s most important export commodity, was completely **nationalised**. That means the mines now belonged to the state.

The reforms were very controversial. One part of the population supported Allende, another part sharply rejected his policy. The economy got into difficulties, with high price rises and many strikes. The USA too was against Allende’s government and supported his opponents. The tensions in the country grew greater and greater.

On **11 September 1973** the military staged a coup. A **coup** is the violent overthrow of a government. Fighter aircraft bombed the presidential palace **La Moneda** in the capital Santiago. Allende died in the palace. A military government under General **Augusto Pinochet** took power. Parliament was dissolved, and parties were banned.

Under Pinochet thousands of opponents were arrested, and many were killed or disappeared without trace. Among the victims was the well-known singer and songwriter **Víctor Jara**. After the coup he was murdered in a stadium in Santiago that today bears his name. Many people fled abroad, and **Switzerland** also took in refugees from Chile. In 1988 the population voted in a referendum against a further term of office for Pinochet, and in **1990** he gave up the office of head of state.

After 1990 Pinochet remained commander-in-chief of the army. In **1998** he was arrested during a stay in **London**. The basis was an **arrest warrant from Spain** for crimes during his rule. After more than a year he was allowed to return to Chile for health reasons. He died in 2006 without having been convicted.

gewusst: The arrest of Pinochet in London was an important signal: even former heads of state can be called to account abroad for crimes.
The La Moneda palace was originally a mint, hence its name, because “moneda” means coin.

teile.einleitung: The Soviet Union was once the largest state in the world and consisted of 15 Union republics. Between 1989 and 1991 this huge state broke apart step by step. In the end 15 independent countries emerged, including Russia, Ukraine and the Baltic states.
wichtigste: Before its dissolution the Soviet Union consisted of 15 Union republics.
From 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev tried to modernise the country with reforms.
On 11 March 1990 Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare independence.
The August coup of 1991 against Gorbachev failed after three days.
Boris Yeltsin became the symbol of resistance to the coup plotters.
In a referendum on 1 December 1991 about 92 per cent of Ukrainians voted for independence.
At the end of December 1991 the Soviet Union ceased to exist.

abschnitte.text: The **Soviet Union**, abbreviated USSR, was founded in 1922 and stretched from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific. In the end it consisted of 15 **Union republics**, such as Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Kazakhstan and the three Baltic states. It was ruled by the Communist Party, and there were no free elections. In the 1980s the economy was deep in crisis, and simple goods were often missing in the shops.

In 1985 **Mikhail Gorbachev** became head of the Communist Party. With **glasnost**, meaning openness, people were allowed to speak more freely and raise problems. With **perestroika**, restructuring, he wanted to improve the economy. But the new freedom led many peoples in the Soviet Union to demand more self-determination or even independence.

On 23 August 1989 around two million people in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania formed a human chain, the **Baltic Way**. They were marking the 50th anniversary of the Hitler-Stalin Pact, through which their countries had fallen to the Soviet Union in 1940. On 11 March 1990 **Lithuania** became the first Soviet republic to declare independence. On 13 January 1991 Soviet troops attacked the television tower in Vilnius, and 14 people died.

On 17 March 1991 about 76 per cent voted in a referendum for a renewed union. Several republics such as the Baltic states, however, did not take part at all. On 12 June 1991 **Boris Yeltsin** was elected president of the Russian Soviet Republic in a free election. A new **Union Treaty** was to give the republics more rights and was to be signed on 20 August 1991.

On 19 August 1991 communist hardliners tried to seize power and prevent the Union Treaty. The official figurehead of their State Committee on the State of Emergency was **Gennady Yanayev**. Gorbachev was held at his dacha in Foros in Crimea. In Moscow Boris Yeltsin climbed onto a tank in front of the **White House**, the seat of the Russian parliament, and called for resistance. After three days the **coup** collapsed.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Soviet Union
abschnitte.text: After the coup many republics declared their independence, Ukraine as early as 24 August 1991. In the **referendum** of 1 December 1991 about 92 per cent of Ukrainians voted for it. On 8 December Russia, Ukraine and Belarus founded the **Commonwealth of Independent States** (CIS). On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned, and the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin. With that the Cold War was finally over too.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the 15 constituent states of the Soviet Union, similar to a large member state.
Russian word for openness: people were allowed to speak and criticise more freely.
Russian word for restructuring: Gorbachev's plan to renew the economy and the state.
An attempt by a small group to seize power in a state by force.
A popular vote on an important question.

gewusst: The human chain of the Baltic Way was over 600 kilometres long and linked the capitals Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius.
Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990 but later became very controversial in his own country.
In area the Soviet Union was about 540 times as big as Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Operation Overlord was the great landing of the Allies in Normandy in the north of France during the Second World War. On 6 June 1944, the so-called D-Day, tens of thousands of soldiers went ashore. It was the largest landing operation by sea that there has ever been.
wichtigste: The landing in Normandy began on 6 June 1944.
The Allied commander-in-chief was the US General Dwight D. Eisenhower.
The troops landed on five beaches: Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword.
Through the deception “Fortitude” the Germans believed the main landing would come at the Pas-de-Calais.
Artificial harbours, the Mulberry harbours, ensured supplies.
Erwin Rommel was responsible for the German coastal defence.
Paris was liberated on 25 August 1944.

abschnitte.text: Since 1940 National Socialist Germany had held France occupied. The Allies, above all the USA, Britain and Canada, wanted to open a second front in the west. As the place they chose the coast of **Normandy** in northern France. The supreme command was held by **Dwight D. Eisenhower**, and the land forces were led by the British General Bernard Montgomery.

With the deception operation **Fortitude** the Allies faked a huge army in south-east England. There were dummy tanks made of rubber and false radio messages. The German leadership therefore expected the main landing at the **Pas-de-Calais**, where the English Channel is narrowest. Because of bad weather Eisenhower postponed the attack by a day to 6 June.

During the night paratroopers jumped behind the coast. In the morning soldiers from thousands of ships and boats landed on five beaches: the Americans at **Utah** and **Omaha**, the British at Gold and Sword, the Canadians at Juno. At Omaha Beach the losses were especially high, because the German positions there were hardly damaged. By the evening around 150,000 soldiers had come ashore.

Field Marshal **Erwin Rommel** had the coast strengthened with bunkers, mines and obstacles on the beach, the so-called Atlantic Wall. Because the Allies could not capture a large port straight away, they simply brought their harbours with them. The **Mulberry harbours** were put together off the coast from huge concrete sections. Through them came tanks, lorries, fuel and food ashore.

After weeks of hard fighting the Allies broke out of Normandy in the summer. On 15 August 1944 a second landing on the French Mediterranean coast followed with **Operation Dragoon**.
