On 25 August 1944 **Paris** was liberated. The landing was a decisive step towards the end of the Second World War in Europe, which came in May 1945.

Every year on 6 June memorial ceremonies take place in Normandy. In large military cemeteries, such as the American cemetery near Colleville-sur-Mer, thousands of fallen soldiers lie. Museums and remains of bunkers recall the fighting. Many people visit the beaches to remember the victims.

begriffe.erklaerung: The military name for the day on which an attack begins, here 6 June 1944.
The allied countries that fought against Germany, such as the USA, Britain and Canada.
A chain of German bunkers and barriers along the coast from Norway to France.
An artificial harbour made of floating and sunken concrete sections.
The entry of troops into an area, here from the sea.

gewusst: For the deception “Fortitude” the Allies built inflatable rubber tanks that looked real from the air.
One of the two Mulberry harbours was destroyed by a severe storm only two weeks after the landing.
The time of the landing was chosen so that the Moon and the tides were as favourable as possible.

teile.einleitung: A hooped skirt is a wide skirt that is held in shape by hoops underneath. Over several centuries distinguished ladies in Europe wore such skirts, sometimes so wide that they could hardly fit through a door.
wichtigste: A hooped skirt is a wide skirt with hoops underneath.
The hoops were made of wood, cane, whalebone or later steel.
Hooped skirts showed that a woman was distinguished and rich.
Under the dress ladies wore a corset tight around the upper body.
With a wide hooped skirt it was difficult to get through a door.

abschnitte.text: A **hooped skirt** is an underskirt in which several **hoops** are sewn. Over it one wore the actual dress, which as a result stood out wide and bell-shaped. The hoops were made of wood, cane or **whalebone**, which comes from the mouth of whales. In the 19th century thin **steel** hoops were used. Hooped skirts came up in the 16th century in Spain and then spread to the princely courts of Europe.

The hooped skirt showed that a woman was **distinguished**. With such a dress one could hardly work, and the great amount of fabric was expensive. Under the dress ladies wore a **corset** tight around the upper body. It was reinforced with firm stays and laced tightly so that the waist looked slim. In the 18th century hooped skirts were popular that stood out wide above all at both sides. In the 19th century the round **crinoline** followed.

Some hooped skirts were **so wide** that the wearers could not simply walk through a door. They had to turn sideways or squeeze the skirt together a little with their hands. Even sitting, getting into a carriage or climbing stairs was tiresome. Two ladies side by side needed a lot of room. Later fashion became narrower and more comfortable again.

gewusst: With the crinoline of light steel hoops women needed fewer heavy petticoats to make the skirt wide.

teile.einleitung: Extermination camps were camps that the Nazis built during the Second World War solely to murder people on a massive scale. Most of the victims were Jewish people from all over Europe. The extermination camps stand for the greatest crime in human history, the Holocaust.
wichtigste: Extermination camps served mainly for the immediate murder of the deportees.
All the extermination camps were in occupied Poland.
The first extermination camp is considered to be Chelmno (Kulmhof), where from December 1941 Jews were murdered in gas vans.
Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka belonged to “Operation Reinhard”.
About 1.1 million people were murdered in the Auschwitz camp complex.
The Red Army liberated Auschwitz on 27 January 1945.
In the Holocaust the Nazis murdered around six million Jewish people.

abschnitte.text: In **concentration camps** the Nazis locked people up and made them work in cruel conditions, and many died there. **Extermination camps** such as Treblinka, on the other hand, served mainly for the immediate murder of the people who were brought there. Most of the victims were killed in **gas chambers** on the very day they arrived. The perpetrators tried to keep their crimes secret.

The Nazis persecuted Jewish people out of hatred and racist delusion. From 1941 they moved on to systematic mass murder, which is called the **Holocaust** or, in Hebrew, the **Shoah**. At the **Wannsee Conference** in January 1942, senior officials discussed how to organise this murder. People from all over Europe were deported to the east in goods trains.

All the extermination camps were in occupied Poland. The first is considered to be **Chelmno** (Kulmhof), where from December 1941 Jews were murdered in gas vans. The camps of Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka belonged to **Operation Reinhard**. People were also murdered in gas chambers in Majdanek and in the **Auschwitz** camp complex.

Auschwitz was a concentration camp and an extermination camp at the same time. In the part of the camp called **Auschwitz-Birkenau** there were large gas chambers. About 1.1 million people were murdered in the camp complex, the great majority of them Jews. Poles, Sinti and Roma, and Soviet prisoners of war were also among the victims.

Even in the camps, prisoners fought back. In August 1943 there was an **uprising** in Treblinka and in October 1943 in Sobibor, in which some prisoners managed to escape. On 27 January 1945 the **Red Army** liberated the Auschwitz camp. There it found only a few thousand survivors, seriously ill and emaciated.

27 January is now **International Holocaust Remembrance Day**. In Auschwitz there is a memorial site that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is visited by many school classes every year. Survivors have written down and told their memories so that nobody forgets. In Switzerland, too, there is discussion about how the country treated Jewish refugees at that time, whom it sometimes turned away at the border.

begriffe.erklaerung: The mass murder of around six million Jewish people by the Nazis.
The Hebrew word for the Holocaust, meaning catastrophe.
The forced removal of people to another place.
A place where victims and crimes are remembered.

gewusst: To hide their crimes, the perpetrators tore down the camps of Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka as early as 1943 and planted trees there.
The diary of Anne Frank is among the best-known testimonies from this period; she died in 1945 in the Bergen-Belsen camp.
In Israel the Yad Vashem memorial commemorates the victims and honours people who saved Jews.

teile.einleitung: The Renaissance was a time of new beginnings in Europe, from about 1400 to 1600. People rediscovered the art and knowledge of the ancient Greeks and Romans and created famous works of art and inventions.
wichtigste: Renaissance means “rebirth”.
The Renaissance lasted from about 1400 to 1600.
Immediately before it came the Middle Ages.
People admired the art of the ancient Greeks and Romans again.
From about 1450 printing helped to spread knowledge quickly.
The rich banking family of the Medici supported many artists.
Leonardo da Vinci painted the “Mona Lisa”.

abschnitte.text: The French word **Renaissance** means **“rebirth”**. What is meant is that the art and knowledge of the **ancient Greeks and Romans** came to life again. The Renaissance began around **1400** in Italy and spread over the whole of Europe until about **1600**. Before it came the **Middle Ages**. Many people now put the human being and his abilities more at the centre. This way of thinking is called **humanism**.

One centre of the Renaissance was the city of **Florence**. There lived the rich banking family of the **Medici**. They gave artists, architects and scholars commissions and money. Such supporters are called **patrons**. Thanks to them magnificent paintings, statues and buildings arose. Popes in Rome and princes in other cities also had great artists create works for them.

The painters of the Renaissance learned **perspective**. With it pictures look spacious and deep, as if one could walk into them. They studied exactly how people, animals and plants look. **Leonardo da Vinci** painted the famous **“Mona Lisa”**. Other great artists were **Michelangelo** and **Raphael**. Leonardo was also an inventor and researcher and drew plans for flying machines.

Around **1450** **Johannes Gutenberg** in Mainz invented **printing** with movable metal letters. Before that, books had to be laboriously copied out by hand. Now many books could be made quickly and more cheaply. So new knowledge and new ideas spread throughout Europe. **Basel** also became an important city of printing.

In **Basel** the first university in Switzerland was founded in 1460. The famous scholar **Erasmus of Rotterdam** lived and worked in the city for many years. The painter **Hans Holbein the Younger** worked in Basel for a long time. Among other things he painted portraits of Erasmus and murals for houses in the city. Later he became court painter to the English King Henry VIII.

gewusst: Leonardo da Vinci wrote many of his notes in mirror writing, from right to left.
The Kunstmuseum Basel owns one of the largest collections of works by the Holbein family.

teile.einleitung: The American Civil War, also called the War of Secession, lasted from 1861 to 1865. The Northern states fought against the breakaway Southern states. It was above all about slavery.
wichtigste: The war lasted from 1861 to 1865.
The Northern states (the Union) fought against the Southern states (the Confederacy).
Eleven Southern states founded the Confederate States of America.
The war began in April 1861 with the attack on Fort Sumter.
The Battle of Gettysburg in 1863 is regarded as the turning point.
General Lee surrendered in April 1865 at Appomattox.

abschnitte.text: In the Southern states of the USA millions of enslaved people worked, above all on plantations. In the North **slavery** was banned. The dispute over it grew ever fiercer. When Abraham Lincoln was elected president in 1860, several Southern states left the Union. This leaving is called **secession**, hence the name of the war.

On one side stood the **Union** of the Northern states. On the other side eleven Southern states founded the **Confederate States of America**, whose president was Jefferson Davis. The North had more people, factories and railways. The South had experienced officers and mostly fought on its own ground.

In April 1861 troops of the Southern states shelled **Fort Sumter** in South Carolina. With that the fighting began. In July 1863 the army of the Southern states was beaten at **Gettysburg** in Pennsylvania. After that the South could no longer push into the North. The battle is therefore regarded as the turning point of the war.

The best-known general of the Southern states was **Robert E. Lee**. He was regarded as a very skilful commander. On the Northern side **Ulysses S. Grant** led the troops to victory. Grant later became President of the USA himself, from 1869 to 1877.

On 9 April 1865 Lee surrendered at **Appomattox Court House** in Virginia. With that the war was practically over. The war had cost a very great number of lives. Shortly afterwards slavery was abolished throughout the USA. The country now had to grow together again.

gewusst: The Civil War cost more American soldiers’ lives than most of the other wars of the USA.
President Abraham Lincoln was murdered only a few days after the end of the war.

teile.einleitung: Trenches are long ditches dug into the earth in which soldiers sought protection from enemy fire. In the First World War they stretched along the Western Front from the North Sea to the Swiss border.
wichtigste: When the fronts hardly move in trenches, it is called trench warfare.
The area between the enemy trenches was called No Man’s Land.
Barbed wire protected the trenches further.
If the feet stayed wet and cold for a long time, soldiers got trench foot.
In 1915 the German army used poison gas on a large scale for the first time at Ypres.
In the south the trenches of the Western Front reached the Swiss border.
At Christmas 1914 there was a spontaneous truce, the Christmas Truce.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the **First World War** in 1914 the armies advanced quickly. Soon, however, the soldiers dug themselves into **trenches** to protect themselves from rifles and cannon. The fronts afterwards hardly moved for years. This way of waging war is called **trench warfare**. The trenches of the **Western Front** stretched from the North Sea coast in Belgium to the **Swiss border** in the south, near Bonfol in what is now the canton of Jura.

The trenches ran in a zigzag so that an enemy who broke in could not fire along the whole trench. There were dugouts for sleeping, communication trenches and trenches for supplies. In rain the soldiers often stood in **mud** and water. If their feet stayed wet and cold for a long time they got **trench foot**, a painful illness of the feet. Rats and lice were a constant plague.

abschnitte.titel: No Man’s Land and barbed wire
abschnitte.text: Between the enemy trenches lay **No Man’s Land**. It was full of shell craters, and anyone who entered it was in great danger. In front of the trenches the soldiers strung **barbed wire** to hold up attacking soldiers. In attacks the troops tried to reach the enemy trenches across No Man’s Land. Mostly this succeeded only with very great losses.

To end trench warfare the armies used new weapons. In 1915 the German army used **poison gas** on a large scale for the first time at the Belgian town of **Ypres**. Soon the other armies also used gas. The soldiers therefore received **gas masks**. Later **tanks** were added, which were meant to drive over trenches and barbed wire.

At **Christmas 1914** something astonishing happened at some places on the Western Front. Without orders soldiers stopped shooting. They sang Christmas carols, met in No Man’s Land, exchanged small presents and buried their dead. This spontaneous truce is called the **Christmas Truce**. The army commands did not want to allow anything like it again, and in the following years there was hardly anything similar.

gewusst: The Western Front was around 700 kilometres long.
At some Christmas meetings in 1914 soldiers are said even to have played football in No Man’s Land.

teile.einleitung: The Treaties of Rome were signed in Rome in 1957. With them six states founded the European Economic Community, an important forerunner of today’s European Union.
wichtigste: The Treaties of Rome were signed in 1957.
Six states signed them.
With them the European Economic Community, EEC for short, was founded.
At the same time the European Atomic Energy Community came into being.
Britain did not belong to the founding states.
The EEC is a forerunner of today’s EU.

abschnitte.text: On **25 March 1957** representatives of **six states** signed two treaties in **Rome**. These states were **Belgium**, the **Federal Republic of Germany**, **France**, **Italy**, **Luxembourg** and the **Netherlands**. Because the signing took place in Rome, they are called the **Treaties of Rome**. They came into force on 1 January 1958. After the terrible wars the countries wanted to secure peace and prosperity through cooperation.

With the first treaty the **European Economic Community**, **EEC** for short, was founded. Its aim was a **common market**. Goods were to be traded between the member countries without customs duties. Towards other countries common tariffs applied. Later people, money and services were also to be able to move freely. With the second treaty the **European Atomic Energy Community** came into being for the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

**Britain** did not belong to the founding states. At that time it did not want to enter into such close cooperation. Together with other countries it founded the **European Free Trade Association**, **EFTA** for short, in 1960. **Switzerland** was also a founding member of EFTA. Britain joined the European Community in 1973 and left the EU again in 2020.

abschnitte.titel: From the EEC to the EU
abschnitte.text: The EEC gradually became the **European Union**. In 1993 the EU came into being with the Maastricht Treaty. More and more countries joined. The treaty founding the EEC still applies in altered form today. **Switzerland** is not a member of the EU, but regulates its relations with many **bilateral treaties**. The EU is a very important trading partner for Switzerland.

gewusst: For the 60th anniversary of the Treaties of Rome the heads of state and government of the EU met in Rome again in 2017.
The six founding states had already founded the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951.

teile.einleitung: The Titanic was a huge British passenger ship. In the night of 14 to 15 April 1912 she sank on her first voyage after colliding with an iceberg. It is one of the best-known shipwrecks in history.
wichtigste: The Titanic sank in April 1912 on her maiden voyage.
She set off from Southampton and was to go to New York.
In the North Atlantic she collided with an iceberg.
Many had thought her unsinkable beforehand.
There were too few lifeboats for everyone on board.
Of around 2,200 people over 1,500 died.
The Carpathia picked up the survivors from the boats.

abschnitte.text: The Titanic was one of the largest ships of her time. She was regarded as especially safe, and many called her **unsinkable**. On 10 April 1912 she left **Southampton** in the south of England. The destination was **New York** in America. It was her very first journey, the **maiden voyage**.

In the night of 14 to 15 April 1912 the Titanic was sailing through the cold **North Atlantic**. There she struck an **iceberg**. The hull was torn open, and water poured in. After less than three hours the ship sank. The disaster showed that the Titanic was not unsinkable.

On the Titanic only about half of the people had room in the **lifeboats**. Of around 2,200 people on board **over 1,500** died. Only about 700 survived. After the disaster the rules were changed: since then every ship needs enough lifeboats for everyone.

The Titanic sent **distress calls** by radio. The ship **Carpathia** received them and hurried to the scene. She arrived only after the sinking. The Carpathia rescued the people from the lifeboats and brought them to New York.

The wreck of the Titanic lies in the **Atlantic** at a depth of around 3,800 metres. Only in 1985 was it found by researchers. The ship has broken into two large parts. To this day books, museums and films recall the disaster.

gewusst: The wreck of the Titanic was discovered only in 1985, more than 70 years after the sinking.
Because of the Titanic there have been international rules for safety at sea since 1914.

teile.einleitung: The Tokugawa shogunate was the rule of the Tokugawa family over Japan from 1603 to 1867. During this time the shoguns, who were military rulers, governed the country while the emperor had hardly any power. In this period Japan largely closed itself off from the world.
wichtigste: Tokugawa Ieyasu became the first shogun of the Tokugawa period in 1603.
The shoguns ruled from Edo, which is now Tokyo.
The closing off of Japan is called Sakoku.
Only the Dutch were allowed to trade, on the island of Dejima in Nagasaki.
The Sankin-kōtai system forced the lords to live at the shogun's court in alternate years.
In 1853 the American Matthew Perry forced Japan to open up.
The rule of the Tokugawa ended in 1867.

abschnitte.text: After long wars, **Tokugawa Ieyasu** came out on top in the struggles that followed the death of the ruler Hideyoshi. In 1603 he was appointed **shogun**. A shogun was a supreme military ruler. The emperor stayed in **Kyōto** but had hardly any power. The Tokugawa family ruled Japan until 1867, which is more than 250 years.

The shoguns ruled from **Edo**, which is now Tokyo. In the 18th century Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world. Under the **Sankin-kōtai** system, the lords, called **daimyō**, had to live with the shogun in Edo every second year. Their families stayed there permanently. The costly journeys weakened the daimyō financially, so they remained dependent on the shogun.

From the 1630s onwards Japan largely closed itself off. This policy is called **Sakoku**, which means roughly “closed country”. Japanese people were no longer allowed to leave the country, and foreign trade was strictly limited. After the **Shimabara Rebellion** of 1637 and 1638, in which many Christian peasants took part, Christianity was persecuted even more harshly. In 1639 the Portuguese were expelled.

Only a few foreigners were still allowed to trade. Of the Europeans, it was only the **Dutch**. They lived on the artificial island of **Dejima** in the harbour of Nagasaki. The Dutch East India Company was seen as harmless because it did not try to convert people. Western knowledge, for example about medicine, reached Japan through Dejima.

In 1853 the American commodore **Matthew Perry** appeared with warships in the Bay of Edo. The Japanese called them the **“Black Ships”**. In 1854 Japan had to open ports to American ships in the Treaty of Kanagawa. The power of the shoguns grew weaker. In 1867 the Tokugawa shogunate came to an end, and the emperor took over the government again.

gewusst: In the 18th century Edo, today's Tokyo, was one of the largest cities in the world.
The island of Dejima was built up artificially and was so small that you could walk around it in a few minutes.

teile.einleitung: The Opium Wars were two wars in the 19th century between China and European powers. Britain wanted to sell the narcotic opium in China, and China wanted to prevent that. China lost both wars and afterwards had to give up many rights.
wichtigste: The First Opium War lasted from 1839 to 1842.
In it China fought against Britain.
China was then ruled by the Qing dynasty.
In 1839 Lin Zexu had over 1,000 tonnes of British opium destroyed at Humen.
In the Treaty of Nanking in 1842 China had to cede Hong Kong.
In 1860 European troops destroyed the Old Summer Palace near Beijing.
The Chinese call such treaties “Unequal Treaties”.

abschnitte.text: In the 18th and 19th centuries the British drank a great deal of **tea** from China. They paid for it with **silver**. China hardly wanted to buy any British goods. So more and more silver flowed to China. To stop this **outflow of silver**, British merchants sold **opium** to China. The drug was grown in India, which at that time was under British rule.

China was then ruled by the **Qing dynasty**. Many people became addicted to opium and fell ill. The emperor banned the trade, but it went on in secret. In 1839 he sent the official **Lin Zexu** to Canton as imperial commissioner. At **Humen** Lin Zexu had over 1,000 tonnes of British opium seized and destroyed. Britain then sent warships.

The **First Opium War** lasted from **1839 to 1842**. The British steamships and cannon were far superior to the Chinese troops. China lost the war. In the **Treaty of Nanking** it had to cede the island of **Hong Kong** to Britain in 1842. In addition China had to open five ports to trade and pay a high compensation.

From 1856 to 1860 the **Second Opium War** followed. This time Britain and France fought together against China. In 1860 their troops reached Beijing. There they looted and destroyed the **Old Summer Palace**, a magnificent imperial complex with gardens and palaces. China had to open further ports, and the opium trade was allowed.

The treaties that China had to conclude under pressure in the 19th century are called in China the **Unequal Treaties**. They gave foreign powers many advantages, but China hardly any rights. Many Chinese still see this time today as a time of **humiliation**. Hong Kong stayed British for a long time. Only in 1997 did Britain give Hong Kong back to China.

gewusst: At Humen the opium was mixed with salt and lime and flushed into the sea.
The ruins of the Old Summer Palace in Beijing can still be visited today.

teile.einleitung: Simón Bolívar was a South American freedom fighter. He led several countries of South America to independence from Spain. To this day he is revered as “El Libertador”, the Liberator.
wichtigste: Bolívar was born in 1783 in Caracas, today the capital of Venezuela.
He fought against Spanish rule in South America.
In 1819 he founded the state of Gran Colombia.
Bolivia is named after him.
The currency of Venezuela is also called the bolívar.
He died in December 1830 near Santa Marta in present-day Colombia.

abschnitte.text: Simón Bolívar was born in 1783 in **Caracas**. He came from a rich family. As a young man he travelled through Europe. In August 1805 he swore on **Monte Sacro**, a hill near Rome, not to rest until South America was freed from Spanish rule.

At that time large parts of South America belonged to **Spain**. Brazil, by contrast, was a colony of Portugal. Bolívar led armies against the Spanish troops. After defeats he received help from **Haiti** in 1815 and 1816: President Alexandre Pétion gave him weapons and ships. In return Bolívar promised to abolish slavery in the liberated territories.

In 1819 Bolívar founded the state of **Gran Colombia**. It covered roughly the present-day countries of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Panama. Bolívar dreamed of a united South America. But there was a great deal of quarrelling between the regions. In 1830 and 1831 Gran Colombia fell apart again into separate states.

In the south of the continent **José de San Martín** was fighting at the same time. He led the independence of Argentina, Chile and Peru. In 1822 the two liberators met in Guayaquil. In 1825 **Bolivia** received its name in honour of Bolívar, and he was the first president of the country.

At the end Bolívar was ill and politically stripped of power. He died in December 1830 near **Santa Marta** on the Caribbean coast. In 1842 his remains were brought to Caracas. Today many squares, streets and the currency of Venezuela bear his name.

gewusst: A whole country, Bolivia, bears the name of Simón Bolívar.
In almost every larger city in South America there is a Plaza Bolívar or a monument to him.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of the Somme was one of the largest and costliest battles of the First World War. It took place in 1916 in northern France and lasted several months.
wichtigste: The battle took place in 1916 on the Somme in Picardy.
British and French attacked the German positions.
For a week the attack was preceded by continuous artillery bombardment.
On the first day the British army suffered the highest daily losses in its history.
In September 1916 the British used tanks for the first time.
In all, more than a million soldiers were killed, wounded or missing.

abschnitte.text: The battle took place on the **Somme**, a river in **Picardy** in northern France. It began on **1 July 1916** and lasted until November. At that time the First World War was already almost two years old. The fronts in the west hardly moved, and the soldiers lay facing each other in **trenches**. The **British** and the **French** wanted to break through the German lines and at the same time relieve the French troops at **Verdun**.

For a week the British shelled the German positions without a break with **artillery**, that is, with large guns. They hoped in this way to put the defenders out of action. But many German soldiers had survived in deep dugouts. When the British attacked on 1 July they hardly made progress. On this one day the **British army** suffered the highest losses in its history. The commander-in-chief was General **Douglas Haig**.

In **September 1916** the British used **tanks** for the first time on the Somme. This new weapon was meant to be able to drive over trenches and barbed wire. The first tanks, however, were slow and loud and often got stuck or broke down. Even so they showed how war would change in future. Later tanks became one of the most important weapons.

After about four and a half months the attackers had gained only a few kilometres of ground. In all, **more than a million soldiers** were killed, wounded or missing. Among the British soldiers was the young officer **J. R. R. Tolkien**, who later wrote “The Lord of the Rings”. Today many cemeteries and memorials in Picardy recall the battle.

gewusst: Many British volunteers fought in units together with friends and neighbours from the same town.
Tolkien fell ill on the Somme and was sent home, where he began his first stories about Middle-earth.

teile.einleitung: Mercantilism was an economic policy pursued in many European states from the 16th to the 18th century. The state was to become rich and powerful by selling more goods than it bought. Absolutist kings in particular, such as Louis XIV in France, used this idea.
wichtigste: The most important aim was a favourable balance of trade, with more exports than imports.
The French form is called Colbertism, after the minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert.
Typical were high duties on imported finished goods and low duties on raw materials.
Colonies were to supply raw materials and buy goods from the mother country.
In the German states the variant was called cameralism.
Adam Smith criticised mercantilism in 1776 in his work on the “wealth of nations”.
The Physiocrats set against it the motto “Laissez faire, laissez passer”.

abschnitte.text: In mercantilism people believed that a country’s wealth consists above all of gold and silver. Because this amount seemed limited, a country was to bring in as much money as possible and let little go out. That is why a **favourable balance of trade** was aimed at, that is, more exports than imports. With the money the king could pay for the army, the fleet and the court.

To protect its own economy, the state demanded high **duties** on imported finished goods. Raw materials, on the other hand, could enter the country cheaply so that they were processed at home. The state founded and promoted **manufactories**, large workshops in which many workers produced goods with a division of labour. Roads and canals were also built so that goods could be transported faster.

In France **Jean-Baptiste Colbert** headed the finances of King Louis XIV from 1665. He promoted the making of luxury goods such as mirrors, tapestries and silk. He also had trading companies founded and a strong fleet built up. After him the French form of mercantilism is called **Colbertism**.

In mercantilism colonies had a clear task: they supplied cheap **raw materials** such as sugar, cotton or tobacco and bought goods from the mother country. In 1651 England issued the **Navigation Act**. After it, goods could be brought to England only in English ships or in ships of the country of origin. This was directed above all against the Netherlands, which then dominated sea trade.

In the German states the variant was called **cameralism**, after the princely chamber that managed the finances. It was strongly geared to state finances and good administration. Princes such as the kings of Prussia tried to bring more inhabitants into the country so that more work was done and more taxes were paid. In this way Brandenburg-Prussia took in numerous Huguenot refugees from France in 1685.

In the 18th century mercantilism was criticised more and more. The French **Physiocrats** demanded more freedom for the economy with the motto “Laissez faire, laissez passer”. The Scottish economist **Adam Smith** explained in 1776 that wealth arises from work and free trade and not from hoarded gold. When states today protect their economy with high duties, this is called protectionism.

begriffe.erklaerung: A comparison between the value of the goods a country exports and those it imports.
A fee that has to be paid when goods are taken across a border.
A large business in which many people make goods by hand with a division of labour.
The sending of goods out to another country.
Protection of one’s own economy from foreign competition, for example through duties.

gewusst: The word mercantilism comes from the Latin word for merchant, “mercator”.
The famous Gobelin tapestries from Paris were made in a royal manufactory that Colbert promoted.
The term mercantilism was only coined later by the critics of this policy.

teile.einleitung: The Second Industrial Revolution began around 1870. Electricity, chemistry and cheap steel fundamentally changed people's work and daily lives.
wichtigste: The Second Industrial Revolution from about 1870 was shaped by electrical engineering and chemistry.
With the Bessemer process of 1856, steel could be made cheaply in large quantities.
In 1883 Emil Rathenau founded what became AEG as the “Deutsche Edison-Gesellschaft”.
In 1891 a line from Lauffen to Frankfurt proved that electricity can be transmitted over long distances.
The Basel chemical industry began with synthetic dyes.
From 1913 the Haber-Bosch process made ammonia for artificial fertiliser possible.
Large corporations with their own research laboratories emerged.

abschnitte.text: The **First Industrial Revolution** was based on steam engines, coal and textile factories. From about **1870** new industries were added: **electrical engineering** and **chemistry**. Large **corporations** with their own research laboratories came into being. Science and industry now worked closely together. New inventions reached the factories much faster.

Steel is harder and tougher than iron, but was long expensive. **Henry Bessemer** found a new process in 1856. In the **Bessemer converter**, **air is blown through liquid pig iron**. This burns off the excess carbon, and steel is produced in a few minutes. Now rails, bridges, ships and machines could be built in large quantities from steel.

Light bulbs, electric motors and trams conquered the cities. In 1883 **Emil Rathenau** founded the **Deutsche Edison-Gesellschaft**, which from 1887 was called **AEG**. In 1891 **three-phase current** was sent about 175 kilometres **from Lauffen to Frankfurt**. This proved that electricity can be transmitted over long distances. The **Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon** in Zurich played a major part in it.

Chemists learned to make substances artificially in the laboratory. In 1880 **Adolf von Baeyer** succeeded in the first synthesis of the blue dye **indigo**. BASF brought synthetic indigo onto the market in 1897. In **Basel**, firms such as **Geigy, Ciba and Sandoz** first produced **coal-tar dyes** for the textile industry. Later they turned to medicines, and out of this grew today's Basel pharmaceutical industry.

Plants need **nitrogen** to grow. **Fritz Haber** developed a method for making **ammonia** from nitrogen and hydrogen. **Carl Bosch** made the process usable industrially at BASF, and production began in 1913. **Artificial fertiliser** is made from ammonia. The **Haber-Bosch process** increased harvests all over the world.

gewusst: In 1891 the firm Brown, Boveri & Cie. was founded in Baden in Aargau, which built generators and electrical machines.
Until the synthesis, indigo was obtained from plants grown mainly in India.

teile.einleitung: With the telephone one can talk to one another over long distances. Alexander Graham Bell received the patent for it in 1876 in the USA. Even earlier the German teacher Philipp Reis had built an early telephone.
wichtigste: Alexander Graham Bell was born in 1847 in Edinburgh in Scotland.
He was living in Boston in the USA when he invented the telephone.
In 1876 Bell received his patent for the telephone.
The telephone turns the voice into electrical signals.
Bell’s assistant was called Thomas Watson.
Philipp Reis built around 1861 an apparatus that he called “Telephon”.

abschnitte.text: **Alexander Graham Bell** was born in 1847 in **Edinburgh**, the capital of Scotland. Later he moved to America and lived in **Boston**. Bell worked as a teacher of **deaf people**. He therefore concerned himself a great deal with speech, sound and hearing. This knowledge helped him in inventing the telephone.

In 1876 Bell received the **patent** for his telephone. A patent is a document that protects an invention. Only the inventor may then use or sell it for a time. That is about 150 years ago. Bell’s telephone quickly became known, and soon the first telephone networks arose.

Bell built the telephone together with his assistant **Thomas Watson**. During an experiment Bell called through the telephone that Watson should come to him. Watson was in the other room and heard him. The telephone turns the **voice** into **electrical signals**. At the other end sound is made from them again.

Even before Bell others tried to transmit sounds with electricity. The German teacher **Philipp Reis** built around 1861 an apparatus that could transmit sounds. He already called it a **“Telephon”**. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “far voice”. Reis’s device, however, still transmitted speech badly.

The first telephones were connected with long **wires**. Later operators in exchanges connected the lines by hand. In Switzerland the first telephone networks arose from 1880, first in Zurich. Only much later came **mobile phones**, which telephone without a cable by radio.

gewusst: The word “telephone” translated from Greek means roughly “far voice”.
In the past telephone operators made every connection by hand by moving plugs.

teile.einleitung: The Dutch East India Company, VOC for short, was a trading company from the Netherlands. It was founded in 1602 and for almost two hundred years traded in spices and other goods from Asia. In doing so it also waged wars and ruled whole territories.
wichtigste: The VOC was founded in 1602.
It was one of the first companies to issue freely tradable shares to a wide public.
Its supreme governing body was called “the Gentlemen Seventeen”.
In 1619 it founded Batavia as its main base in Asia.
On the island of Dejima near Nagasaki it long ran the only European trading post in Japan.
In 1652 Jan van Riebeeck set up a supply station at the Cape of Good Hope.
In 1799 the VOC was finally dissolved.

abschnitte.text: In 1602 several Dutch trading companies joined together to form the **United East India Company**, **VOC** for short. It received the sole right to trade with Asia from the Netherlands. Many people could buy parts of the company, so-called **shares**. These shares could be freely resold in Amsterdam. That is why the VOC is regarded as a **milestone in economic history**. It was run by the **Gentlemen Seventeen**.

The VOC was allowed to conclude treaties, build forts and even wage wars. In 1619 it founded on the island of Java the city of **Batavia** as its main base. Today the city is called Jakarta and is the capital of Indonesia. In Japan Europeans were for a long time allowed to trade only on the small artificial island of **Dejima** near Nagasaki. There the Dutch had their post.

Spices were very valuable in Europe. **Nutmeg** and **mace** at that time grew almost only on the small **Banda Islands** in Indonesia. The VOC wanted to control the trade in them entirely alone. In 1621 it conquered the islands in a brutal war. A large part of the inhabitants were killed, driven out or enslaved. The VOC also used enslaved people as labour in other places.

The ships of the VOC were away for months. On the way the sailors needed fresh water, meat and vegetables. That is why **Jan van Riebeeck** set up a **supply station** at the **Cape of Good Hope** in 1652, at the southern tip of Africa. From it later came the city of **Cape Town**. Many men from Switzerland also went to Asia for the VOC as soldiers or sailors.

In the 18th century the VOC did worse and worse. Wars, debts and bribery in its own administration weakened the company. Other countries such as England also competed with it. In 1799 the VOC was finally dissolved. Its territories in Asia were taken over by the Dutch state.

gewusst: In Dutch the company was called “Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie”, hence the abbreviation VOC.
VOC shares are regarded as some of the oldest shares in the world, and individual certificates survive to this day.

teile.einleitung: Human rights are rights that belong to every person simply because they are a human being. They include, for example, the right to life, to freedom and to a fair trial. They apply to everyone, regardless of origin, sex, skin colour or religion.
wichtigste: Human rights belong to all people from birth and cannot simply be taken away from them.
Early forerunners were the English Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 and the Virginia Declaration of Rights of 1776.
In 1789 the French National Assembly proclaimed the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
On 10 December 1948 the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights with 30 articles.
The commission that drew up this declaration was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt.
Switzerland joined the European Convention on Human Rights in 1974.
The UN Human Rights Council meets in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: Human rights are based on the idea that every person has an inviolable **dignity**. They protect the individual above all against encroachments by the state. They include rights of freedom such as freedom of speech and freedom of religion. But there are also social rights, for example the right to education, to food and to health.

The English **Habeas Corpus Act** of 1679 already protected against arbitrary arrest. The American Declaration of Independence of 1776 stated that all people are created equal. In the same year the **Virginia Declaration of Rights** appeared, one of the first modern declarations of human rights. These ideas came from the Enlightenment, in which thinkers such as John Locke wrote about natural rights.

In 1789 the French National Assembly proclaimed the **Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen**. It said that people are born free and equal in rights. However, people thought mainly of men in this. That is why Olympe de Gouges wrote a “Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen” in 1791.

After the crimes of the Second World War the world wanted to set down human rights together. A UN commission under the chairmanship of **Eleanor Roosevelt** drew up a declaration. On 10 December 1948 the UN General Assembly in Paris adopted the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** with 30 articles. Article 4, for example, bans slavery, and 10 December is now International Human Rights Day.

In 1950 European states concluded the **European Convention on Human Rights**. Anyone who finds that their rights have been violated can, in the end, bring a case before the European Court of Human Rights in **Strasbourg**. The Court then examines whether a state has violated the Convention. Member states must carry out its judgments.

Switzerland joined the European Convention on Human Rights in 1974. The Swiss Federal Constitution contains a catalogue of its own of **fundamental rights**, such as equality before the law and freedom of speech. In **Geneva** the UN Human Rights Council meets, and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights also has its seat there. In addition the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child applies in Switzerland, which gives children special rights.

begriffe.erklaerung: The worth that every person has and that must always be respected.
Human rights that are written into the constitution of a state.
A treaty between several states.
Latin for “you shall have the body”, a principle protecting against arbitrary detention.
When people are held, bought and sold like property.

gewusst: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is among the most translated texts in the world.
Olympe de Gouges was executed in 1793 during the French Revolution.
The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted in 1989 and is the human rights treaty signed by the most states.

teile.einleitung: Saint Petersburg is a large city in the north-west of Russia. Peter the Great founded it in 1703, and for about 200 years it was the capital of the Russian Empire.
wichtigste: Peter the Great founded Saint Petersburg in 1703.
The city lies on the Baltic Sea.
The Neva flows through Saint Petersburg.
For about 200 years it was the capital of Russia.
The Ticinese Domenico Trezzini was an important architect of the city.
Because of its many canals it is called the “Venice of the North”.

abschnitte.text: **Peter the Great** founded the city in the year **1703**. He wanted a port on the **Baltic Sea** for Russia and a “window to Europe”. First he had the **Peter and Paul Fortress** built on an island. The ground was marshy, and the building work was very hard for the many workers. Peter brought architects from all over Europe, who planned the city on a Western model.

One of the most important architects was **Domenico Trezzini** from what is now the canton of **Ticino**. He worked for many years in Saint Petersburg. Among other things he built the **Peter and Paul Cathedral** with its tall, golden spire. Later too many Ticinese architects and craftsmen worked in Russia. They helped to shape the look of the city.

Through the city flows the **Neva**, which runs into the Baltic Sea. Saint Petersburg is built on many islands and has numerous **canals** and hundreds of bridges. That is why it is also called the **“Venice of the North”**. In summer some large bridges are raised at night so that ships can pass through. In June it hardly gets dark, which is called the **White Nights**.

From 1712 Saint Petersburg was for about **200 years** the **capital of Russia**. Here the Tsars lived in the magnificent **Winter Palace**. Today part of the **Hermitage**, one of the largest art museums in the world, is housed in it. In 1918 Moscow became the capital again. The city was later called Petrograd and then Leningrad. Since 1991 it has been called Saint Petersburg again.

gewusst: The Peter and Paul Fortress was the first building of the city and still stands today.
After Moscow, Saint Petersburg is the second largest city in Russia.

tk7xw3e.t: Genocide of the Herero and Nama

teile.einleitung: In the German colony of German South West Africa, now Namibia, German troops killed tens of thousands of Herero and Nama from 1904. Today this is regarded as the first genocide of the 20th century.
wichtigste: German South West Africa was a German colony from 1884 to 1915 and largely corresponds to present-day Namibia.
In January 1904 the Herero under Samuel Maharero rose up against colonial rule.
After the Battle of Waterberg the Herero were driven into the dry steppe of the Omaheke.
Later the Nama also rose up against German rule.
Many prisoners died in camps, for example on Shark Island near Lüderitz.
In 2011 the Berlin Charité returned skulls of victims to Namibia.
In 2021 the German federal government officially described the crimes as genocide.

abschnitte.text: From 1884 the German Empire made the territory in the south-west of Africa into the colony of **German South West Africa**. It largely corresponds to present-day **Namibia**. German settlers took more and more land and cattle away from the native peoples. The **Herero** were cattle farmers, and cattle were very important to them. The native people had hardly any rights and were often treated unjustly.

In **January 1904** Paramount Chief **Samuel Maharero** called on the Herero to rise up. They were resisting the seizure of land, the loss of their cattle and their lack of rights. The German Empire then sent many soldiers. In August 1904 the **Battle of Waterberg** took place. After it Samuel Maharero fled with part of his people into the British territory of Bechuanaland.

After the battle the Herero were driven into the **Omaheke**, a dry region without enough water. The German troops sealed off the **waterholes** at its edge. Thousands of people, including women and children, died of thirst while fleeing. The German commander **Lothar von Trotha** wanted to destroy the Herero deliberately. That is why today we speak of a **genocide**.

In the autumn of 1904 the **Nama** in the south of the colony also rose up. The German troops waged a harsh war against them too. Captured Herero and Nama were put into **concentration camps**. Particularly many died on **Shark Island** near the port town of Lüderitz of cold, hunger and forced labour. In all, a large part of the Herero and about half of the Nama lost their lives.

Skulls of victims had been brought to Germany and used for racist research. In 2011 the Berlin **Charité** ceremonially returned 20 skulls to a Namibian delegation. In May **2021** the German federal government officially described the deeds as genocide in an agreement with Namibia. It promised support of **1.1 billion euros**. Many representatives of the Herero and Nama criticised the agreement as inadequate.

gewusst: Germany lost the colony of German South West Africa in 1915 during the First World War.
Namibia became an independent state only in 1990.

teile.einleitung: The NSDAP was the party of Adolf Hitler. It ruled Germany from 1933 to 1945 as a dictatorship and was responsible for the Second World War and the genocide of the Jews of Europe. After the war it was banned.
wichtigste: NSDAP stands for National Socialist German Workers’ Party.
The party arose in 1920, and from 1921 Adolf Hitler was its leader.
Its symbol was the swastika.
The SA was its fighting force in brown shirts.
In 1933 the NSDAP came to power in Germany.
Joseph Goebbels became Minister for Propaganda in 1933.
In 1945 the victorious powers banned the party.

abschnitte.text: The party arose in 1920 in Munich from a small group and called itself the **National Socialist German Workers’ Party**, **NSDAP** for short. From 1921 **Adolf Hitler** was its leader. In 1923 he tried to seize power with a coup in Munich, but the attempt failed. The party spread **racism** and hatred of Jews, which is called **antisemitism**. It rejected democracy.

On the flag of the NSDAP one could see the **swastika**, a black sign in a white circle on a red background. The party had its own fighting force, the **SA** (Sturmabteilung). Its members wore brown shirts and used violence against political opponents. Later the **SS** became the party’s most important force. Today showing the swastika is banned in Germany.

Around 1930 many people in Germany had no work because of a severe **economic crisis**. The NSDAP promised simple solutions and in 1932 became the strongest party in elections. On 30 January 1933 Hitler became **Reich Chancellor**. In the same year all other parties were banned. **Joseph Goebbels** became Minister for Public Enlightenment and **Propaganda**. He decided what was shown in newspapers, on the radio and in the cinema.

Under the NSDAP Germany became a **dictatorship**. Anyone who held a different opinion was persecuted and locked up. In 1939 Germany began the **Second World War**. The National Socialists murdered around six million Jews, a crime called the **Holocaust**. Many other people were also persecuted and killed. In 1945 Germany lost the war, and the victorious powers banned the NSDAP.

gewusst: In Switzerland in the 1930s so-called Fronts arose that held similar ideas but had little success.
After the war many leading National Socialists had to answer for themselves in court in the Nuremberg trials.

teile.einleitung: In the Battle of Adwa in 1896 the army of Ethiopia defeated the troops of Italy. The victory secured Ethiopia’s independence and became a symbol of resistance to colonial rule in Africa.
wichtigste: The Battle of Adwa took place in 1896.
Emperor Menelik II led the Ethiopian army to victory.
The Italian troops were commanded by General Oreste Baratieri.
The trigger was a dispute over the Treaty of Wuchale of 1889.
In the peace of 1896 Italy recognised the independence of Ethiopia.
Alfred Ilg from Thurgau was a close adviser of Menelik II.
In 1935 Italy under Mussolini attacked Ethiopia again.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 19th century European powers divided almost the whole of Africa among themselves. **Italy** already owned territories on the Red Sea and wanted to rule **Ethiopia** too. In 1889 both countries concluded the **Treaty of Wuchale**. The Amharic and the Italian versions, however, read differently. According to the Italian version Ethiopia was to come under Italian protection, according to the Amharic one not. Emperor **Menelik II** rejected this, and war followed.

On **1 March 1896** the armies met near the town of **Adwa** in the north of Ethiopia. The Italian troops were under the command of General **Oreste Baratieri**. The Ethiopian army under Menelik II was much larger and well equipped with rifles. The Italians clearly lost the battle. Empress **Taytu**, Menelik’s wife, also played an important role in the war.

In the **peace of 1896** Italy had to recognise the **independence of Ethiopia**. Ethiopia thus remained one of the very few African countries that did not become a colony. The victory gave courage to many people in Africa and all over the world. In Ethiopia the anniversary of the battle is still a public holiday today. In 1935 Italy under **Mussolini** attacked Ethiopia again, partly to avenge the defeat at Adwa.

abschnitte.titel: A man from Thurgau at the imperial court
abschnitte.text: A close adviser of Emperor Menelik II was the Swiss engineer **Alfred Ilg** from **Thurgau**. He came to Ethiopia as a young man and worked for the emperor for many years. He helped with the building of bridges and water pipes and with the planning of a railway. Later he even became **Ethiopian minister of state**. Ilg also represented Ethiopia in negotiations with European states.

gewusst: Adwa was one of the greatest victories of an African army over a European colonial power.
The railway line from Djibouti to Addis Ababa, in whose planning Alfred Ilg took part, was finished in 1917.

teile.einleitung: Victoria was Queen of the United Kingdom from 1837 to 1901. A whole era is named after her: the Victorian era.
wichtigste: Victoria came to the British throne in 1837 at the age of 18.
She came from the House of Hanover and was the last British ruler from that house.
In 1840 she married Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha.
She had nine children and was called the “grandmother of Europe”.
From 1876 she also bore the title “Empress of India”.
She reigned for over 63 years and died in January 1901.
Her successor was her eldest son Edward VII.

abschnitte.text: Victoria was born in London in 1819. When her uncle **William IV** died in 1837, she became queen at only **18 years old**. She came from the **House of Hanover**. The British kings had long also been rulers of Hanover. But since women were not allowed to inherit there, the two crowns separated when Victoria took office.

In **1840** Victoria married her cousin **Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha**. Prince Albert became her most important adviser. He promoted science, technology and art and helped to organise the first **World's Fair** in London in 1851. The couple had **nine children**. Many of them married into European royal houses, which is why Victoria is called the “grandmother of Europe”.

Prince Albert died in 1861. Victoria was deeply shaken. She withdrew from public life for a long time and wore **black mourning clothes** for the rest of her life. With time she appeared in public more often again. In old age she was very popular with the people. Her jubilees in 1887 and 1897 were celebrated on a grand scale.

Her reign is called the **Victorian era**. **Industrialisation** changed the country: railways, factories and large cities appeared. At the same time strict rules of behaviour and morals applied. The **British Empire** reached an enormous size. In 1876, at the instigation of Prime Minister **Benjamin Disraeli**, Victoria received the title “Empress of India”.

Victoria died in **January 1901** on the **Isle of Wight**. The 20th century had begun shortly before. She had reigned for over **63 years**, longer than any British ruler before her. Her eldest son became king as **Edward VII**, and he was already almost 60 years old at the time. Only Queen Elizabeth II later reigned even longer.

gewusst: Victoria was the first British ruler to live in Buckingham Palace.
Many places are named after Queen Victoria, for example Lake Victoria in Africa and Victoria Falls.

teile.einleitung: A sewing machine joins pieces of cloth with thread, much faster than by hand. It was invented in the 19th century and greatly changed the making of clothes. Today it stands in many homes and in factories all over the world.
wichtigste: On the needle of a sewing machine the hole for the thread is near the point.
For the normal stitch the machine needs two threads.
The bobbin thread is wound on a small spool.
Many old sewing machines were driven by the foot.
Josef Madersperger from Austria built an early sewing machine.
The American Elias Howe had an important sewing machine patented in 1846.
With sewing machines clothes could be made much faster.

abschnitte.text: On an ordinary sewing needle the eye, that is, the hole for the thread, is at the back. On a sewing machine it is different: the hole is **near the point**. The needle pierces the cloth and takes the thread down with it. There the thread forms a small loop. In this way the machine can stitch again and again very fast.

For the normal stitch the sewing machine needs **two threads**. The **upper thread** comes from above through the needle. The **bobbin thread** is wound on a small **spool** under the cloth. A hook catches the loop of the upper thread and guides it around the bobbin thread. In this way the two threads interlock in the middle of the cloth. This stitch is called the **lockstitch**.

Many people tried to build a sewing machine. The tailor **Josef Madersperger** from **Austria** was already working on a machine in Vienna at the beginning of the 19th century. Commercially, however, he had no success. In 1846 the American **Elias Howe** had a sewing machine with a lockstitch patented. Later Isaac Singer improved the machine and sold it in large numbers.

In the past there were no electric sewing machines yet. Many machines were driven **by the foot**. Under the table there was a broad pedal that you moved to and fro. A wheel and a belt transmitted the movement to the needle. Some smaller machines also had a crank for the hand. Today sewing machines mostly run on an electric motor.

With the sewing machine **clothes** could be made much faster than by hand. In factories women workers now sewed large quantities of shirts, trousers and skirts. As a result clothing became cheaper. Many families also sewed their clothes themselves at home. In Switzerland Karl Friedrich Gegauf founded the firm in Steckborn in Thurgau in 1893 from which the well-known sewing machine brand **Bernina** came.

gewusst: Modern industrial sewing machines manage several thousand stitches a minute.
The first sewing machines in France were destroyed by angry tailors who feared for their work.

teile.einleitung: The Spanish Armada was a huge war fleet that King Philip II of Spain sent against England in 1588. The attack failed. Fireships, fighting and severe storms cost Spain many ships.
wichtigste: The Armada sailed against England in the summer of 1588.
King Philip II of Spain sent it off.
It numbered around 130 ships.
The commander-in-chief was the Duke of Medina-Sidonia.
Off Calais the English sent burning ships drifting towards the Armada.
On the way back severe storms destroyed many ships.

abschnitte.text: **Philip II** was King of Spain, then one of the most powerful countries in the world. He was Catholic and wanted to conquer **Protestant England** under Queen Elizabeth I. He was also angry because England supported the rebellious Netherlands against Spain. In addition English privateers repeatedly raided Spanish ships.

The **Armada** numbered around 130 ships with many thousands of sailors and soldiers. The word “armada” means fleet in Spanish. The commander-in-chief was the **Duke of Medina-Sidonia**. He had little experience at sea. The experienced admiral who was meant to have the command had died shortly before.

One of the most important English commanders was **Francis Drake**. Earlier he had raided Spanish ships as a privateer and sailed round the world as a captain. The English ships were smaller and more manoeuvrable than the Spanish ones. They also had guns that could shoot further.

The Armada anchored off **Calais** on the French coast. In the night the English sent burning ships drifting towards the Armada. Such ships are called **fireships**. The Spaniards panicked, cut their anchor cables and lost their formation. After that the English attacked.

The Armada could not return through the English Channel. It had to sail round **Scotland and Ireland**. There the ships ran into severe **storms** and were wrecked on the coasts. Many ships were lost. How many exactly came back is disputed among experts.

gewusst: After Calais the Spaniards had to sail on without many of their anchors, which put them in extra danger in the storms.
Francis Drake was the first English captain to sail around the whole world.

teile.einleitung: Risorgimento is the name of the movement that in the 19th century united the many states of the Italian peninsula into one common country. At the end stood the Kingdom of Italy with Rome as its capital.
wichtigste: Risorgimento means roughly “resurgence”.
Before unification Italy was divided into many states.
Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, steered unification politically.
In 1859 France and Sardinia-Piedmont defeated Austria at Solferino.
In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II became the first King of Italy.
In 1870 Italian troops took Rome.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 19th century there was no united Italy. The peninsula was divided into several states, such as the **Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont**, the **Papal States** of the Pope and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in the south. In the north **Austria** ruled over Lombardy and Venetia. Many people wished for a common, free country. This movement was called the **Risorgimento**, which means roughly “resurgence”.

The Prime Minister of Sardinia-Piedmont, **Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour**, steered unification politically. He was a skilful diplomat and won **France** as an ally against Austria. Another important thinker was **Giuseppe Mazzini**. He dreamed of an Italian republic and inspired many young people with enthusiasm for the unity of Italy.

In 1859 France and Sardinia-Piedmont defeated Austria in the **Battle of Solferino**. After that Lombardy came to Sardinia-Piedmont. In 1860 **Giuseppe Garibaldi** went to Sicily with around a thousand volunteers and conquered the south. His fighters wore red shirts. Garibaldi handed the conquered territories over to the King of Sardinia-Piedmont.

In 1861 **Victor Emmanuel II** was proclaimed the first **King of Italy**. But Venetia and Rome were still missing. Venetia was added in 1866. Rome was protected by French soldiers who supported the Pope. When these withdrew in 1870, Italian troops took **Rome**. In 1871 Rome became the **capital** of united Italy.

The Genevan **Henry Dunant** came by chance in 1859 after the Battle of **Solferino** on to the battlefield. He saw that thousands of wounded soldiers were left without help, and helped to care for them. He wrote a book about it. His ideas led in 1863 in **Geneva** to the founding of the **Red Cross**. Many Italian freedom fighters, Mazzini among them, also found refuge in Switzerland for a time.

gewusst: As a united state Italy is younger than the Swiss Federal Constitution of 1848.
In 1901 Dunant received the very first Nobel Peace Prize.

teile.einleitung: The Weimar Republic was the first democracy in Germany and lasted from 1918 to 1933. It is named after the city of Weimar, where the constitution was drawn up in 1919. Despite modern ideas and a lively culture, it failed because of crises, violence and its enemies, and in 1933 the Nazis came to power.
wichtigste: On 9 November 1918 Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed the republic from the balcony of the Reichstag.
The Weimar Constitution came into force on 14 August 1919 and also brought votes for women.
Article 48 allowed the Reich President to issue emergency decrees.
The Kapp Putsch of 1920 failed because of a general strike.
In 1923 Germany experienced hyperinflation, and one trillion paper marks were exchanged for one Rentenmark.
With the Locarno Treaties of 1925 Germany recognised its western border.
In the Great Depression the Nazi Party became the strongest party in 1932 with 37.3 per cent.

abschnitte.text: At the end of 1918 Germany had lost the First World War, and workers and soldiers were on strike everywhere. Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated and fled to the Netherlands. On 9 November 1918 **Philipp Scheidemann** of the SPD proclaimed the German republic. Because Berlin was unsettled, the elected National Assembly met from February 1919 in quiet **Weimar**. The first Reich President was the Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert.

The **Weimar Constitution** came into force on 14 August 1919. It guaranteed basic rights and for the first time also allowed women to vote and to stand for election. The Reich President was elected directly by the people and had a lot of power. Under **Article 48** he could, if security and order were in danger, issue emergency decrees, that is, laws without parliament. This rule was later abused.

The young republic was attacked from the left and the right. In March 1920 right-wing officers tried to seize power in the **Kapp Putsch**, but a general strike and the refusal of the civil servants made it fail. In 1922 the far-right organisation Consul murdered Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau. In January 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied the **Ruhr**, because Germany was behind with reparations. In November 1923 Hitler failed in Munich with an attempted putsch.

In 1923 money lost value almost daily, because the state kept printing more and more banknotes. In the end a loaf of bread cost billions of marks, and wages were collected in laundry baskets. Many people lost all their savings. On 15 November 1923 the **Rentenmark** was introduced: for one trillion paper marks you got one Rentenmark. After that the situation calmed down.

Between 1924 and 1929 Germany recovered. Foreign Minister **Gustav Stresemann** improved relations with the neighbours; in 1925 Germany concluded the Locarno Treaties, and in 1926 it joined the League of Nations. Berlin became a world city with cinemas, theatres and jazz clubs. The art school **Bauhaus** shaped architecture and design right up to today. After Ebert's death, the old First World War general Paul von Hindenburg became Reich President in 1925.

The Great Depression from 1929 brought millions of unemployed. From 1930 chancellors governed with the president's emergency decrees instead of with a majority in parliament. Radical parties such as the Nazi Party and the Communist Party gained strongly, and in the election of 31 July 1932 the Nazi Party received 37.3 per cent. On 30 January 1933 Hindenburg appointed **Adolf Hitler** Reich Chancellor. Within a few months the Nazis destroyed democracy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state without a king or emperor, in which the people decide who governs.
A violent attempt to overthrow the government and seize power.
When money loses value and everything gets more and more expensive.
A law that the president can issue without the consent of parliament.

gewusst: On that same 9 November 1918, only a few hours after Scheidemann, the communist Karl Liebknecht proclaimed a “socialist republic”.
In 1923 banknotes were so worthless that children played with them and some people burned them for fuel.
The Basic Law of the Federal Republic of 1949 was deliberately designed so that the mistakes of the Weimar Constitution would not be repeated.

teile.einleitung: Migration means that people move their home for a longer time or for good to another area or another country. People have always migrated, for example because of work, war, persecution or hardship. Switzerland too was once a country of emigration and is now an important country of immigration.
wichtigste: Migration is the lasting move of one’s home to another region or another country.
Push factors drive people away from their homeland, pull factors draw them to a new place.
The Geneva Refugee Convention of 1951 forbids sending refugees back to a state that persecutes them.
In 1685 around 200,000 Huguenots fled from France, many coming via Geneva.
From 1934 the Swiss seasonal worker status allowed time-limited stays without family reunion.
Since 2002 the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons with the EU has applied.
In March 2022 Switzerland activated protection status S for the first time for refugees from Ukraine.

abschnitte.text: Migration research distinguishes **push factors** and **pull factors**. Push factors drive people away, for example war, persecution, poverty or natural disasters. Pull factors attract people, for example work, safety, education or family members. Someone who moves voluntarily for work is a migrant, and someone who flees persecution is a **refugee**.

With the **Edict of Fontainebleau** the French king Louis XIV banned the Reformed faith in 1685. Around 200,000 Huguenots then fled from France. For a time Geneva took in more refugees than the city had inhabitants. Many moved on, others stayed and advanced crafts such as watchmaking and textile production.

abschnitte.titel: Switzerland as a country of emigration
abschnitte.text: In the 19th century poverty and years of hunger were widespread in Switzerland. Many Swiss people therefore emigrated to America, especially to the USA, Argentina and Brazil. In 1845 emigrants from the Glarus region founded the village of **New Glarus** in Wisconsin. Only towards the end of the 19th century did more people come into Switzerland than left it.

After the Second World War Switzerland brought in many workers, above all from Italy, later also from Spain, Portugal and Yugoslavia. The **seasonal worker status** of 1934 allowed only time-limited stays without family reunion, and children often had to stay behind or be hidden. In the Mattmark disaster in Valais on 30 August 1965 a glacier collapse killed 88 workers, 56 of them from Italy. The Schwarzenbach Initiative, which on 7 June 1970 wanted to limit the share of foreigners to 10 per cent, was rejected.

After the Second World War the UN created the High Commissioner for Refugees **UNHCR** in 1950, with its seat in Geneva. The **Geneva Refugee Convention** of 1951 lays down who counts as a refugee. Its most important principle is **non-refoulement**, the ban on sending people back to a state that persecutes them. The protocol of 1967 lifted the restriction to events before 1951.

In 2002 the **Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons** with the EU came into force, and with it the seasonal worker status lost its validity for EU citizens. On 9 February 2014 the electorate narrowly accepted the initiative against mass immigration with 50.3 per cent yes. In March 2022 Switzerland activated **protection status S** for the first time for refugees from Ukraine. Today about a quarter of the people in Switzerland do not have a Swiss passport (as of about 2024).

begriffe.erklaerung: The movement of people to a new home, often in another country.
A person who had to leave their homeland because of war or persecution.
Protection that a state grants to persecuted people.
The principle that nobody may be sent back to a country where they face persecution.
The growing together of newcomers and locals in one society.

gewusst: Well-known Swiss firms such as Nestlé were founded by immigrants; Henri Nestlé came from Frankfurt.
In New Glarus in the USA a festival with Swiss traditions is still celebrated today.
In 1956 Switzerland took in thousands of refugees from Hungary.

teile.einleitung: Solar energy is energy from the light and heat of the sun. One can make electricity from it or heat water. Switzerland is closely linked to this technology through the solar aircraft Solar Impulse and the Tour de Sol.
wichtigste: “Sol” is the Latin word for sun.
Solar cells convert sunlight directly into electricity.
Solar collectors use the heat of the sun to heat water.
When it is cloudy solar cells produce less electricity.
In 1985 the first Tour de Sol for solar cars took place in Switzerland.
Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world in 2015 and 2016 using only solar energy.

abschnitte.text: Every day the sun sends huge amounts of energy to Earth. The word **solar** comes from the Latin “sol”, sun. Solar energy is a **renewable energy**: it does not run out as long as the sun shines. In operation it also causes no exhaust gases.

**Solar cells** convert sunlight directly into electric current. Many solar cells together form a **solar panel**, which one mounts, for example, on roofs. Solar cells need light. When clouds cover the sun, less light arrives, and less electricity is produced. At night they supply no electricity at all.

There is a second way of using the sun: **solar collectors**. They capture the heat of the sun. With it water is heated, for showering or for heating. Solar collectors and solar panels can be seen on more and more house roofs in Switzerland.

In 1985 the first **Tour de Sol** took place in Switzerland. It was one of the first races for **solar cars** in the world. The vehicles drove right across Switzerland using only solar power. The race was meant to show what is already possible with solar energy.

The Swiss **Bertrand Piccard** and **André Borschberg** flew around the world in 2015 and 2016 in the aircraft **Solar Impulse 2**. On the wings sat over 17,000 solar cells. The aircraft needed not a drop of fuel. In the cockpit there was room for only one person, so the two took turns as pilots.

gewusst: Solar Impulse 2 had over 17,000 solar cells on its wings.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to travel from the sun to the Earth.

teile.einleitung: In 1683 a large Ottoman army besieged the city of Vienna. After two months the city was relieved in the Battle of Kahlenberg.
wichtigste: The Ottoman grand vizier Kara Mustafa led the army to Vienna in 1683.
The sultan of the Ottoman Empire at the time was Mehmed IV.
Emperor Leopold I left Vienna before the siege and went to Passau.
City commander Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg defended Vienna for about two months.
On 12 September 1683 a relief army under the Polish king Jan III Sobieski freed the city.
In 1684 the emperor, Poland and Venice formed the Holy League.
The war ended in 1699 with the Peace of Karlowitz.

abschnitte.text: The **Ottoman Empire** was a great power in the 17th century. It ruled the Balkans and large parts of Hungary. The sultan was **Mehmed IV**, but the army was led by the grand vizier **Kara Mustafa**. He wanted to conquer **Vienna**, the emperor's capital. In July 1683 his huge army surrounded the city. The Ottomans had already besieged Vienna once in vain in 1529.

**Emperor Leopold I** left Vienna with his court before the Ottomans arrived. From **Passau** he worked to obtain help. In the city Count **Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg** took over the defence as city commander. With a few soldiers and the citizens he held out for about **two months**. The situation grew ever more difficult, because food was lacking and diseases spread.

A **relief army** of Polish and German troops came to Vienna's aid. The Polish king **Jan III Sobieski** had the supreme command. The army moved over the **Kahlenberg**, a hill north of Vienna. On **12 September 1683** it put the Ottoman army to flight. A great charge by the Polish **cavalry** decided the battle. Among the fighters was also the young **Prince Eugene** of Savoy, only 19 years old at the time.

After the defeat the sultan had Kara Mustafa executed in the same year. In 1684 the emperor, Poland and Venice formed the **Holy League** against the Ottoman Empire, encouraged by Pope Innocent XI. Later Russia joined too. In the **Great Turkish War** the allies won back wide territories. Prince Eugene became Austria's most successful commander. Mehmed IV was deposed in 1687.

The war ended in **1699** with the **Peace of Karlowitz**. The Ottoman Empire had to hand over almost all of **Hungary** to Austria. With that Austria became a **great power** in Europe. For the Ottoman Empire, on the other hand, a long period began in which it lost territory. In Vienna monuments and street names still recall the year 1683.

gewusst: Many legends surround the siege, for example about the founding of the first Viennese coffee houses.
The Kahlenberg is now a popular viewpoint with a view over the whole of Vienna.

teile.einleitung: “Operation Barbarossa” was the code name for the German attack on the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941. It was the largest military campaign in history and was planned from the start as a war of annihilation. The war in the east cost millions of lives and became the turning point of the Second World War.
wichtigste: The German attack on the Soviet Union began on 22 June 1941.
The attack was divided into three army groups: North, Centre and South.
Historians call it a war of annihilation because it was designed around murder, hunger and expulsion.
The “Commissar Order” ordered that captured political commissars of the Red Army be murdered immediately.
Around three million Soviet prisoners of war died in German custody.
The blockade of Leningrad lasted about 872 days.
In November 1942 Operation Uranus encircled the 6th Army at Stalingrad.
Of the German prisoners from Stalingrad only about 5,000 to 6,000 returned home.

abschnitte.text: Although Germany had signed the **Hitler-Stalin Pact** with the Soviet Union in 1939, Hitler had been planning the attack since 1940. The code name recalled the medieval emperor Frederick I, called **Barbarossa**. The Nazis wanted to conquer “living space” in the east and subjugate, expel or kill the population. They expected a victory within a few months.

On 22 June 1941 around three million German soldiers attacked together with allies. **Army Group North** aimed for Leningrad, **Army Group Centre** for Moscow and **Army Group South** for Ukraine. In the first months they conquered huge areas and took millions of soldiers prisoner. The Red Army was at first poorly prepared.

From the start the war was designed around **murder, hunger and expulsion**. The **Commissar Order** of 6 June 1941 ordered that captured political commissars be murdered at once. Behind the front, so-called **Einsatzgruppen** shot hundreds of thousands of Jews, for example in September 1941 in the ravine of Babyn Yar near Kyiv. Around three million Soviet prisoners of war died in German custody, many of them starving.

In autumn 1941 rain turned the roads into mud, and then an icy **winter** arrived. The German soldiers had no winter clothing. Shortly before Moscow the Red Army launched a **counter-offensive** on 5 December 1941. With that the plan for a quick victory had failed.

German troops encircled **Leningrad**, now Saint Petersburg, from September 1941. The **blockade** lasted about 872 days, until January 1944. About a million inhabitants died, most of them from hunger and cold. In winter food arrived only along the **Road of Life**, a route across the frozen Lake Ladoga.
