In 1942 the Wehrmacht attacked in the south and reached **Stalingrad** on the Volga. In November 1942 the Soviet **Operation Uranus** encircled the 6th Army there. At the beginning of 1943 the last troops surrendered, and some 90,000 to 110,000 Germans were taken prisoner. Only about 5,000 to 6,000 returned home after the war. After that the Red Army pushed the Wehrmacht back as far as Berlin by 1945.

begriffe.erklaerung: A war that is aimed deliberately at the murder and destruction of people.
A very large formation made up of several armies.
Cutting a city off from all supplies.
The army of the Soviet Union.
A political officer who watched over loyalty to the party in the Red Army.

gewusst: The Soviet Union lost, by estimate, around 27 million people in the Second World War, more than any other country.
In Leningrad, scientists at a seed collection chose to starve rather than eat the stored seeds.
Napoleon had also attacked Russia in June, 129 years earlier in 1812, and had also failed.

teile.einleitung: Today the tomato is one of the most popular vegetables in the world. It originally comes from the Americas. It only reached Europe after the voyages of discovery, and at first people there did not trust it.
wichtigste: The tomato comes from Central and South America.
It came to Europe after the voyages of discovery.
At first many Europeans thought it was poisonous.
So for a long time it was grown only as an ornamental plant.
The tomato is related to the potato.
In botany the tomato is a fruit, more precisely a berry.

abschnitte.text: The tomato originally grew in **Central and South America**. Wild tomatoes had only small fruits. People in Central America had been growing them for a long time. The word “tomato” comes from the language of the Aztecs. It was only after the Europeans' **voyages of discovery** that the tomato reached Europe in the 16th century.

In Europe many people did not trust the new plant. They thought the tomato was **poisonous**. So for a long time it was grown only as an **ornamental plant** in gardens. Only little by little did people start to eat the fruits. The tomato became popular early on, especially in Italy. In Austria it is still also called “Paradeiser” today.

The tomato belongs to the **nightshade** family. This family also includes the **potato**, the aubergine and the pepper. The green parts of the tomato plant, that is the leaves and stems, contain substances that should not be eaten. It is also better not to eat unripe green tomatoes raw.

In **botany** the tomato is a **fruit**. It grows from the flower and contains seeds. Strictly speaking it is even a **berry**. In the kitchen, however, it is usually counted as a vegetable because it is not eaten sweet. In Switzerland tomatoes grow in gardens in summer or all year round in greenhouses.

gewusst: For experts, the tomato is a berry.
The word “tomato” comes from the language of the Aztecs in Mexico.

teile.einleitung: Nicolaus Copernicus was an astronomer, physician and churchman who was born in Toruń in 1473. He realised that the Sun does not circle the Earth, but the Earth circles the Sun. This idea changed people’s view of the world so strongly that people still speak of a Copernican revolution today.
wichtigste: Copernicus was born in 1473 in Thorn, today’s Toruń in Poland.
In the Copernican view of the world the Earth and the planets circle the Sun.
Around 1509 he first sketched his theory in the unprinted “Commentariolus”.
His main work “De revolutionibus orbium coelestium” appeared in 1543 in Nuremberg.
His pupil Georg Joachim Rheticus urged him to publish it.
For most of his life Copernicus was a canon in the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia.
In 1616 his work was placed on the Index of forbidden books until individual passages were corrected.

abschnitte.text: Nicolaus Copernicus was born on 19 February 1473 in **Thorn** on the Vistula, today’s Toruń in Poland. After the early death of his father his uncle Lucas Watzenrode looked after him, who later became Bishop of Warmia. Copernicus studied in Kraków and then for several years in Italy, among other places in Bologna and Padua. He learned canon law, medicine, mathematics and astronomy.

For most of his life Copernicus was a **canon** in the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia and lived in Frauenburg, today’s Frombork. As a canon he managed estates of the Church, worked as a physician and even dealt with money and coins. He pursued astronomy alongside these duties. From a tower he watched the stars and planets, entirely without a telescope, because that was only invented later.

abschnitte.titel: The new view of the world
abschnitte.text: Since antiquity most scholars had believed in the **geocentric view of the world** of Ptolemy, in which the Earth stands still at the centre. Copernicus instead put the Sun in the middle, which is called the **heliocentric view of the world**. According to it the Earth turns once a day on its own axis and once a year around the Sun. In this way, for example, the strange looping paths of the planets in the sky could be explained more simply.

Around 1509 Copernicus sketched his theory in the **Commentariolus**, a short text that was passed on only by being copied out by hand. For a long time he hesitated to publish his whole work. His pupil **Georg Joachim Rheticus** made the doctrine known in 1540 with the “Narratio prima” and urged him to have it printed. In 1543, the year Copernicus died, “De revolutionibus orbium coelestium” appeared in Nuremberg, but an anonymous preface by Andreas Osiander claimed that the model was only a mathematical hypothesis for calculation.

At first the new doctrine found only a few followers, because it contradicted appearances and some passages of the Bible. Later Johannes Kepler and Galileo Galilei built on it and supplied new proofs. In 1616 “De revolutionibus” was placed on the **Index** of forbidden books until individual passages were corrected. Today Copernicus is regarded as one of the founders of modern natural science, and the “Copernican revolution” stands for any fundamental upheaval in thinking.

begriffe.erklaerung: The idea that the Sun stands at the centre and the planets circle around it.
The old idea that the Earth stands at the centre of the universe.
A clergyman who belongs to the body that runs a bishop’s church and has administrative duties.
A list of books that the Catholic Church used to forbid people to read.

gewusst: Copernicus still imagined the paths of the planets as perfect circles; only Kepler found out that they are ellipses.
His pupil Rheticus came from Feldkirch in Vorarlberg, very close to the Swiss border.
The chemical element number 112 was named copernicium in his honour.

teile.einleitung: The Safavids were a ruling dynasty that governed Persia, today’s Iran, from 1501 into the 18th century. They made the Shia branch of Islam the state religion, which still shapes the country today.
wichtigste: Ismail I founded Safavid rule in Tabriz in 1501.
The Safavids made Twelver Shia the state religion of Persia.
Warrior tribes with red headgear, the Qizilbash, brought them to power.
In 1514 they were defeated by the Ottomans at the Battle of Chaldiran.
Shah Abbas I moved the capital to Isfahan in 1598.
In 1722 Afghan tribal warriors conquered Isfahan.

abschnitte.text: In **1501** **Ismail I** had himself crowned shah in the city of **Tabriz**. Shah is the Persian title for king. He was still very young at the time. He was supported by Turkmen tribal warriors, the **Qizilbash**. The name means “red heads”, because they wore red headgear. Ismail made **Twelver Shia**, a branch of Shia Islam, the **state religion**. To this day the majority of people in Iran are Shia.

In the west Persia bordered the powerful **Ottoman Empire**, whose rulers were Sunni. In 1514 the Ottoman sultan **Selim I** defeated the Safavids in the **Battle of Chaldiran**. The Ottomans had many cannon and guns, while the Safavids fought mainly with horsemen. Afterwards there were long wars still. Only the **Peace of Qasr-e Shirin** fixed a border in 1639. It corresponds roughly to today’s border between Iran and Iraq.

The best-known Safavid ruler was **Shah Abbas I**. He strengthened the army and the empire. In 1598 he moved the capital to **Isfahan**. There he had a huge square built with magnificent mosques, a palace and a great bazaar. Isfahan became one of the most beautiful cities in the world. The square is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In the 17th century the empire grew weaker. Many later rulers cared little about governing. In **1722** **Afghan tribal warriors** conquered the capital Isfahan. With that Safavid rule was in effect at an end, even if individual members of the family were still installed as rulers for some years.

gewusst: Under the Safavids precious carpets were woven in Persia, which can be seen today in great museums.
Because of its splendour Isfahan was also called “half the world”.

teile.einleitung: In the First World War the Western Front was the line of battle between Germany on one side and France, Britain, Belgium and later the USA on the other. It stretched for around 700 kilometres from the Belgian North Sea coast to the Swiss border in the Jura. Millions of soldiers died in its trenches, often without the front moving.
wichtigste: The Schlieffen Plan was to defeat France quickly first and then fight Russia.
The Battle of the Marne stopped the German advance on Paris in September 1914.
After that the front froze into trench warfare.
The Battle of Verdun began on 21 February 1916 and was meant to wear down the French army.
On the first day of the Battle of the Somme, 1 July 1916, around 20,000 British soldiers fell.
New weapons such as poison gas, aircraft and tanks made the war even crueller.
The armistice of Compiègne ended the fighting on 11 November 1918.

abschnitte.text: Germany feared a war against France and Russia at the same time. The **Schlieffen Plan** was to defeat France first in a few weeks and then turn the troops against Russia. For this, German armies marched through neutral **Belgium** in August 1914. Because of this breach of neutrality, Britain entered the war.

In September 1914 the German troops were close to Paris. In the **Battle of the Marne** the French and British managed to stop the advance. Chief of the General Staff Helmuth von Moltke the Younger was replaced afterwards, and his successor was Erich von Falkenhayn. Both sides now dug in in **trenches**, protected by barbed wire and machine guns. Between the trenches lay the deadly “no man's land”.

On 21 February 1916 Germany attacked the fortress town of **Verdun**. Falkenhayn wanted to weaken the French army by attrition, which is called a **battle of materiel**. France brought soldiers and supplies up along the road from Bar-le-Duc, which was called the Voie Sacrée, the Sacred Way. The battle lasted until December 1916 and cost hundreds of thousands of lives on both sides together. In the end the front had hardly shifted.

On 1 July 1916 the British-French offensive on the **Somme** began. After days of artillery fire the soldiers ran towards the German trenches and were mown down by machine guns. On this single day around 20,000 British soldiers fell. In September 1916 the British used **tanks** for the first time on the Somme. By November the Allies had gained only a few kilometres of land.

In April 1915 the German army used **poison gas** on a large scale for the first time, at Ypres in Belgium. Soon both sides used gas, and soldiers had to wear gas masks. Aircraft were first used for reconnaissance, and later fighter pilots fought in the air. Artillery turned whole landscapes into fields of craters, some of which can still be seen today.

In 1917 the **USA** entered the war on the side of the Allies. A large German spring offensive in 1918 failed, and from August the Allies pushed the German troops back. On 11 November 1918 at 11 o'clock the **armistice** of Compiègne came into force. The southern end of the front lay at Bonfol in the canton of Jura, on the Swiss border. In Basel and in the Jura the thunder of the guns was often heard.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, deep ditch in which soldiers sought protection from enemy fire.
A war in which the fronts hardly move because both sides are dug in.
A battle in which huge quantities of ammunition and weapons are used.
The contested ground between the opponents' trenches.

gewusst: At Christmas 1914, in some sections of the front, soldiers spontaneously laid down their weapons, sang songs and met in no man's land.
The front ended at Bonfol in the Jura, where Swiss soldiers stood guard right on the border.
On the former battlefield of Verdun, unexploded shells are still lying about, and some destroyed villages were never rebuilt.

teile.einleitung: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923 and was its first president. With many reforms on the European model he transformed the country. Several of these reforms have a link to Switzerland.
wichtigste: Mustafa Kemal was born in Thessaloniki in 1881.
He became known as an officer in the Battle of Gallipoli in the First World War.
The Treaty of Lausanne recognised the borders of the new Turkey in 1923.
On 29 October 1923 the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed.
Ankara became the new capital in 1923.
The Turkish Civil Code of 1926 followed the Swiss Civil Code.
In 1928 Turkey introduced a Latin alphabet.

abschnitte.text: Mustafa Kemal was born in **Thessaloniki** in 1881. The city then belonged to the **Ottoman Empire**; today it lies in Greece. He attended military schools and became an officer. In the **First World War** the Ottoman Empire fought on Germany’s side. In 1915 Ottoman troops repelled a landing of British and French troops in the **Battle of Gallipoli**. Mustafa Kemal became known there as a successful commander.

After the war the victorious powers wanted to divide large parts of the Ottoman Empire among themselves. Mustafa Kemal led a **war of independence** against this and succeeded. In 1923 a peace treaty was signed in **Lausanne** that recognised the borders of the new Turkey internationally. On 13 October 1923 **Ankara** became the capital, and on **29 October 1923** the **Republic of Turkey** was proclaimed. Mustafa Kemal became its first president.

Mustafa Kemal wanted a modern state in which religion and state are separate. This is called **secularism**. In 1926 Turkey took over the **Swiss Civil Code** almost word for word as its own law. It regulates, for example, family, inheritance and property. Laws from other countries in Europe also served as models. Women received the right to vote at national level in 1934, much earlier than in Switzerland.

Until 1928 Turkish was written with **Arabic letters**. In 1928 Turkey introduced a **Latin alphabet**, that is, letters as in German, with some special characters. Many adults learned to read and write anew in courses. In 1934 all Turks had to choose a family name. Mustafa Kemal received the name **Atatürk**, which means “Father of the Turks”.

Atatürk ruled with great power, and other parties were hardly admitted for a long time. His reforms were pushed through from above, and some people rejected them. He died on 10 November 1938 in Istanbul. His great mausoleum stands in Ankara. In Turkey he is still very much revered today, and his picture hangs in many schools and offices.

gewusst: On Atatürk’s day of death, many people in Turkey stand still for a moment every year at 9.05 a.m.
The Treaty of Lausanne was signed in the Palais de Rumine, which today houses museums.

teile.einleitung: India was ruled by the British for around 200 years and was seen as the “jewel in the crown” of the British Empire. After a long struggle led by Mahatma Gandhi, India became independent on 15 August 1947. At the same time the country was divided into India and Pakistan.
wichtigste: After the great uprising of 1857 the British Crown took over the rule from the East India Company.
In 1885 the Indian National Congress was founded in Bombay.
In 1906 the All-India Muslim League was formed in Dhaka.
On 13 April 1919 British troops fired on an unarmed crowd in Amritsar.
Mahatma Gandhi led the non-violent resistance against British rule.
From 1929/30 the National Congress demanded complete independence with “Purna Swaraj”.
In August 1942 the “Quit India” movement began.
On 15 August 1947 India and Pakistan became independent.

abschnitte.text: From the 18th century the British **East India Company** conquered large parts of India. In 1857 Indian soldiers and others rose up against it. After this great uprising the **British Crown** took over the rule itself in 1858. A viceroy governed the country, and in 1877 Queen Victoria became Empress of India.

In 1885 educated Indians founded the **Indian National Congress** in Bombay. When the British divided the province of Bengal in 1905, the **Swadeshi** movement arose, which boycotted British goods and preferred local products. In 1906 the **Muslim League** was founded in Dhaka. It represented the interests of Muslims, who were a minority in India.

In 1919 the **Rowlatt Act** allowed arrests without trial, which set off major protests. On 13 April 1919 British soldiers fired on an unarmed crowd in the **Jallianwala Bagh** in Amritsar. Hundreds of people died. After that many Indians turned finally against British rule.

**Mahatma Gandhi** returned from South Africa in 1915 and became the most important leader of the movement. He relied on **non-violent resistance**: boycotts, strikes and peaceful protests. In 1928 the movement boycotted the Simon Commission because it did not include a single Indian. In 1930 Gandhi led the famous **Salt March**, about 390 kilometres on foot to the sea, to protest against the British salt tax.

From 1929/30 the Congress demanded complete independence with **Purna Swaraj**. In 1939 the viceroy declared India a participant in the war without consulting anyone, after which the Congress governments in the provinces resigned. In 1940 the Muslim League demanded states of their own for areas with a Muslim majority in the **Lahore Resolution**. In August 1942 the **Quit India** movement demanded the immediate withdrawal of the British, and Subhas Chandra Bose even fought on the side of Japan against Britain.

After the Second World War Britain was weakened and gave way. On 15 August 1947 **India** and **Pakistan** became independent, and Jawaharlal Nehru became India's first prime minister. During the **partition**, millions of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims fled across the new borders, and very many people died in acts of violence. Gandhi was murdered by a Hindu nationalist on 30 January 1948.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area that is ruled by a foreign state.
When you deliberately do not buy something or do not take part, in order to protest.
Resistance without weapons and without hurting people.
The representative of the British monarch who governed India.
The splitting of British India in 1947 into India and Pakistan.

gewusst: In 1971 the eastern part of Pakistan became the separate state of Bangladesh.
26 January, the day on which Purna Swaraj was proclaimed in 1930, is now Republic Day in India.
As a sign of self-sufficiency, Gandhi wore simple clothes made of cloth he had spun himself.

teile.einleitung: The social question was the great problem of industrialisation in the 19th century. Many factory workers lived in poverty, lived in cramped flats and were not covered in case of illness or accident. The state, the churches, employers and the labour movement looked for answers.
wichtigste: The social question means the hardship of the working class through poverty, housing shortage and lack of protection.
Pauperism means mass poverty in the early 19th century.
Friedrich Engels described the condition of the working class in England in 1845.
Otto von Bismarck introduced health insurance in the German Empire in 1883.
With it Bismarck also wanted to keep the workers away from social democracy.
Pope Leo XIII took a position in 1891 with the encyclical Rerum Novarum.
In Switzerland the Factory Act of 1877 limited working hours.

abschnitte.text: With **industrialisation** many people moved from the countryside to the cities in order to work in factories. Working days often lasted 12 to 16 hours, and children also had to work. Wages were low, and anyone who fell ill often lost work and income. This hardship of the working class was called the **social question**.

Already in the early 19th century there was mass poverty in many areas, **pauperism**. In the growing cities families lived crowded together in dark flats, often without clean water. Diseases such as cholera and tuberculosis spread easily. **Friedrich Engels** described these conditions in 1845 in his book on the condition of the working class in England.

Workers joined together in **trade unions** to demand better wages and shorter working hours. They founded cooperatives and social democratic parties. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels demanded a revolution in 1848 in the Communist Manifesto. Others wanted to achieve improvements step by step through reforms.

In the German Empire Chancellor **Otto von Bismarck** introduced social insurance: in 1883 health insurance, in 1884 accident insurance and in 1889 old-age and disability insurance. He wanted to help the workers, but also keep them away from social democracy. In Switzerland the **federal Factory Act** of 1877 limited working hours to eleven hours a day and banned factory work for children under 14. The AVS was introduced in Switzerland only in 1948.

The churches also cared about the hardship: the priest **Adolph Kolping** founded associations that offered lodging and education to travelling journeymen. Pope Leo XIII in 1891 in the encyclical **Rerum Novarum** demanded fair wages and protection for workers. Some manufacturers, in the spirit of **employer paternalism**, built workers’ housing estates and employed company doctors. In this way they wanted to tie workers to their firm.

From the answers to the social question the present-day **welfare state** arose. It includes insurance against illness, accident, old age and unemployment. Laws today protect employees and ban child labour. In many countries of the world, however, child labour and exploitation are still a great problem today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The shift from handwork to production with machines in factories.
Mass poverty, especially in the early 19th century.
An association of employees that campaigns for their rights.
An official circular letter of the Pope.
Insurance that helps people financially in case of illness, accident or in old age.

gewusst: The canton of Glarus already issued a progressive factory law in 1864 with a twelve-hour day.
The Kolping organisation, which goes back to Adolph Kolping, still exists today in Switzerland too.
Children often used to work in spinning mills, because with their small hands they could reach between the machines.

teile.einleitung: The Nazi era in Germany lasted from 1933 to 1945. In these twelve years Adolf Hitler and his party, the Nazi Party, ruled the country as a dictatorship. They persecuted and murdered millions of people and started the Second World War.
wichtigste: On 30 January 1933 Adolf Hitler was appointed Reich Chancellor.
With the Reichstag Fire Decree of 28 February 1933 basic rights were suspended.
The Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 allowed the government to pass laws without parliament.
From July 1933 the Nazi Party was the only party allowed in Germany.
With Gleichschaltung, the state and society were completely aligned with Nazi rule.
Jewish people were step by step deprived of their rights, persecuted and murdered in the Holocaust.
With the attack on Poland on 1 September 1939 the Second World War began.
Nazi rule ended with Germany's unconditional surrender in May 1945.

abschnitte.text: After the Great Depression, millions of people in Germany were unemployed and dissatisfied. The **Nazi Party** became the strongest party in the Reichstag election of July 1932. On 30 January 1933 Reich President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler **Reich Chancellor**. Many conservative politicians believed at the time that they could control Hitler, but that was a serious mistake.

In the night of 28 February 1933 the Reichstag building in Berlin burned. The very next day the **Reichstag Fire Decree** suspended basic rights such as freedom of speech and of the press. On 23 March 1933 the Reichstag passed the **Enabling Act** in the Kroll Opera House in Berlin, by 444 votes to 94. Only the SPD voted against, and its chairman Otto Wels gave the last free speech in the Reichstag. The Communist Party deputies had by then already been arrested or had fled.

**Gleichschaltung**, or “coordination”, means aligning the state and society with Nazi rule. The federal states lost their independence, and other parties were banned or dissolved themselves. From the law of 14 July 1933 the Nazi Party was the only permitted party. The free trade unions were smashed and replaced by the **German Labour Front**. Clubs, newspapers, radio and schools also had to follow Nazi ideology, and children were put into the Hitler Youth.

As early as March 1933 **Dachau concentration camp** began operating near Munich. Political opponents were locked up there without a court ruling and abused. In the so-called **Röhm Putsch** in the summer of 1934 Hitler had the leadership of the SA and other opponents murdered. The secret state police, the Gestapo, watched the population, and anyone who voiced criticism risked imprisonment or death.

The Nazis spread a cruel **antisemitism**, that is, hatred of Jewish people. With the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 they were deprived of their rights, and in the pogrom night of November 1938 synagogues burned. From 1939 Germany waged war and occupied large parts of Europe. In the **Holocaust** the Nazis murdered around six million Jewish people, as well as Sinti and Roma, sick and disabled people and many others.

On 30 April 1945 Hitler took his own life in Berlin, and on 8 May 1945 the Wehrmacht surrendered unconditionally. In the **Nuremberg Trials** leading Nazis were put on trial. During this time Switzerland was strongly threatened by Nazi Germany and from summer 1940 almost completely surrounded by the Axis powers. Today memorials, museums and **Stolpersteine** (stumbling stones) recall the victims, so that nothing like this is ever repeated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of rule in which one person or party has all the power and the people may not have a free say.
A law of 1933 with which Hitler's government was allowed to make laws without parliament.
Everything in the state and in society had to obey the Nazis.
Camps in which people were locked up, tortured and murdered without a verdict.
The mass murder of around six million Jewish people by the Nazis.

gewusst: For the Enabling Act the Reichstag met in an opera house, the Kroll Opera, because the Reichstag building had burned out.
In his courageous speech Otto Wels said that Social Democrats could be robbed of freedom and life, but not of honour.
More than 100,000 Stolpersteine have been laid in Europe so far, small brass plates in the pavement in front of the last homes of victims of the Nazis.

teile.einleitung: The Western Campaign was the German attack on France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg in early summer 1940. In only about six weeks the German Wehrmacht defeated these countries, which surprised the whole world. For Switzerland it meant that it was almost completely surrounded by the Axis powers.
wichtigste: The attack began on 10 May 1940.
Erich von Manstein developed the so-called Sickle Cut plan.
The main thrust of the German tanks led, to everyone's surprise, through the wooded Ardennes.
On 14 May 1940 the German Luftwaffe bombed Rotterdam.
In Operation Dynamo around 338,000 Allied soldiers were rescued from Dunkirk to England.
On 22 June 1940 the armistice was signed in the forest of Compiègne.
On 25 July 1940 General Guisan gathered the senior officers for the Rütli Report.

abschnitte.text: In September 1939 Germany had invaded Poland, whereupon France and Britain declared war on Germany. For months hardly anything happened in the west, and people spoke of the “Phoney War”. On 9 April 1940 Germany occupied Denmark and Norway in **Operation Weserübung**. France trusted in the **Maginot Line**, a strong line of fortresses on the border with Germany.

The Allies expected the main attack through Belgium, as in the First World War. **Erich von Manstein** proposed sending the tanks instead through the wooded and hilly **Ardennes**. On 10 May 1940 the Wehrmacht attacked the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg, and the Allies advanced into Belgium. At the same time German tanks pushed through the Ardennes and crossed the Meuse at Sedan. As if with a sickle, they cut off the Allied armies in the north from the rest of France.

On 14 May 1940 the German Luftwaffe bombed the centre of **Rotterdam**, and hundreds of people died. Soon afterwards the Netherlands surrendered, and the queen fled to London. Belgium surrendered on 28 May. On 10 May **Winston Churchill** had become prime minister in Britain, determined to fight on.

The British and many French troops were trapped on the coast at **Dunkirk**. At the end of May and the beginning of June 1940, in **Operation Dynamo**, warships but also fishing boats and yachts brought around 338,000 soldiers to England. They had to leave their heavy weapons behind. That so many were rescued was important so that Britain could carry on fighting.

On 14 June 1940 German troops marched into Paris. Marshal Philippe Pétain asked for an **armistice**, which was signed on 22 June in the forest of Compiègne. For this Hitler had the very same railway carriage fetched in which Germany had had to surrender in 1918. France was divided: Germany occupied the north and the Atlantic coast, and in the south Pétain governed from **Vichy**. General Charles de Gaulle called for resistance from London.

abschnitte.titel: Switzerland after the fall of France
abschnitte.text: In June 1940 over 40,000 French and Polish soldiers fled into Switzerland and were **interned**. Now Switzerland was almost completely surrounded by Germany, Italy and occupied France. On 25 July 1940 General **Henri Guisan** gathered all the senior officers on the Rütli. He declared that Switzerland would defend itself. The army later withdrew to the **Réduit** in the Alps.

begriffe.erklaerung: The armed forces of Nazi Germany.
A fast attack with tanks and aircraft that is meant to take the enemy by surprise.
When an army or a state gives up and ends the fighting.
Foreign soldiers are held in a neutral country until the war ends.
The defensive position of the Swiss army in the Alps in the Second World War.

gewusst: In the First World War the Germans had tried in vain for four years to defeat France; in 1940 they needed only about six weeks.
In May and June 1940 Swiss fighter aircraft shot down several German aircraft that had violated Swiss airspace.
Hundreds of small private boats crossed the English Channel for the rescue at Dunkirk.

teile.einleitung: Pepper is a perfectly ordinary spice today. In the past, however, it was so valuable that sailors and merchants undertook long and dangerous journeys to get it.
wichtigste: Pepper originally comes from India.
Peppercorns are the dried fruits of a climbing plant.
Because it was so expensive, pepper was called “black gold”.
The search for spices was an important reason for the great voyages of discovery.
The Moluccas were also called the “Spice Islands”.

abschnitte.text: Pepper grows on a **climbing plant** that winds its way up trees or poles. Originally it comes from the south-west coast of **India**. The plant forms long clusters with small, round fruits. Peppercorns are therefore **dried fruits**. For black pepper they are harvested while still unripe and dried, and in doing so they turn dark and wrinkled. For white pepper ripe fruits are used and the outer skin is removed.

In Europe pepper was very expensive for a long time, because it had come a long way. Merchants brought it over land and sea to Europe, and every middleman earned something from it. That is why pepper was called **“black gold”**. Rich merchants who traded in spices were mockingly called **“pepper sacks”**. Cities such as **Venice** became rich through the spice trade.

The Europeans wanted to get the spices themselves, without middlemen. That is why they looked for a **sea route to India**. The Portuguese Vasco da Gama in 1498 was the first European to reach India by sea around Africa. Still further east lie the **Moluccas**, which were called the **“Spice Islands”**. There valuable spices such as cloves and nutmegs grew. Later Portuguese, Spanish and Dutch fought over these islands.

gewusst: The heat of pepper comes from a substance called piperine.
When something is very far away, people still say today that it is where “the pepper grows”.

teile.einleitung: A personal computer, PC for short, is a computer for a single person. In the past computers filled whole rooms and belonged only to large firms or universities. From the 1970s they became so small and cheap that they fitted on a desk.
wichtigste: PC is the abbreviation for personal computer.
Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded the firm Microsoft in 1975.
Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak founded the firm Apple in 1976.
IBM brought out its first personal computer in 1981.
With the mouse one moves the pointer on the screen.
A laptop is a portable computer that opens like a book.
The Swiss firm Logitech was founded in 1981 and became world famous for computer mice.

abschnitte.text: The first computers came into being in the 1940s. They were as big as a room and very expensive. Only experts could operate them. Thanks to tiny electronic components, the **microprocessors**, computers became much smaller in the 1970s. Now even a single person could afford a computer. In this way the **personal computer** came about.

In 1975 **Bill Gates** and **Paul Allen** founded the firm **Microsoft**. It wrote above all **software**, that is, programs for computers. In 1976 **Steve Jobs** and **Steve Wozniak** founded the firm **Apple**. Their Apple II of 1977 became one of the first successful home computers. Both firms are today among the largest companies in the world.

In 1981 the large American firm **IBM** brought out its first **personal computer**. The operating system for it came from Microsoft. An **operating system** is the basic program that controls the computer. Many other firms soon copied similar computers. That is why people still often say “PC” of such machines today.

In the past one had to type commands into the computer. Then came screens with little pictures and windows. With the **mouse** one moves the pointer on the screen by sliding it across the table, and clicks on what one wants. In 1984 the Apple Macintosh made this way of working well known. The Swiss firm **Logitech**, founded in 1981 in the canton of Vaud, became world famous for computer mice.

Later computers became smaller still. A **laptop** is a portable computer that opens like a book. Screen, keyboard and battery are built into one flat device. So one can work on the train, at school or on the move. Today there are also tablets and smartphones, which are likewise small computers.

gewusst: The name laptop means “on the lap”.
At ETH Zurich Niklaus Wirth developed the programming language Pascal, with which many people learned to program.

tyifrtn.t: The Reformation and Counter-Reformation in Switzerland

teile.einleitung: After the Reformation the Confederation was split into Reformed and Catholic places. The Catholic places renewed their faith in the Counter-Reformation, and the two camps faced each other mistrustfully for a long time. Nevertheless the Confederation was held together.
wichtigste: The Bern Disputation led to the Reformation in Bern in 1528.
In Basel the Reformation prevailed in 1529 under Johannes Oekolampad.
The Kappel milk soup stands for the peaceful settlement of the First War of Kappel in 1529.
The Second Peace of Kappel of 1531 stopped the spread of the Reformation in German-speaking Switzerland.
Heinrich Bullinger wrote the Confessio Helvetica posterior in 1566.
With the Golden League of 1586 the Catholic places allied to protect their faith.
Appenzell was divided into two half-cantons in 1597 for religious reasons.

abschnitte.text: After Zurich other towns also became Reformed. In Bern the **Bern Disputation** took place in 1528, a great debate after which the council introduced the Reformation. In Basel the reformer **Johannes Oekolampad** prevailed in 1529. In St Gallen the humanist and mayor Joachim von Watt, called **Vadian**, introduced the new teaching.

In 1529 the five Catholic places allied with Austria in the **Christian Union**. Zurich marched against them in the First War of Kappel, but no battle took place. The Glarus Landammann **Hans Aebli** mediated successfully between the opponents. According to legend soldiers of both sides ate a milk soup together from one pot on the border.

In 1531 war did come after all, and the Catholic places won at Kappel am Albis, where Zwingli fell. The **Second Peace of Kappel** of 20 November 1531 allowed each place to keep its denomination. In this way the spread of the Reformation in German-speaking Switzerland was stopped. In French-speaking Switzerland, however, Bern still brought the Reformation to the conquered Vaud in 1536.

The Catholic places renewed their Church following the decisions of the Council of Trent. The Archbishop of Milan **Charles Borromeo** opened the **Collegium Helveticum** in Milan in 1579 for the training of Swiss priests. Jesuits founded schools, for example in Lucerne and Fribourg, and Capuchins built monasteries. In 1586 the Catholic places concluded the **Golden League** to preserve the old faith.

The Reformed also strengthened their teaching. **Heinrich Bullinger**, Zwingli’s successor in Zurich, wrote the **Confessio Helvetica posterior**, the Second Helvetic Confession, in 1566. It was recognised in many countries of Europe as a Reformed confession of faith. Geneva with John Calvin became an important centre for Reformed refugees from all over Europe.

Because the religious camps in Appenzell could not agree, the place was divided in 1597. So arose the Catholic **Appenzell Inner Rhodes** and the Reformed Appenzell Outer Rhodes, which exist to this day. In the Villmergen Wars of 1656 and 1712 the denominations fought against each other again. Only in the federal state from 1848 was freedom of belief gradually secured.

begriffe.erklaerung: The renewal of the Catholic Church as an answer to the Reformation.
The highest officeholder in a canton with an open-air assembly, such as Glarus.
A canton that arose from the division of an old place.
A text that sums up the most important articles of faith of a church.

gewusst: The Kappel milk soup was later shown by the painter Albert Anker in a famous picture.
The Golden League is also called the Borromean League after Charles Borromeo.
The division of Appenzell in 1597 is the reason why there are still two Appenzell cantons today.

teile.einleitung: Nationalism is an idea according to which a people or a nation forms a special community that should have a state of its own. In the 19th century nationalism greatly changed the map of Europe. It could inspire people for freedom, but also lead to hatred and war against others.
wichtigste: Nationalism puts one’s own nation at the centre of political thinking.
Johann Gottfried Herder shaped the notion of a “national spirit” of its own for every people.
Johann Gottlieb Fichte gave the “Addresses to the German Nation” in 1807 and 1808.
In 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed, and on 18 January 1871 the German Empire in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
Ernest Renan described the nation in 1882 as a “daily plebiscite”.
Switzerland is regarded as a nation by will, because it is based on the will to live together and not on a common language.
In the late 19th century nationalism became increasingly aggressive and linked with imperialism.

abschnitte.text: A **nation** is a large community of people who feel they belong together. Often they are linked by a common language, history or culture. The French scholar **Ernest Renan** thought in 1882 that a nation was a “daily plebiscite”, that is, a vote that people take anew every day. For him it was above all the will to live together that counted.

The philosopher **Johann Gottfried Herder** believed that every people has a “national spirit” of its own, which shows itself in language and songs. That is why people at the time collected folk songs and fairy tales, the Brothers Grimm for example. During the French occupation **Johann Gottlieb Fichte** gave the “Addresses to the German Nation” in Berlin in 1807 and 1808. In them he called on the Germans for national renewal.

Italy was divided for a long time into many small states, some under Austrian rule. In 1831 **Giuseppe Mazzini** founded the secret society “Young Italy”, which demanded a united, free Italy. With wars and the volunteer expedition of Giuseppe Garibaldi the country was united little by little. In 1861 the **Kingdom of Italy** was proclaimed.

Germany too consisted of many individual states. Under the leadership of Prussia and its minister-president Otto von Bismarck it was united after three wars. On 18 January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the **Hall of Mirrors at Versailles**. For France, which had lost the war, this was a great humiliation.

Around 1830 nationalism was often linked with freedom and democracy. In the late 19th century it became increasingly conservative, aggressive and linked with **imperialism**. An exaggerated nationalism that belittles other nations is called **chauvinism**. From 1891 the Pan-German League demanded an aggressive power policy, and Pan-Slavism aimed at the unity of all Slavic peoples, which contributed to the tensions before the First World War.

abschnitte.titel: Switzerland as a nation by will
abschnitte.text: Switzerland does not fit the idea of “one people, one language, one state”. Here people with four national languages and different religions live together. That is why it is called a **nation by will**, based on the common will to live together. In 1897 the First Zionist Congress took place in Basel, where Theodor Herzl campaigned for a state of their own for the Jewish people.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large community of people who feel linked by history, culture or common will.
A vote of the people.
Exaggerated nationalism that despises other nations.
The striving of states to extend their power through colonies and conquests.
A nation that is based not on a common language but on the will to live together.

gewusst: Many European national anthems and national holidays arose in the 19th century.
The word chauvinism goes back to a figure called Nicolas Chauvin, an excessively enthusiastic soldier of Napoleon.
The Zionist Congress met in the Basel Stadtcasino.
